This study investigates the predictive capability of two-layer neural networks for solving the high-dimensional Schrödinger equation when the potential is selected from a pre-defined set of potential classes. In our analysis, selected potentials are viewed as complex examples of a given basic potential, and existing methods are extended to address the added complexity. By deriving estimates of the out-of-sample prediction error, our findings demonstrate that neural networks are capable of approximating potential classes at optimal rates, and also reveal that they can achieve nematic phase predictions with minimal training data requirements. Furthermore, a method is proposed for estimating the approximation dimension of a potential class in the context of neural network solutions, and it is applied in a simulated study. To illustrate the practical implications of our results, a study of the effect of neutron star mass on neutrino rates is also conducted. At http://neuralnetworksforpdes.github.io, public code and data are accessible for replication and review. Through our research, we aim to establish tangible evidence of the generalization capability of two-layer neural networks for solving complex physics problems. In computational neuroscience, reconstructing neural activity patterns is vital for grasping the brain's underlying functioning and for developing effective treatments for neurological disorders. We apply machine learning techniques, specifically Recurrent Neural Networks, to construct and classify distinct patterns of neuronal behavior in Caenorhabditis Elegans, a well-studied nervous system model. Using long-term fluorescence imaging data of neurons from the Light Microscopy Dataset, we successfully construct a model that predicts the probability of specific behavioral patterns in this organism. Utilizing metrics such as the Normalized Mutual Information metric and the Loss Function of our multiclass cross-entropy model, we evaluate the accuracy of our Recurrent Neural Network. We also explore methods to enhance our model's performance, including the application of data augmentation and the creation of synthetic time series generation to address class imbalance issues. Our study contributes to the development of a potential low-cost, high-throughput system for reconstructing neural activity patterns in animals. We hope that the presented work will facilitate the advancement of this field and inspire future advancements. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/TechGuy123/Neural-Reconstr-Models. The Data used in this project is from https://sites.google.com/view/neural-mc/. Given a nonnegative real number x and a positive integer n, the point (x,n) lies on a specific curve known as Arnold's tricuspoid. This paper explores the stable points of the forest surrounding Arnold's tricuspoid with the metric being the maximum of the absolute values of three functions, where each metric is derived from the coordinates of a point. The initial forest is formed by iterating a billiard process in a rectangle with the domain bounded by the parabola u = v^2 - x and the line v = 2 |u - x|. This study determines the limits of the points in this forest as the domain approaches a semi-parabola and demonstrates that these limits lie on a new, smaller curve called the regionally stable point forest. We also establish the relationship between the regionally stable point forest and Arnold's tricuspoid, specifically that the former lies inside the latter. In addition, for any point on the regionally stable point forest with x >= 0, the forward orbit under the Arnold's tricuspoid diffeomorphism must reside in this forest and converge to its corresponding point on the curve. Similar properties are found for the regionally stable point forest with x <= 0. Finally, this study embeds the regionally stable point forest with x >= 0 and x <= 0 into the Arnold's tricuspoid using a specific map and demonstrates that this forest is globally stable within the entire phase space. Furthermore, this study describes all the asymptotic trajectories in the Arnold's tricuspoid as well as its modifications and the impact of its compactifications on the metric. Last but not least, this study demonstrates that these compactified metrics are well-defined and perfectly regular. As such, this study provides a mathematical framework for modeling systems with the Arnold's tricuspoid metric, and it offers valuable insights into the behavior of these systems in the context of Hamiltonian dynamics and the triaxial rotation of asteroids. Exoplanetary systems with near 3:2 orbital resonances are relatively rare, and identifying systems in the final stages of resonance progression is challenging due to the noisy data from space missions. Further complicating the process is the fact that most numerical integration techniques can't replicate the observed orbital configurations without exceeding computational limits, for low mass ratio systems. However, researchers have developed a novel approach by numerically integrating various Newtonian variations to track the hypothetical host star's motion and its impact on the evolving orbital configurations of its planets. Applying this methodology to the K2-138 system allowed scientists to reconstruct its full resonance sequence and confirm that it follows a specific 3:2 resonance chain: $k:m$. Moreover, they discovered new findings that could explain a discrepancy in astronomical observations by showing that the planets actually lie at slightly different distances than previously thought. These results were obtained using various Newtonian variations to verify the sequence. When they used their algorithm without modifications, the results suggested a possible period shift of less than 0.1%, which could potentially explain the observed disparity. However, when they ran the model with artificially enhanced noise levels mimicking space mission conditions, the results showed that precision of less than 0.2% is required to reproduce the observed period ratio of the planets. Finally, they ran several numerical integrations with each possible $k:m$ resonance chain, and determined that the most likely sequence for K2-138 is 3:2, 3:4, 2:7, and 1:7. However, the model couldn't confidently exclude other possible combinations such as 2:3, 4:2, and it couldn't reproduce the observed planetary motion when in the $k=m+1$ resonance chain. Therefore, while the model significantly enhances our understanding of the K2-138 system, it still has some limitations that need to be addressed. Furthermore, the researcher notes that the model produced the expected results when run with the correct numerical integration approach, and suggests its applicability to similar cases. One such system that it can be applied to is K2-251, which is at the final stages of its resonance progression with the second planet. However, when it was run with the correct Newtonian variation, it produced the expected results showing that the planets at near 3:2 resonance typically follow a specific $k:m$ chain. However, when it was run with the correct Newtonian variation for the $k=m+1$ resonance chain, it failed to reproduce the observed planetary motion

It is found that $W_{aq}$ yields the quantum counterpart of the classical Schur--Weyl duality. To achieve this goal, we first outline the framework of the Yoneda embedding within the context of presheaf categories and then apply this understanding to compute the two-fold colimit of the image of the authentic Whittaker vector functors. To present an alternative description of this result, we establish the representation theory of the algebra resulting from a quadratic extension of the quantum number field. Ultimately, through the application of Tannaka reconstruction, we obtain the parametrizing space of the Whittaker points. However, the Isabelle archive poses a barrier due to its dispersed nature, with various types of proofs and model-based descriptions, lacking a unified framework that could streamline research access to these proofs. Following a thorough examination of a randomly selected subset consisting of 10% and 20% of the archive's content, our discrete evaluation reveals a distinct preference for theoretical computer science proofs over 50%, in contrast to practical proof-based descriptions, with a ratio of 33% exhibiting some connection to data and program executions. Subsequently, we present the Isabelle archive analyzer, an engine capable of systematically reviewing Isabelle files to determine the theorem status or evidence associated with them. Utilizing this tool, we categorize the proof types within the selected archive subsets and present a discourse on their implications. Ultimately, we outline the prospective benefits of proof-based categorization, discussing the Isabelle archive's structure and proof types in detail, with the ultimate aim of enhancing the verifiable theorem count through the identification of optimal methodologies. As such, we suggest and demonstrate the proposed Isabelle archive framework, aimed at structuring the content and aiding researchers in their pursuit of significant verification achievements. The presented framework enables content categorization by proof types and offers a systematic means to locate relevant proofs. Moreover, it enables content filtering by evidence-related parameters such as proof types, keywords, and the Isabelle archive code. The proposed framework is expected to streamline the verification process of significant programs, encompassing both theoretical and practical domains. As such, it is envisioned that the Isabelle archive framework will facilitate considerable advancements in formal verification. Preliminary evaluation studies have revealed the robustness and efficiency of the Isabelle archive framework, with the capability to review 100% of a 20% selected subset consisting of 1828 files within 30 seconds, as quickly as the more modest 10% selected subset consisting of 182 files. The traditional knowledge representation frameworks rely heavily on graphs, but graph models that incorporate textual information are often inadequate due to their fundamental frame-based structure. The key shortcomings of existing node-pair approaches are; (a) relationship emphasis with no regard to the relative significance of these connections and (b) failure to encompass the hierarchical structure inherent in textual data. To address these limitations, we propose the Text Declaratve Knowledge Graph (TDKG), an innovative recall-based framework, and the Hierarchical Information Representation Model (HIRM). HIRM is an expansion of the traditional vector representation, allowing for the incorporation of hierarchical knowledge and nuanced relationships. By incorporating a structured knowledge tree and an information abstraction hierarchy, HIRM is capable of efficiently capturing knowledge from the underlying corpus. We demonstrate the superiority of TDKG-HIRM as a unified text representation model by applying it to diverse natural language processing and deep learning tasks. Experimental results indicate a remarkable enhancement in performance, and in addition to providing efficient and declarative text retrieval, HIRM also achieves substantial improvements in semantic representation, as evidenced by its achievements in tasks such as machine translation, name entity recognition, text classification and machine learning. The proposed model is expected to serve as a foundational structure for the development of advanced computational systems and the creation of intricate multi-layered textual information repositories in the future. The pre-trained models and related information can be found at https://amirveysehve.github.io/declaratve-kg-nli-models. Additionally, the corresponding author's account on the Arxiv platform, established in 2011, can be accessed at https://arxiv.org. A graph theory approach, known as "graphical suns," is used to analyze a type of infinite groups with exponential growth. This theory is applied to classify certain subgroups of free products of finitely generated groups. Specifically, groups with exponential growth and a specific property (residual finiteness) are studied. It is demonstrated that some subgroups of the symmetric groups satisfy residual finiteness and have a connected fundamental group of a specific graph, known as the "graphical sun." Using this theory, it is shown that certain products of the cyclic groups of prime order meet specific criteria based on their graph structure. Firstly, it is proven that for a given prime number p, the infinite product of the cyclic groups A_n satisfies certain criteria based on the graph structure of the sequence of groups as n approaches infinity. Secondly, it is proven that for a specific set of primes, the product of the cyclic groups has a graph consisting of connected components that are the graphical suns, and this product depends on the prime numbers p in the set. Lastly, it is acknowledged that some subgroups of the symmetric groups have a graph consisting of connected components that are the graphical suns, and this group depends on the integer n, but for a specific set of groups, particularly 2-groups, the product of these groups has a graph consisting of connected components that are the graphical suns, and this group depends on n in the set. We delve into the stability analysis of an Euler-Bernoulli beam mounted on a star-shaped graph structure. The outer edges represent its main beam and have a different Young's modulus compared to the inner points that connect them. Our aim is to find the general minimum energy levels corresponding to even and odd functions, utilizing two methods. First, by utilizing the Freidkin-Kalfus theorem, we derive the asymptotic minimum energy levels for even and odd functions. Concurrently, we apply the in and out analysis method by Copeland and Hirst. Both approaches yield the same quadratic stabilizing estimates for the energy levels, and simulations demonstrate the behavior of associated spectra. Moreover, we address the question of exponential stability using optimal control and minimum time problems. However, we observe that when time is factored into these problems, we cannot achieve uniform stability results. However, we address a related problem with zero input time, yielding partial stability results, especially exponential stability for even functions in the minimum energy level. Lastly, we explore a time-fractional version of the problem in the minimum time model, resulting in a diverse minimum energy level. Our analysis reveals distinct qualitative behavior in the minimum energy for time-fractional versus time-differential problems. Moreover, we observe a trade-off between time-fractional and time-differential parameters in the minimum energy. Conversely, when optimizing the minimum energy with control, we cannot recover this trade-off, and neither does it depend on parameters. Unfortunately, we cannot achieve a complete classification of the minimum energy behavior. Nevertheless, we observe a distinct transition in the minimum energy behavior on the line separating even and odd functions. Our results are confirmed by the behavior of the spectra in the uncontrolled problem, as seen in the star graph. Furthermore, we see that behavior in the minimum energy in time-fractional problems is also universal, as seen from time-fractional Schrodinger equation. Lastly, we discuss possible impact of these findings in the context of quantum mechanics. The corresponding video supplementing the research can be accessed at https://youtu.be/q3QDiz2jO6I. The theoretical framework of Electromagnetics has a fundamental concept called pull or anti-push, which is peculiar in optics and is often associated with weights rather than forces. This article will explore the optical pull through the lens of a minimal, classical two-level system by examining its underlying dynamics. By using a basic framework with coherent and incoherent light interactions, we can determine conditions that lead to significant optical pull effects in scenarios involving incoherent light pull and reveal an intriguing possibility of pull without forces. Our work primarily focuses on principles rather than technical applications. Despite being grounded in a classical approach, our findings may also offer insights relevant to quantum optical contexts. One of the key relationships we identify in this paper - $-{\bf F}_p\propto{\bf F}_l $ - could potentially hold valuable applications in light engineering. This relationship suggests that linear momentum forces are related to spin or angular momentum pull forces, which is an intriguing similarity that existing momentum conservation laws do not fully utilize. Moreover, we can derive the pull force coefficients $F_{\alpha}$ by combining principles of pull forces with that of momentum coupling, an approach that is an extension of Minkowski's co-energy and power relations. This is an original contribution of this study. Pull force coefficients provide access to various effect measurements, e.g. optical magnetoelectric effect, and are essential for understanding within and extrinsic properties. This is another key finding of our work. Our work further extends beyond even push-pull optics by enabling measurement of coherent state effects that go beyond the reach of magnetoelectric measurements due to potential non-coherent effects. Finally, we can use our model to determine unidirectional effects that are absent from magnetoelectric measurements, thus further expanding the frontiers of pull optics. This is an additional key finding of our work. Our work is thus an advancement beyond existing knowledge in magnetoelectric physics and optics that bridges coherent and incoherent optics with magnetoelectric physics. This is an accompanying article to a recent publication in the journal New Journal of Physics. In this article, we have further developed and extended our model of optical pull to include path-averaging average momentum pull effects that are also explored in the companion article. Moreover, we have further extended our model to include electron pull effects. This article complements our work in the companion article by delving into electron pull effects. One of the key findings of this article is the possibility of achieving coherent effects that correspond to significant optical pull effects even in incoherent light conditions.

This resource is unique, comprising four distinct datasets, each focusing on different aspects: population growth, urban expansion, transportation systems, and residential patterns. The H4M dataset is characterized by its diverse sources, including government reports, satellite imaging, transportation data, and social media platforms. It is further defined by four distinct modalities, viewing angles, and demographic distributions. The H4M dataset is comprised of four separate datasets, each consisting of four distinct layers, totaling 3.56 Terabytes in capacity. This work introduces the H4M dataset, outlining its distinct features, and highlights its potential applications, research opportunities, and analytics tools for studying Beijing's socioeconomic development. We have published a comprehensive dataset paper, and a competition with detailed guides and codes have been launched on the website at https://h4m.biot-bu.edu.cn. A new family of biological-inspired perceptual fields, known as On-Off Center-Surround (OCS) fields, have been developed for enhanced image classification. By weighing local image patterns more heavily when they conform to expectations and assigning lower importance when they deviate significantly, OCS fields improve the accuracy and resilience of deep neural networks. This is accomplished through the calculation of a dichotomous weight value, '1' or '0', for every pixel in the local field, where a value of '1' indicates conformity and '0' indicates disparity. OCS fields incorporate two key components: a centre operator that weighs average pixel values and a surround operator that assigns weights based on contextual consistency. OCS fields can take on Gaussian or Linial forms and incorporate diversity of views through rotation, thereby increasing robustness. Experimental findings indicate that networks utilizing OCS fields for representation learning exhibit superior performance and increased resilience against noise and semantic adversarial attacks on standard image classification tasks. The models adopt a more granular, yet precise data representation, thereby reducing correlations within colour channels. Integration of OCS fields into existing deep networks enhances their precision and robustness, thereby suggesting their potential as a universal perceptual prior for image classification. Implementation details and the model architecture are publicly accessible via the repository https://github.com/kaidongyang/On-Off-CS-Nets. Evaluation metrics, code, and pre-trained models can be found at https://github.com/kaidongyang/On-Off-CS-Nets/tree/master/OCSEvaluation. Video illustrations can be accessed at https://github.com/kaidongyang/On-Off-CS-Nets/tree/master/VideoIllustrations. The study is published in the journal Neural Networks and Learning Systems. Analysis of key findings and implications are discussed in Section 7 of the dissertation at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2022.100101. Furthermore, the pressure-induced transition was found to be associated with the gradual disappearance of both iridium and lithium-based magnetic moments, as evidenced by the simultaneous drop in the ratios of conductive to dielectric responses. This paper introduces a synthesis of synthetic control and causal framework techniques
to address treatment effects in policy consultations. By viewing the treated unit's pre-intervention history as part of a larger source pool, and considering post-intervention outcomes as targets for prediction, we develop a formal optimization framework for constructing synthetic control units. Focusing on long-term outcomes, we find that the most effective control combinations are those achieving causal force balance - where the unit's pre-intervention characteristics are mirrored in the source pool. By combining synthetic control with causal balance techniques, we identify key features contributing to balanced causal effects, and reveal properties of high-quality treatment effect estimators. Building on this framework, we extend it to multi-group causal models and prediction problems. In addition, we re-interpret the classical Neyman's Causal Model within our proposed framework, and discuss how to apply such a framework in real-world policy consultations. Lastly, we apply our methods to two prominent US case studies: the national abortion law in the US and the gun control laws in Texas. In these examples, we use data from the American National Election Studies. Our results show that utilizing our method yields more accurate treatment effect estimators and confidence intervals compared to traditional techniques. Moreover, we reveal important new insights derived from the applied causal balance techniques. The generalized Ermakov system in multiple dimensions is now better understood due to the discovery of a fundamental integral that expresses the system's symmetries in terms of invariants. Building on this, we've determined that system's conserved quantities, which include invariants that arise from the Poisson vector fields associated with the system. These conserved quantities not only encompass the time-independent invariants, but also include new first integrals obtained through a reduction process applied to the time-dependent invariants. By computing these first integrals explicitly, we're able to provide the complete integration of the system in terms of invariants, thereby allowing us to find a solution that integrates the system's partial differential equation. This partial differential equation, in turn, yields a solution to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a specific potential. Consequently, we're able to provide a time-independent solution to the generalized system and express it in terms of invariants, leading to a new integral transformation that maps solutions from one system to another. The existence of certain potentials that allow the system's invariants to be expressed in closed form is also demonstrated. These potentials include the most recent solution to the generalized Ermakov system in two dimensions, as well as new solutions in three and four dimensions. The study of these potentials serves to bridge the gap between classical and contemporary research on the generalized system in multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we're able to provide a new representation for the system in terms of complex vector fields, allowing the system in four dimensions to be mapped onto a coadjoint orbit. We study a theoretical model of effective Brillouin interaction between LE$_{01}$ and HE$_{11}$ modes in solid-core photonic crystal fibers, where the intensity of the fundamental mode drives geo-magnetic brain-cell contractions that enhance the electrostrictive coupling between the fundamental and HE$_{11}$ modes. The mechanism is enabled by the flexibility of solid-core photonic crystal fibers, where mechanical contractions induce phase shifts in the fundamental mode through electrostriction and mode coupling. The maximum conversion efficiency we observed was approximately 90%, occurring after a 10-meter fiber with 50-mW input power and an optimized frequency detuning of 10 MHz from the fiber's natural resonance frequency. The observed interaction scheme is universal and can be applied to a range of modal effective Brillouin interactions through the flexure of solid-core photonic crystal fibers. This research offers a flexible platform for optical power transfer between different modes and could be applied in a range of optical parametric processes, such as mode conversion in optical communications, and nonlinear spectroscopy in various multi-mode structures. The discovered interaction is not limited to fundamental and HE$_{11}$ modes and can be extended to a range of LE$_{01}$ and HE$_{11}$ mode pairs in solid-core photonic crystal fibers. The capability to transfer power between the LE$_{01}$ and HE$_{11}$ modes and other HE$_{11}$ pairs holds great potential for optical communications, as it allows for a low-dispersion coupling between the modes. Notably, power conversion between the HE$_{11}$ and HE$_{21}$ modes occurred with a 71% efficiency and a 20-MHz detuning from the HE$_{11}$ mode's natural resonance frequency. The use of solid-core photonic crystal fibers in this work enables a new degree of flexibility in optical power transfer and coupling between optical modes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mechanical properties of solid-core photonic crystal fibers can be utilized effectively to modulate light within the structures by utilizing thermo-optic effects to couple multiple light modes together. Notably, power conversion between the LE$_{01}$ and HE$_{11}$ modes occurred with a near-ideal 98% efficiency and a 20-MHz detuning from the HE$_{11}$ mode's natural resonance frequency. The flexibility of solid-core photonic crystal fibers, when combined with the capabilities of spatially structured light, holds great potential for a range of applications in and nonlinear optics, including spectroscopy and communications

Our theorem broadens the scope of this earlier result by removing the rank constraint and also extends it to include an 'almost normal' subgroup classification. Additionally, we prove an application related to the generation of groups. Specifically, we present a description of the smallest normal subgroup that can be formed from any finite B-type Coxeter group, which is generated by a single element. This investigation was inspired by an earlier challenge issued by Y. Guo. Our approach to solving this problem also allows us to challenge the continuation of a trend identified by Yamgou. Yamgou had noted that for an individual finite rank group, the normal subgroups can be effectively characterized through both logical and algebraic means. Our theorem reveals that in the broader context (of infinite rank groups), the characterization relies solely on algebraic means. Finally, we have also developed a related but independent result related to generating sets within group theory. Specifically, we have shown that for the special linear group SL(n, k) (where k represents a field, which in this case is finite)) the process of selecting a maximal set of elements with relatively prime lengths to form a generating set yields a relatively small normal subgroup, which is generated by this set of elements. This element-generated normal subgroup turns out to be the smallest possible one among all normal subgroups that can be generated by a single element. Ultimately, the calculation shows the order of this smallest normal subgroup generated by a single element to be very close to the order of the group as a whole. Specifically, we have shown that this smallest normal subgroup generated by a single element is such that its order is no more than n times the order of the group as a whole. Our theorem holds the potential of being extended to more general precision characteristics defined in terms of generators over fields with a finite characteristic. In the context of statistical mechanics, a broad class of nonlocal models is investigated, where the interaction term adheres to a symmetric entropy dissipation principle. This analysis initially focuses on the microcanonical ensemble, determining the speed of convergence to the kinetic equilibrium distribution. Subsequently, the analysis shifts to the macroscopic scale, encompassing a selection of examples with applications. Those examples include a model akin to the Burgers equation and a variant of the optimized long-range interaction system. We demonstrate that the macroscopic model derived from the microcanonical ensemble is inherently admissible in the entropy sense and that it can be obtained through a singular limit of the microscopic model. We also establish the rate at which the microscopic model's distribution converges to the kinetic equilibrium in the macroscopic scale, depending on the model's parameters. This research provides a framework for analyzing and understanding the microscopic and macroscopic behavior of a wide array of nonlocal PDEs, including those that might arise in various fields. Several of the models discussed in this study have previously been explored in the literature, while others present promising avenues for further investigation. A primary method employed in this research consists of a combination between the relative entropy method and the linearization/stability analysis techniques used in the context of hyperbolic systems, involving spectral analysis and perturbative expansions. By means of entropy admissibility and convergence rate calculations for the microscopic and macroscopic models, this research fills the existing gap in the literature by providing a unified framework for understanding the distributions at both scales through the creation of a new, broader class of nonlocal models. We define certain types of links, specifically horizon saddle links, and show that they always have a particular property: all points on the surface, except where Morse theory dictates otherwise, exhibit either saddle-like or transverse behavior. Furthermore, any surface with a certain level of smoothness exhibits at most two types of interactions, i.e. hyperbolic or non-hyperbolic behaviors. As a consequence, we identify the criterion for a particular surface to be non-planar. Additionally, we show that horizon saddle links have a particular orientation in relation to the surface's boundary and that any surface with a certain level of smoothness and containing a horizon saddle link always exhibits a complex dynamics, especially along the boundary's central line where you'll find either two singular points or a particular kind of spiral, typically infinite in length. Lastly, we demonstrate a particular surface with a particular kind of dynamics is homeomorphic to a particular kind of spiral surface with a circumferential singularity. A independent line of inquiry shows that a particular set of conditions sufficient for a non-planar, non-trivial surface with a particular kind of dynamics includes, but is not limited to, the presence of a particular kind of saddle link. This theory is based on the concept of a particular kind of surface with a particular topology, as described in another of our papers. We've provided diagrams and figures in an effort to clarify the 3-D concepts being described. We've also addressed a few inaccuracies in a particular explanation of generalized spiral surfaces in order to set the record straight. We've also derived this theory from our analysis of a particular computer program in an effort to clarify the relationship between geometry and dynamics. We claim this theoretical work is the first of its kind in this area of study. We've also included an appendix in an effort to validate the theoretical structure of a particular computer program in this area of study.

Recent advances in big data techniques have led to the creation of complex networks to represent various systems across biology, medicine, and physics. However, the network model has inherent limitations that have been overlooked in research involving functional brain connectivity, which this paper aims to address by developing a fundamental framework for functional brain connectivity based on total association. By utilizing extensive functional MRI data from 1,414 subjects, we generated a map of global and local brain connections and discovered a large-scale network with 90 nodal communities, 16 sub-networks, and 5 super-networks. The subject-specific network structure consisted of a core and a periphery, with the core consisting of secondary sensory, attention, and default mode areas and the perimeter comprising primary sensory, motor, and other non-default mode areas. The large-scale brain network was stable and displayed clustering, weak liquidity, and a specific small-world characteristics, as well as a specific specific distribution of nodal connections. Compared to previous large-scale brain connectivity maps, our functional brain connectivity map displayed higher local clustering, lower characteristic path lengths, and more symmetrical and highly connected nodes. Additionally, we found differences in the large-scale brain connectivity of individuals with high and low autisms, as well as those with multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, and bipolar and depression disorders, which may have significant implications for future research and applications such as brain disease diagnosis, treatment, and optimization of cognitive performance. The database of 1,414 subjects is available for download at http://www.talyork.org-total-association.html. A comprehensive description of the methodology and data is provided in a related paper on graph metrics. The source code for the system is available at https://github.com/bootox/fbc_totalassociation. (Original abstract by Talya N. L. Klein and Hunter L. Gould)

In this research, the sbsuperbosonization equation is utilized to transform the dimensions of specific boson functional integrals into fermion functional integrals, contrasting with the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. It's demonstrated that although both methods yield similar outcomes, they in fact represent distinct four-dimensional supersymmetric quantum mechanics systems. A thorough analysis and interpretation is provided, highlighting the formal and practical implications of each transformation in the context of the underlying theory. In particular, it's acknowledged that the Barbieri and Semenoff transformation, in conjunction with the sbsuperbosonization equation, can be seen as encompassing the generalized HS transformation as a particular case. Moreover, the techniques employed to calculate loop energies using the HS transformation are also applicable to the sbsuperbosonization equation, thus preserving physical integrity. By offering an alternative method for the creation of fermion path integrals, the sbsuperbosonization equation can facilitate the solution of complex bosonic functional integrals, thus serving as a valuable complement to the generalized HS transformation. Finally, the paper concludes by exploring future research directions, suggesting the application of similar transformations to the dimensions of supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory as a potential area of investigation. A preliminary examination by the authors indicates that suitable transformations exist, although determining their physical significance would necessitate further analysis. A separate study on the application of these transformations in the context of quantum gravity is currently in progress. Further research may also reveal that other transformations, beyond the sbsuperbosonization equation and the generalized HS transformation, hold the potential to create novel and interesting path integral constructions. As such, the primary recommendation of this review is that future work should aim to construct more tools, not merely variations. A deeper understanding of the underlying theoretical framework may offer valuable insights into the creation of meaningful and impactful contributions. Furthermore, the methods of distinction between applicable and inapplicable transformations, as well as the identification of potential paths for further research, rely heavily on the interpretation of physical principles rather than solely on mathematical reflections of symmetry breaking and the corresponding scaling of field variables and coupling constants. Thus, the primary governing force driving this review is the hope for future advancements in the field. A separate observation can be made that, despite the similarity in conventions used in this paper with those employed by M. B. and S. B., the general trend of recent publications favors the use of the convention commonly employed in the supersymmetric community, wherein $F_\alpha U^\alpha = \epsilon^{\alpha \beta} F_\alpha U_\beta

Releases of detailed design data in Architecture Engineering Design (AED) are rare, and most studies in AED focus on preliminary sketches with coarsened spatial and temporal details. This paper's goal is to analyze the temporal motion in sketches between consecutive frames or snapshots. We are particularly interested in detailed spatial movements during AED, so we introduce a novel method utilizing hierarchical hidden representations to accurately capture motion characteristics. Building on this, we have developed a spatiotemporal predictive model that takes previous frames and detailed motion features as inputs to predict subsequent sketches. The proposed model's effectiveness was evaluated on two public datasets, SketchRCN and the Huawei Huawei Sketch dataset, with results demonstrating its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods on predicting sketch sequences. Furthermore, we have also conducted an in-depth analysis of the design process, revealing that the models can learn and generate design intentions at successive detail levels. Our findings indicate that integrating motion details with sketch-based methods enhances predictive performance. We have openly shared our source code with the research community. The current design process in AED is primarily restricted to coarsened spatial and temporal details, but detailed motion features play a crucial role in representing design intentions. This research investigates whether incorporating motion details improves the effectiveness of sketch-based methods, resulting in numerical evaluations demonstrating that using motion details in sketch-based methods leads to superior predictive performance. Our study reveals that incorporating motion details in sketch-based methods leads to a performance boost. The importance of motion in design processes is also discussed. The models' ability to accurately capture motion at different resolution levels allows us to analyze the design process at these various resolution levels. Recent advancements in iterative decoding for message passing, specifically list decoding with a polar code subcode, have shown promising results but also introduced significant computational complexities. To address these issues, we propose the Polar Subcode List Decoding (PSLD) scheme, which initially applies belief propagation-based iterative decoding to the polar subcode to generate diverse reliable paths. Subsequently, a density evolution technique determines the optimal number of safe false paths to eliminate, thereby accelerating the subcode decoding process and reducing computational demands. Furthermore, our approach involves the dual subcoding idea, where diverse reliable paths in the original polar code are to broadcasted to the other subcode to enhance collective diversity recovery trajectories. Experimental results show that PSLD outperforms its counterparts with substantial decrements in decoding iterations, thereby achieving substantial computational cost reductions. Simulations also confirm that the dual subcoding strategy can effectively enhance existing polar subcode-based list decoding methods, resulting in superior performance with lower computational requirements. Extensive simulation results are also presented to validate the dependability of the proposed PSLD design. Moreover, our framework suggests a systematic approach to enhancing existing polar subcode-based list decoding methods, as well as other iterative decoding approaches, by integrating the dual subcoding concept. This suggested approach is anticipated to yield significant collective diversity benefits to diverse decoding methods with reduced computational cost. Moreover, due to its versatility and dependability, the proposed framework can effectively be applied to a variety of codes beyond polar codes, such as LDPC codes with collective diversity traits defined by the parity-check matrix. Therefore, further research is recommended to integrate the dual subcoding idea with diverse decoding methods to further enhance collective diversity recovery trajectories. Finally, by extending the proposed framework, it is possible to establish a systematic design methodology for existing diverse decoding methods with the dual subcoding idea, thereby resulting in superior performance with reduced computational cost. Extending this proposed framework is thus an area of recommended future research. Moreover, by adopting the dual subcoding idea, it is possible to effectively improve existing diverse decoding methods with the collective diversity recovery trait, and by extending this proposed framework, it is possible to achieve even better results with higher degrees of parallel decoding in the dual subcoding idea, thereby further increasing computational cost reductions and performance gains. Hence, further research from the dual subcoding idea and the proposed framework is recommended. In a scenario involving two images, our analysis reveals that the orientation matrix, regardless of polarization beam arrangement, does not significantly impact the PSF, implying minimal effect of polarization configurations commonly employed. Conversely, in cases of odd polarization arrangements, the matrix has a non-negligible impact, thereby affecting the PSF, and in turn, affecting PSF correction procedures. Moreover, in cases of odd polarization arrangements, the PSF can be expressed as the convolution of the two individual PSFs and a scalar multiple of the orientation matrix, indicating that the PSF can be corrected by conventional methods only in cases of odd polarization arrangements, and that the PSF in cases of odd polarization arrangements, though distorted, still retains a direct physical relationship with the object of interest. Such behavior is also predicted to occur in cases of higher step numbers within multi-step reconstruction methods. In order to utilize the PSF correction methods effectively for cases of odd polarization arrangements, it is necessary to incorporate an additional correction step that adjusts for the distorted PSF, facilitating the attainment of a defined correlation between the PSF and the object of interest. Such an additional correction step, for instances of two-step reconstruction methods, would involve rectifying the orientation matrix or utilizing an alternative normalization technique. Notably, our analysis predicts that the reconstructed images show varying levels of dependence, with some configurations resulting in near-dependent behavior and others, particularly those of odd polarization arrangements, resulting in images that can be effectively treated as if they were independent of one another. Ultimately, our analysis reveals that the reconstructed images possess a defined physical interpretability, with the PSF correlation, when corrected for in cases of odd polarization arrangements, defining the extent of coherence between these images and the object of interest. Drawn from the root of crystallographic principles, this research advances and refines the existing theory of fracture at a microscopic level as proposed by Kullaa. The underlying idea is that the critical stress required for a crack to propagate is directly related to the amount of deformation previous to the crack formation. The initial model included two key considerations - the influence of surface tension and the amount of plasticity determined by the applied stress relative to the material's hardness. The model has now been broadened by incorporating a new parameter that accounts for the fraction of plastic deformation occurring before a crack forms. As a result, this theory provides a comprehensive framework that encompasses both plasticity-based and elasticity-driven crack propagation mechanisms. Derived from this framework are formulas for fracture toughness, as well as an associated expression for fracture energy, both of which are based on well-established relationships between stress, work, and energy. The model was tested with experiments on high-strength, high-alloy steel found to exhibit significant ductility despite having a low coefficient of plasticity. The presence of ductility in this material enabled the observation of prolonged crack growth preceding the final fracture, thereby allowing the verification of the theoretical predictions using experimental data. The practical utility of this theoretical framework is illustrated through its ability to predict the material's resilience in the absence of comprehensive fracture mechanics analysis. Specifically, this entails using a straightforward design approach to identify the optimal material processing parameters as the key to achieving desirable properties in the material. The theoretical framework presented combines well-established principles from elasticity and plasticity theory to provide a cohesive and comprehensive understanding of fracture at a microscopic level. The resulting theory possesses the simplicity and generality required for practical applications in design and engineering. Furthermore, this framework, grounded in fundamental crystallographic roots, provides a essential understanding of fracture as an intricate part of the microscopic world of crystalline materials and their underlying mechanisms. The associated computational tools and resources, including the CrystallineMaterial class in MATLAB, are conveniently accessible for efficient use in designing and engineering applications involving high-strength alloys like advanced steel and similar materials. The proposed design approach and the related computational tools are intended for widespread adoption in design and engineering applications, while the theoretical framework aims to integrate and consolidate various earlier concepts and ideas. Notably, this framework resembles an elasticity-based model suggested by Kullaa, though it differs significantly in its predictive capabilities and generality. Moreover, this framework has been designed with a user-friendly structure and can serve as a useful starting point for developing future designs and engineering applications. This research paper is focused on resolving the Navier-Stokes equations for periodic initial conditions, and we have derived some theoretical bounds for the solutions in terms of the maximum norm. Our analysis reveals that the norm of the derivative of the velocity vector field is bounded, and we have also established that if the initial velocity is within a certain range of values, then a solution to the Navier-Stokes equations exists and its velocity component adheres to the Cauchy critical norm within that range. Furthermore, by employing a technique of non-regular averaging in a thin domain, we have obtained an a priori estimate for the velocity component within that range. Utilizing our analysis, we have reached the conclusion that if the initial velocity is within a certain range of values and the Navier-Stokes equations are strictly hyperbolic throughout that range, then the quasilinear Navier-Stokes system is well-localized and its solution can be extended indefinitely. A numerical example illustrating the strict hyperbolicity property in a waveguide configuration is presented. We have also demonstrated that if the initial velocity is within a certain range of values and the Navier-Stokes equations are not strictly hyperbolic throughout that range, then the quasilinear Navier-Stokes system is well-localized and its solution can be extended indefinitely, and in this case, the growth of the velocity component can exceed any polynomial function. All our conclusions are based on extensive analytical results, and they are not numerical in nature despite the use of a technique of non-regular averaging in a thin domain. Furthermore, we have verified the consistency between our analytical results and those obtained numerically. The presented findings are analytical and can be extended to other problems such as the Euler and other nonlinear hyperbolic systems, and they are relevant for various applications in science and engineering. However, by taking a different approach where the focus is on confirming the absence of non-zero outcomes instead of directly evaluating their presence, we can resolve the issue with much greater ease. This alternative perspective, coupled with the use of data structures designed for efficient handling, allows us to develop a verification algorithm that works linearly with the size of the input. Furthermore, in addition to constructing this verification algorithm, we also develop another one based on a different logic model where the focus is on verifying the overall context rather than individual components. This alternative, classical verification method has its own set of benefits and applications. It is noteworthy that these algorithms can be used not just for confirming the accuracy of quantum computations but also for evaluating the reliability of measurements obtained from experiments in the field of quantum physics. This efficiency in context-orientated verification methods can, however, decrease to quadratic, depending on the specific size of the input data. This study proposes a novel IoT blockchain framework that incorporates a specific type of computer called an oracle within a blockchain system. The objective is to facilitate adoption of the blockchain technology in the IoT sector by addressing several key issues that have hindered its implementation. A simulated, real-world scenario was developed to test the efficacy of the framework in the domain of smart logistics for food distribution. The outcomes of the experiment revealed that the IoT blockchain framework has a minimal impact in terms of computational overhead, yet offers robust security benefits. Furthermore, the introduction of a specific type of computer within a blockchain system appears to be an highly promising approach to managing and interpreting data from sensors. The experiment showed that to ensure food quality, sensor data from certain nodes is sometimes required, and other times it is unnecessary to minimize overhead. Such dynamic decisions can significantly accelerate processing speed by up to 3 times, depending on the context. The analysis points out several potential limitations of the approach, such as the possibility of unfair decisions due to a lack of standardised sensor data evaluation processes. Cells exhibit vast diversity in shape due to various forms and diseases. Yet, current AI cell prediction models struggle to handle the intricacies of cells, especially in generating novel, imaginary cell examples. In this research, we present an innovative approach based on implicit neural representations to create highly detailed and accurate cell predictions. By utilizing a neural renderer to compute signed depth values, we demonstrate the efficacy of our technique in processing cell data. We also successfully applied this method to the task of generating imaginary cells and outperformed traditional convolutional networks in terms of accuracy and realism. This research explores the worldwide impact of document accessibility, considering it as a vital element of human rights. Through online surveys and interviews with individuals who have difficulty reading due to various disabilities including dyslexia, the research highlighted the necessity of accessibility. Key challenges were also uncovered, such as the under-representation of print-impaired individuals and the lack of consistent accessibility standards across document providers. Consequently, the research suggests potential solutions, including awareness campaigns and a unified accessibility framework that could greatly improve document accessibility. Crucially, the research sheds light on a long-neglected demographic, the print-impaired, and seeks to bring their needs to the forefront. A key finding of this study is that there is no cost-effective technology to enable print-impaired individuals to access essential documents. Consequently, the research calls for policy intervention and investment in research and development to create a more inclusive world. Importantly, the research emphasizes that technological development alone is insufficient and that a more holistic and systematic approach is required. A large-scale data-driven study could help gauge the true magnitude of document accessibility needs worldwide and inform a global document accessibility policy. A potential winner of a prestigious EU funding program, the "Luminoso Prize", our proposal aims to develop AI-powered tools to make documents accessible to print-im impaired individuals. Through comprehensive analysis and rigorous testing, our proposal will be executed in three key locations: Berlin, Germany; Barcelona, Spain; and Lima, Peru. By pursuing this project, we intend to make a significant contribution to the global effort to improve document accessibility and create a more just and equitable world for all. While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. By leveraging permutations of factorization order and masking strategies, XLNet addresses the limitations of BERT and captures richer contextual and positional representations. Benefiting from its enhanced modeling capabilities, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across eleven different tasks, with significant improvements visible in key areas like SQuAD 2.0 and GLUE benchmarking. Importantly, XLNet achieves these gains while processing input sequences at only half the speed of BERT-Large, thereby facilitating large-model finetuning without cost constraints. Furthermore, XLNet's pretraining objectives can be combined in various ways to optimize model performance. These contributions validate XLNet as a Pretrained Language Model benchmark, offering superior performance to BERT in most contexts. Several modeling techniques have been developed to accurately simulate tsunami behavior, especially in disperse wave models. These waves originate from asteroid impacts and fundamentally involve a nonlinear partial differential equation with complex interactions of shocks, rarefactions, and interfaces. In disperse wave models, the equation's hyperbolic nature is preserved, but only under an explicit set expansion speed limit. When this limit is exceeded, the equation loses its hyperbolic properties and becomes non-linear diffusion-based, significantly impacting simulation methods and requirements. This work investigates disperse wave models, focusing on the behavior of the set expansion front over time. It demonstrates that, in ideal cases, the set expansion grows exponentially and analytically derives the associated rate constant. Numerical simulations, using high-resolution grids, reveal that, in real cases, the set expansion converges towards an exponential growth, but is initially constrained by a fixed speed limit. When this limit is breached, the set expansion converges towards the exponential growth, but only after transitioning through a concave-convex'saddle' period. Knowing these temporal behaviors is crucial for choosing an appropriate modeling technique. In cases where the set expansion converges towards an exponential growth with a moderate speed below the expansion speed limit, the Lagrangian method proves to be the most efficient type of disperse wave model. In cases where the set expansion transitions through a'saddle' period before converging towards an exponential growth with a speed above the expansion speed limit, MUSCL and VOF methods prove to be the most efficient types of disperse wave models. Finally, in extremely rare cases where the set expansion transitions through a'saddle' period before converging towards an exponential growth with a speed significantly above the expansion speed limit, the linear disperse wave model may be required. This linear model loses its hyperbolic properties abruptly and typically demands a significant level of resolution and a high degree of adaptability. Therefore, these two types of models, the Lagrangian and MUSCL/VOF, offer the most efficient solutions for disperse wave models, while the linear model represents an area for further advancement and research. Furthermore, numerical results are presented and discussed in a related work [2]. In a related work [3], an algorithm designed to run the disperse wave models locally and in a distributed fashion over multiple processors and CPU's is described. This algorithm aims at reducing the computational complexity of these models and suggests that, in addition to choosing the most efficient modeling technique, choosing the most efficient computational platform may be equally crucial

Our research examines the kinetic dynamics of expanding polymer networks that undergo strain-hardening with light scattering. The kinetic model by Morse et al. was used to generate specific scenarios, which our experiment cannot produce solely based on light scattering measurements alone. To overcome this limitation, we combined the Morse model with the energy framework and conducted novel simulations of photopolymerization and light scattering during kinetic effects. The outcomes reveal that simple scattering measurements can distinguish affine and non-affine models due to their distinct behavior in the Tanada-Morse parameter space. Therefore, we propose that the affine model is insufficient and that the non-affine model provides a more accurate representation of the kinetic dynamics. Nevertheless, we acknowledge the presence of affine kinetic effects and propose the utilization of supplementary methods, such as fluorescence, to dissect the two types of behavior. Ultimately, this approach enables a more detailed understanding of the underlying mechanisms in complex polymer systems. The main challenge in incremental classification, previously referred to as classification growth, lies in effectively merging new data with a pre-existing classification model without compromising its accuracy. By utilizing a self-organizing approach inspired by Kohonen maps to embed new data into a pre-trained task graph, a new method called HyperExpan is able to leverage the efficient geometry of hyperbolic space to achieve this goal. This method incorporates a neuroevolutionary technique to optimize node positions for the most important new data examples, thereby facilitating more efficient incorporation of new data. Furthermore, by applying a contrastive learning framework to task nodes in the graph, HyperExpan is able to maintain the accuracy of its integrated model at or below the combined accuracy of its individual tasks. Our experiments with various new datasets have demonstrated that HyperExpan is able to successfully address the main challenges of classification growth, namely data accommodation and accuracy retention. In addition, by using a method of merging self-organizing representations with deep neural network representations, HyperExran is able to convert its embedded features into a form that is compatible with modern deep neural networks, thereby enabling comparison with existing techniques. Our results show that HyperExpan is superior to all existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in its ability to retain accuracy and improve overall performance. Importantly, HyperExpan is able to achieve these results using a simple implementation of hyperbolic network growth that is easy to use in practical applications. All of the code for HyperExpan has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/mhilsenbeck/HyperExpan. Our work, in combination with the tools that we have developed, may facilitate the creation of more robust, interpretable, and efficient life-long learning systems. Cyber-Physical Systems require robust characteristics to accommodate unpredictable aspects, which can stem from variations in system parameters, external interference, or timing discrepancies. Although general concepts for cyber-physical system robustness exist, they often fail to account for specifications formulated using Temporal Logic languages like STL. As a result, there's a gap between STL-based requirements and practical, timing-dependent approaches, hindering their utilization. To address this disparity, we develop a novel robustness definition that establishes a link between STL formulas and a particular timing model. This definition enables us to gauge the degree of robustness in cyber-physical systems operating within a timeframe and influenced by parameter variations. Furthermore, we outline a practical methodology for evaluating and presenting robustness in a multi-dimensional context. We demonstrate the practical application of our approach by applying it to a celebrated case study, the Sampled-Data Autopilot system. Compared to existing robustness assessment methods, our approach offers a flexible, human-centered method for assessing and visualizing cyber-physical system robustness via a intuitive, 3D chart similar to the ones commonly used. After examining the charts, engineers can adjust system parameters, such as gain (adjusting the feedback) or sampling rate, in order to achieve an optimal balance between performance, safety, and stability. Moreover, we show that the sample points on the robustness charts follow a geometric pattern, allowing us to identify the boundaries of the robust region through a simple calculation based on a relevant vector norm. This approach simplifies the identification of the maximum radius of the robust region, making it easier to achieve an optimal balance between performance and stability. Finally, we compare our approach with a popular tool, UPPAAL, to verify the effectiveness of our 3D robustness visualization method. With the help of our approach, we are able to present a general, model-agnostic strategy for evaluating and presenting cyber-physical system robustness in a timing-based, multi-dimensional context. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive formulation of Concealed Markov Models (CMMs). A CMM is an advanced Markov model, enriched with a hidden unit that restricts observation access. This hidden unit controls when to conceal (i.e., render undistinguishable from the completely random scenario) and, consequently, influences the visible output. Following the development of CMMs, we explore the visibilty property: a predicate indicating whether a CMM's behavior can be recognized through its visible behavior. We demonstrate that CMMs with a determinate hidden unit can recognize visibility, but this capability is not achievable for those with a probabilistic hidden unit. Additionally, we demonstrate a CMM's visibility is independent from its equivalence to a probabilistic finite-state automaton. We provide necessary and sufficient conditions for simulating a CMM in an advanced semiring and establish that CMMs can recognize a more extensive class of languages in an advanced semiring in comparison to a probabilistic finite-state automaton. Lastly, we outline CMMs' potential applications in a distributed setting, highlighting their use in modeling quantitative process security aspects. In the context of pattern formation in fluid dynamics, researchers developed a novel framework incorporating both hydrodynamic velocities and vorticity from the Navier-Stokes and vorticity equations. This approach in a quadruplet space has inherent coherence, displaying traits of a closed invariant subspace within the Navier-Stokes equations. By combining Kolmogorov's energy cascade principles and the view of coherent structures as statistically unique entities, researchers found that coherent patterns follow a normal distribution with statistically nonlocal spread. This nonlocality indicates that distant coherent structures interact through molecular forces, thereby violating the assumption of independence. This analysis provides a potential basis for identifying distinct coherent structures using a normal distribution with their characteristic dimensions as distinct features. This approach could facilitate further investigation of coherent structures as fundamental building blocks of fluid dynamics in a manner similar to turbulent statistics involving fineness scales. Moreover, it shows that coherent structures in symmetric patterns display properties of both determinism and randomness, properties typically seen in the behavior of low-probability, high-energy events. This distinct behavior is predicted to be a general characteristic of all naturally occurring coherent structures. Finally, the approach in coherent quadruplets can be applied to other areas such as stock prices, offering novel avenues for both theoretical and practical applications. Currently, the library contains implementations of three different approaches to coherent structures, all of which can be computed at a standard rate. probability distribution. We introduce the concept of "safe harbour" – a circle 
within the Gaussian region. We develop an algorithm that securely moves the 
user's real-time location to a new Gaussian probability distribution while 
maintaining the constraints of the predefined Gaussian shape. We also modify 
this method to accommodate scenarios with time constraints, demonstrating that

Research has shown that the precise measurement of neural connections between different brain regions, as measured with functional MRI (fMRI), has important benefits. Resting-state fMRI data, which is collected without a specific task, provides valuable insights into the brain's network structure. However, conventional methods used to analyze this data are statistical in nature and can only utilize a limited amount of available data. Consequently, these methods have inherent limitations in their ability to quantify regional and inter-regional brain activity. In order to overcome these limitations, researchers have developed multi-subject modeling approaches which aim to maximize information extraction from available data. This study compares the effectiveness of traditional pair-wise measures with a multi-subimal approach in precision. This more streamlined approach offers a simpler solution for interpreting fMRI data and identifying individual differences in brain connectivity. In systems that use beeping protocols, devices communicate by sending beeps on a specific channel, and assuming $b$ beeps on that channel indicates the message has been transmitted. Unlike wireless media allowing for simultaneous transmission, this assumption requires devices to wait a set time, known as the "bee duration", after sending a message before considering it delivered. Based on this process, a beeping protocol called Power-Saving Beeping (PSB) was developed, improving energy efficiency by using a sensor to track when a node is the sole sender, and thus reducing the delivery time of messages and minimizing energy usage. Our findings show that PSB protocol significantly reduces energy consumption and improves efficiency in wireless systems with random noise, and that using a two-stage protocol can further optimize the PSB results, and even enable the creation of parallel beeping processes to increase its performance. Additionally, a set of beeping protocols were created to show that even under adverse noise conditions, and that resolving these issues does not affect the overall performance of the PSB protocol in ideal conditions and slightly decreases it in noisy ones. One such protocol, Fast One-Shot (FOS), was developed to achieve optimal performance and is just as efficient as PSB in noisy conditions while outperforming it in ideal cases. Another protocol, Parallel Beeping Protocol (PBP), allows for performance gains in systems with high quality noise conditions, and in systems where concurrent beeping is possible. Lastly, both FOS and PBP were adapted into higher levels of programming, and our results show such programming yields energy savings of 80-90% in real-world systems with random noise conditions. In particular, a higher level of programming called RPFOS yielded near optimal performance in all tested levels of noise conditions. In summary, our research shows a set of programming levels that can take advantage of the local two-stage process in beeping protocols, and in doing so achieve energy savings of up to 90%, particularly with a higher level known as RPFOS. What is more, our research is the first to take advantage of local processing in beeping protocols, and in doing so achieves near optimal performance in all tested levels of noise conditions. In particular, our research at the higher levels of programming shows significant gains in efficiency over prior work in beeping and sensing, and in particular, RPFOS shows significant gains in prior sensing protocols such as SPSP and Minimax. Recent advances in NLP have revealed that language models can be sensitive to linguistic and grammatical details, including word order and syntax. While WordPiece encoding has been effective, its ability to capture nuanced word-order information is limited. To address this limitation, researchers have been exploring methods to enhance the performance of language models. This work focuses on code-mixed utterances, which combine two languages with diverse word-order configurations. To capture the inherent word-order information in these utterances, we introduce a novel encoding method known as Transition Point Encoding Technique (PETO). This approach represents transitions between languages as indicators of word-order changes. Experimental results demonstrate that PTO is a valuable complementary encoding method that can be applied in conjunction with WordPiece encoding. Furthermore, to cater to the needs of code-mixed speech datasets, we also develop a positional encoding approach based on the writing system, distinguishing between script types (Latin and Sanskrit). Comprehensive experiments conducted on speech recognition tasks reveal the significance of the language order in code-mixing, and we also observe that combining both PTO and positional encoding leads to superior speech recognition performance. This approach allows us to train a general language model that is adept at handling various language pairs, including English, Hindi, Tamil, and Sanskrit. The underlying code is available for open research purposes. The model's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art results, yielding a word error rate of 6.87 on the SMIC v2.0 dataset. The final model's induction time is approximately two epochs. Furthermore, we also identify that PTO can be applied to translate the text in both forward and reverse directions, indicating its versatility in translation applications. The underlying code for PTO can be found at https://github.com/indianos/smit-pastuo-2022/tree/main/PESTO. The model's integration with Indic languages and language models is still an area of ongoing research. For further model details, readers are advised to consult the original paper. The Indic dataset used in this research, including SMIC v2.0, can be accessed at https://indianos.github.io/SMICv2.0/. The model's performance on other code-mixed datasets can be studied in a related paper published at IJCAI 2021, titled "Combining WordPiece and Transition-based Encoding for Code-mixed Speech Recognition". The model's performance on other code-mixed datasets can be found at https://github.com/indianos/CM-SPEECH-RC.

By examining two different S-H bond lengths in the rock-salt structure of sulfur, the results show that the position of the Fermi energy and the electronic density of states at the Fermi energy strongly depend on the S-H distance. Under 163 GPa of pressure, H$_3$S with a longer interatomic distance has a higher electronic density of states at the Fermi energy. As pressure increases to 226 GPa, the corresponding critical temperature also exhibits an upward trend. Our research suggests that the application of pressure results in the movement of the van Hove singularity from the energy range of $E \sim 2$ eV to $E \sim 0.5$ eV, with a substantial increase in the electronic density of states at the Fermi energy under high-pressure conditions. Our results indicate that the movement of the van Hove singularity from the low energy range plays a key role in the high-temperature superconductivity of H$_3$S. We also discovered that the isotope effect on the critical temperature of H$_3$S at high pressure is primarily influenced by the electronic density of states at the Fermi energy near the bottom of the conduction band around the van Hove singularity. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a model-based approach that utilizes 3D surfel maps to support visual relocalization, leveraging geometric context and deep learning-based feature extraction. This study focuses on a simultaneous channel measurement and beamforming problem, where users can select the uplink channel measurements that best suit their requirements. This is formulated as a group LASSO problem, which is solved by the triple iteration algorithm. Our approach first splits the problem into three smaller tasks, where the first task involves initial channel measurements, the second uses measurement matrices as inputs, and the third uses beamforming matrices as inputs. Numerical simulations demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method compared to a baseline approach that separates channel measurements and beamforming design into distinct tasks. The results show enhanced performance in terms of average rate and complexity. Over a tropical semifield, the rational function semifield of a tropical arc admits a finite set of generators. Additionally, the tropical arc's structure is entirely defined by these generating functions. Consequently, the rational function semifield's degree is equivalent to the maximum of the critical values of these generating functions. It has been established that the existence of a rational function semiffield degree for tropical arcs only relies on the arc itself, not on the arc's embedding. Moreover, the rational function semiffield's degree aligns with its Kodaira dimension, implying that the arc's singularities substantially influence its dimension. The study includes examples to demonstrate the complexity of tropical arcs and tropical moduli spaces, particularly regarding the arc's finite generation over the tropical semifield and the independence of its embedding. The findings extend to more general dimensional contexts via algebraic fibered calculus methods. The study ultimately shows that a particular tropical moduli component has a finite set of algebraic sections. The proof leverages Cartier duality and tropical moduli spaces' properties as semi-Log minimal fibrations. The study incorporates established results on tropical moduli spaces by Bruce, Martinengo, and Rouse, which are crucial for the findings. The study also includes computational examples to illustrate the complexity of tropical arcs and their relationships with tropical moduli spaces and logarithmic Gromov-Witten theory. The example with the Deligne-Mumford moduli space demonstrates that the results are applicable to established tropical moduli spaces, while the example with the K3 surface tropical moduli space showcases the application of the findings to individual cases. The study ends with the conclusion that further connections between tropical geometry and algebraic geometry through logarithmic Gromov-Witten theory remain unexplored. The study's primary goal is to extend the findings to higher dimensions, which requires the use of established results on algebraic fibered calculus by Gompf and Maydim. The study was completed during a three-week research period at the University of Warwick in January 2020. The code for the computational examples is included in the appendix and is written in a mix of Mathematica and Python, with a focus on interfacing with Sage. The study incorporates the use of tropical geometry, algebraic geometry, and computational methods. The study may have generated 57 figures. The deligne-mumford file was generated by Christian Haase. Authorizing short memory and taking the limit as N approaches infinity, we simplify the properties of N-times repeated independent experiments, allowing us to derive useful results for large N. Considering a Markov chain with transition probabilities P and starting composition π, we define consistent statistical properties for such chains as N approaches infinity. These properties converge to those of a Markov process, Q, having transition probabilities π(i)P(j | i), independent of N. We define a class of functions, called F, and show that a sequence of functions, where L(N, i, j), equals P(i, j) to the power of N, where i, j are in [1, N], in total N times, with the condition that L(N, i, j) equals π(i) * P(j | i) when i has a positive weight in π, does so consistently.
