This research explores a demand-side management approach through a more accurate forecasting technique that takes into account controllable load estimations and real-time feedback from current energy usage. By utilizing a forecasting method that considers multiple future time slots and allows for adjustment of forecasting parameters, participants can set specific targets for their controllable loads. In addition, a real-time feedback mechanism applies a penalty or reward or other forms of adjustment to users' actual energy usage. Our proposed algorithm generates optimal parameters for controllable load forecasting that yield the optimal collective output in terms of minimizing the Sum of the Squares error. However, in situations where users have inherently different preferences for energy usage during various time slots, the Collective Optimal Point may not satisfy all participants' individual interest in maximum collective output. Therefore, the paper adapts a noncooperative game model, specifically the Logit Game, to facilitate participants making their own decisions in a way that the play of the game converges towards the Collective Optimal Point. Simulation results validate the convergence of the game model while highlighting the distinct characteristics of the Logit Game in contrast to other game models. Moreover, the implementation of the proposed approach has been demonstrated using a test project involving 120 controllable appliance loads and 10 random users, all operating controllable loads in a Controllable Demand Side Management system. The approach has been implemented using a mobile application as part of a test project in an university campus in Malaysia. Data collected from the experiment further confirms the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed approach with data collected over the period from March to April 2017. One of the key findings from the experiment is that users' energy usage pattern is still distinct from one another even after the play of the game has converged for several days. This implies a reduced possibility for collective convergence of controllable loads during the play of the Logit Game, however, the proposed approach enables users to collectively optimize their controllable loads in such a way as to minimize the total energy usage during various time slots and ultimately results in a near optimal collective output. Experimental results further reveal an interesting trade-off existing between computational complexity of the proposed approach, number of controllable loads and the number of users involved in the game model. Therefore, future work may involve the adaptation of the proposed approach to resolve multi-objective optimization problems in Smart Grids. In addition, the proposed approach could be further implemented as a tool for advising purposes in contemporary Energy Management Systems. Identifying the precise timing and location of incidents such as crimes, accidents, or social protests is crucial for various research areas including criminology, urban planning, and sociology. Given the vast amount of data uploaded on social media platforms each second, instantiating the timing and location of incidents presented in posts is a key focus of our study. We propose a two-stage method for determining the incident timing and location. First, we use a deep learning model to estimate the timing of individual posts, incorporating time gaps between posts to ensure accurate referencing. Additionally, we employ a temporal influence model to calculate the weighted average timing of posts related to the same incident. Experimental results on datasets from Twitter and Reddit reveal that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches, boasting a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.95 or more for timing estimates and a mean absolute error of no more than 8.5 miles in location estimates. Given that Twitter's posting limit is 3 minutes and Reddit's is 5 minutes, these findings demonstrate remarkable accuracy and reliability. Such estimated timing and location data of incidents can facilitate a variety of applications, such as mapping crime distributions or predicting social mobilizations. Therefore, we also present an online demonstration of our method. Please note that due to various content restrictions on social media platforms, available data on incidents are generally confined to a relatively recent time frame. Hence, our study primarily targets locations where Twitter or Reddit platforms are widely used to gather timely insights into incident patterns. Furthermore, our work incorporates the use of temporal influence models, analogous to those in diffusion models, to determine the aggregate timing of incident-related posts. Therefore, our study is partially inspired by research in social network influence modeling. However, our work diverges from this area by leveraging these models as post aggregation techniques to instantiate the timing and location of incidents. As a result, our study incorporates novel applications of temporal influence models, distinct from the existing research scope. Following current platform trends, our study combines geometric and atmospheric distance considerations to evaluate location estimation accuracy. We have categorized the underlying location estimation model as non-deep learning-based to distinguish it from other models, despite the incorporation of a deep learning model in the first estimation stage. Consequently, our study incorporates novel location-based factors such as road and aerial distances, which have not been utilized in previous work, to refine incident location estimates. Using comprehensive databases and computational models, researchers identified and analyzed potential cobalt-rich compounds within the Y-Cobalt-Boron system. Through computational modeling, researchers obtained the mechanical properties of 102 cobalt-rich candidates, and ranked them based on their thermal expansion coefficients. With the assistance of machine learning, researchers' experimental tests revealed that two newly discovered Y2Co3B5 and Y5Co12B3 cobalt-rich compounds exhibit superior mechanical properties when subjected to high-temperature, high-pressure conditions. Testing the properties of Y2Co3B5 and Y5Co12B3 under various temperatures revealed that Y2Co3B5 has a negative thermal expansion while Y5Co12B3 exhibits typical positive thermal expansion. Furthermore, researchers found that Y2Co3B5 has a stress ratio of 0.85 and Y5Co12B3 has a stress ratio of 0.78, indicating that they are highly resistant to stress at high temperatures. When subjected to a 600 MPa stress, Y2Co3B5 has an 18% increase in strain, while Y5Co12B3 has a 9% increase in strain. Researchers found both materials demonstrate superior mechanical properties including stress ratio and strain resistance. Using X-ray diffraction, researchers confirmed that Y2Co3B5 and Y5Co12B3 have unique crystal structures, with the former exhibiting a monoclinic structure and the latter a tetragonal structure. Scanning electron microscopy revealed that both materials have cobalt-rich compositions on their surfaces. With the assistance of wave-dispersive spectroscopy, researchers confirmed Y2Co3B5 and Y5Co12B3 have an intrinsic cobalt content of 83.54 and 86.52 respectively. Overall, researchers' tests confirmed that both Y2Co3B5 and Y5Co12B3 have superior mechanical properties that qualify them as excellent heat-resistance materials and for use in high-stress environments. Using computational models, researchers were able to design cobalt-rich compounds with enhanced mechanical properties, exhibiting superior stress ratios and strain resistance. With the assistance of machine learning, researchers were able to discover and rank cobalt-rich compounds with outstanding mechanical properties, exhibiting superior stress ratios and strain resistance. Furthermore, researchers were able to discover newly designed cobalt-rich compounds with exceptional negative thermal expansion properties. Ultimately, researchers were able to uncover Y2Co3B5 and Y5Co12B3 as superior heat-resistant materials and for use in high-stress environments.

In the field of display advertising, online publishers auction off ad spaces to achieve a high revenue. Many advertisers partake in this auction, each submitting a bid. Upon an ad request, publishers determine the ad order and revenue based on the bid amount. An optimal bidding strategy, therefore, must balance ad conversion against cost, requiring precise estimation of ad value, known as bid price, to maximize return on investment within a set budget. While ad value is difficult to estimate and varies widely, researchers have made significant strides in this area. This study investigates adaptive bidding under a budget constraint in a competitive environment. Unlike previous studies, which assumed known ad value, this work involves estimating unknown and dynamic ad values. Our solution utilizes an adaptive algorithm, modifying its strategy as new observations become available. We prove this algorithm converges to an optimal solution, providing the foundation for our method. In our experiments, we have obtained up to a 25% higher return on investment on real-world traffic. Our results also highlight key challenges in real-world data, such as ad value variability and winning probability. We have also analyzed the impact of budget on return on investment, revealing a budget expiration results in a lower return on investment. We have also demonstrated the value of our method in an auction environment. Our code is available on github for public use. Our work has also received the Best Paper Award at ACM CIKM 2020. However, constructing reward functions typically requires extensive trial and error, a time-consuming process. To accelerate reward learning, one solution is to split the state space into smaller clusters and learn their respective policies first, a more manageable approach. Current techniques, though promising, still suffer from slow learning due to the inadequate utilization of information inherent in the state clusters. To improve upon this, we introduce VACRank, which optimizes the trial efficiency for reward learning by integrating two key components: 1) a clustering algorithm tailored for state observations, and 2) a novel trial allocation strategy within those clusters that maximizes information gain. Our approach is validated by comprehensive real-world experiments, demonstrating significantly faster learning performance across a range of complex control tasks compared to state-of-the-art counterparts. Furthermore, VACRank facilitates more accurate estimation of the optimal trajectory and yields better task performance. The code for VACRank is available at https://github.com/whsee/vacrank. To ensure that autonomous systems function safely and in accordance with legal standards, their interpretability must be formally assessed.  By combining insights from artificial intelligence, psychology, and philosophy, this paper proposes a comprehensive framework for measuring the interpretability of algorithms through the perspective of human learning.  This comprehensive framework, known as the Human-Learning-Oriented Interpretability Framework (HLOIF), encompasses three fundamental dimensions of interpretability: accuracy in capturing the underlying model, comprehensiveness in covering all aspects, and specificity in avoiding unnecessary details.  Furthermore, we introduce the Concept Intricacy Degree (CID) to quantify the cognitive difficulty of learning, and establish a measurement tool, the Cognitive Intricacy Degree (CID) score, to evaluate the ease of learning through various transformations of the explanatory data.  Utilizing our CID score, we conduct a formal interpretability assessment of decision trees, recursive partition, deep neural networks, and Gaussian mixture models, which provides a theoretical foundation for comparing the interpretability of these models, as well as that of other algorithms.  Moreover, this study offers a practical approach for evaluating and benchmarking the interpretability of any algorithm by considering a specific task within the domain of chemical substance classification.  Our results provide valuable insights into how to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models.  Due to its versatility, the HLOIF and the associated CID score can be widely applied across various fields of study.  At the same time, the proposed framework is capable of addressing the distinct requirements and constraints of diverse domains.  Ultimately, the HLOIF and the CID score offer a unified and systematic approach for understanding and quantifying the interpretability of machine learning models, which in turn facilitates their learning and diagnosis by humans.  A software program written in Python for implementing the HLOIF and the CID score has been made available for download on the China Knowledge Grid Snapshot Estimation Tecnology website.  Utilizing this tool enables users to easily evaluate and calculate the interpretability of machine learning models, as well as to learn and diagnose these models through interactive training sessions facilitated by the program. To gain insights into the dynamics of confined, Brownian particles, we investigate the exit times of single-file diffusion escaping a confined, one-dimensional space with different boundary conditions. We find that the distribution of exit times depends on the confinement's length for hard-walled confinement but becomes independent for soft, harmonic confinement when normalized. Additionally, we demonstrate the absence of a waiting time in single-file diffusion, which is a distinct contrast to the behavior observed in conventional diffusion. We also explore the second-order moments of exit times and discover a correlation between the waiting time and the confinement's length, emerging from the exclusion interaction between particles. Our key finding lays a foundational understanding of diffusion processes with directed motion, which can be generalized to particles moving in semi-circular confinement and may be applicable to certain biological systems, such as mitochondria's movement within cells. This paper demonstrates that the underlying principles of classical inference remain relevant when applied within the constraints of the Hilbert space framework, albeit on a quantum mechanical framework. However, these principles are breached when inferences are drawn using probabilities drawn from quantum mechanics' measurement process. To resolve this disparity, a quantum variation of Bayes' Theorem is proposed and exemplified through its application in both probabilistic and epistemic quantum scenarios. Furthermore, this quantum theorm is capable of generating inferences consistent with those derived from classical probability theory while generating more nuanced outcomes within the context of quantum mechanics. This example serves as a testament to the fact that quantum mechanics does not necessarily necessitate novel inference methods but, instead, often the implementation of existing concepts within a modified framework. This analysis ultimately aims to shed light on the broader implications of inferences drawn using quantum mechanics, particularly with regard to the distinction between probabilistic and epistemic formulations of quantum mechanics. Although the discussion is confined to the probability theorem, the conclusions drawn are considered versatile and potentially applicable across a range of quantum inference scenarios. A comprehensive list of relevant references is included at the paper's conclusion. Finally, Appendix C highlights the application and significance of quantum probability theorm, particularly in terms of emerging contexts. A complete derivation of both the standard and quantum variations of Bayes' Theorem in Hilbert space is presented in the paper's supplementary materials. We introduce a novel image representation called dynamic neural-guided probability hourglass (D-NHPH), which outperforms previous methods in natural image segmentation by leveraging a probabilistic spatial probability hourglass. This model enhances its spatial probability maps through an adaptive neural guide, derived from an early convolutional neural network. By fine-tuning this guide, D-NHPH improves its segmentation performance and efficiently handles long-term dependencies in dynamic images. Notably, D-NPHH achieves superior results without relying on traditional hourglass network architecture components. Furthermore, we propose a probabilistic prediction strategy, which reduces false alarms and maintains consistent segmentation across frames in video. Extensive experiments validate the benefits of our spatial-hourglass integration and probabilistic prediction scheme, enabling state-of-the-art performance in natural image segmentation and probabilistic object detection. Physical keyless authentication protocols aim to establish a secure connection with an unverified party by utilizing the inherent properties of physical systems. A distinct feature of such schemes is the absence of a predefined secret key. Existing keyless protocols rely heavily on open-channel communication, making them vulnerable to adversary attacks. In response, a novel keyless authentication protocol, 'Disturbance Recognition', was introduced and demonstrated the capacity to securely communicate with a single trusted party. In the present study, a modified version of the Disturbance Recognition protocol is proposed for use in AWGN channels. In these channels, legitimate users and communicators possess access to noise-generating equipment, whereas the adversary does not. A theoretical framework for the Disturbance Recognition protocol is developed and applied to AWGN channels. A security analysis via entanglement-based attacks confirms the protocol's robustness against adversary tactics. Notably, the proposed scheme does not require a predefined secret key and can securely establish a connection with a single trusted party in AWGN channels. A performance comparison with the passive authentication protocol is conducted and demonstrates superior security and randomness levels. In addition, the theoretical framework is applied to AWGN channels, providing quantitative measures of protocol performance. In particular, the curve plots of keyless authentication and keyless encryption are shown to outperform those of the existing protocols. In conclusion, the Disturbance Recognition protocol offers a level of security equivalent to that of existing randomized keyless authentication protocols, including the passive and DD protocols. In particular, the Disturbance Recognition protocol achieves a higher level of keyless authentication randomness than the DD protocol. In terms of practicality, the proposed protocol is more feasible to implement and easier to understand than the keyless encryption protocol while generating more randomness. In terms of capabilities, the Disturbance Recognition protocol achieves a higher level of keyless authentication security and keyless encryption security than the passive protocol. In particular, the Disturbance Recognition protocol achieves a higher level of keyless authentication security and keyless encryption security than the passive protocol by a factor of $10^{15}$ and $10^{12}$ respectively. In addition, the keyless authentication and keyless encryption protocols demonstrate a higher level of security than the existing protocols for bit lengths beyond 512 bits. The findings of the study provide an in-depth analysis and understanding of the Disturbance Recognition protocol as well as the existing protocols in the context of entanglement-based attacks. Estimating impulse responses in vector autoregressions can be challengning due to limited data and noise. In the case of impulse response identification through orthogonal projections, high correlation among series hinders orthogonality, while noisy data complicates model optimization. These issues worsen with small datasets. Our research introduces the Adaptable Local Projections (ALP) approach, which tackles these problems by dividing the data into neighboring subsets and projecting impulse responses locally, thereby avoiding correlations between sets and using robust estimators that can handle noisy conditions. We also analyze the statistical and computational efficiency of the ALP method and demonstrate its superiority through simulations across various scenarios. The findings show the ALP approach consistently outperforms existing techniques in estimation accuracy. The approach is further illustrated by analyzing the euro area inflation rate and its determinants. The associated software is written in Python and is made available for reference. The theoretical underpinnings of the ALP method are elaborated in the paper's companion. The efficient estimation of the impulse responses is achieved through the optimization of the three-parameter estimator using an algebraic method, which is subsequently generalized to high-dimensional applications with the help of the Toeplitz matrix identeness property. Our results are based on a Monte Carlo analysis that evaluates the performance of the impulse-simulation, two-stage least-squares, three-parameter, and ALP estimation techniques across different scenarios with or without structural breaks in the data. The simulation results show that the ALP estimation consistently produces more accurate and robust estimates of the impulse responses than the other methods. Furthermore, the ALP estimation is not only computationally efficient but also yields highly interpretable results. The estimation results are also visually presented in a forest plot and a 3-dimensional heatmap to facilitate easy comparison and interpretation. The final section of the paper demonstrates the practical application of the ALP estimation technique by estimating the impulse responses of the euro area inflation rate and its key economic indicators. The estimated impulse responses reveal interesting information about the dynamic relationships between these variables. For instance, the response of the inflation rate to a contraction in Germany's economic performance is relatively significant and persistent, whereas the response to a contraction in other euro area countries is relatively modest and brief. The ALP estimation and analysis of the impulse responses provide valuable insights into the economic systems of Germany and the other 18 countries included in the sample for evaluation purposes. The estimated impulse responses can be utilized by euro area policymakers and researchers to inform their monetary and economic strategies. We investigate how the electromagnetic vacuum's Casimir momentum is affected by a charge q moving in a Landau level with orbital quantum number l. The resulting memory of this motion is embodied in the electric field's non-zero momentum. The field equations reveal that this momentum's magnitude approaches an integer value of ql when l is large and the charge's speed is much slower than the relevant Landau level frequency. This situation can be considered as an embodiment of the concept known as "electron orbiting its own vacuum." Furthermore, we establish that the total momentum of the vacuum, which comprises both the electromagnetic and quantum electronic components, remains at zero for any charge configuration. The latter part of this research involves examining how an electronic charge affects the electromagnetic vacuum's Casimir pressure at the interface of two mirrors. It is discovered that for charges in the ground state or those moving slowly, the surface Casimir pressure is unchanged and increases in the direction of the charge's velocity. Ultimately, we discuss these findings through the lens of the concept known as the "quantum vacuum electrodynamics" of an electron. It is argued that these results can be regarded as a mild manifestation of the electron itself. The research ultimately concludes that it is more accurate to regard these phenomena as a consequence of the electron's field, which incorporates both its spin and orbital components, as opposed to a phenomenon arising from the vacuum's "excitation." The electronic vacuum's complex behavior, particularly its interaction with orbital angular momentum, differs significantly from that of the photon vacuum. The study's conclusions are considered in light of the broader context of the quantum electron. The electron's capacity to give rise to these vacuum phenomena may serve as a powerful reminder of its profound influence on the behavior of other particles. The interaction between the electron and vacuum fields is a fundamental source of various processes, including those governed by radiative corrections. The external characteristic of the electron's field, in the form of a manifest spin-orbit combination, significantly distinguishes the behavior of slow-moving charges from that of photons. A new class of multi-player games, known as nonlocal contests with noisy maximally intertwined states, has been introduced. In this type of game, players choose from states that are maximally intertwined with each other, but due to noise, players' selections do not always reflect their true intentions. We have shown that determining the most strategic choice for each player in these contests is always possible, regardless of the noise and the distribution of payoff rewards. Moreover, if the payoff rewards have a certain level of consistency, it is also possible to find the best possible strategy for each player. These findings build on a previous discovery that nonlocal quantum correlations can be optimized in contests with noisy maximally intertwined states. However, when payoffs are complex and entail multiple measurements, it was previously difficult to identify the optimal strategy, leading to the hypothesis that this limitation might be inherent to all nonlocal games. Our current results validate this idea that nonlocal games with noisy maximally intertwined states are generally unsolvable unless highly consistent payoff rewards are offered. In a surprising twist, it is now clear that determining the most strategic choice for each player in these contests is always a feasible task, even in the absence of consistent payoff rewards. The solution to this seemingly intractable problem reveals that nonlocal quantum correlations can be perfectly achieved through a combination of projective measurements, which was previously thought to be impossible. We have also demonstrated that nonlocal quantum correlations can be realized not only through projective measurements, but also through positive operator-preserving (POPM) measurements that are often considered a more stringent requirement. Furthermore, each player can implement these POPM measurements using only two distinct measurement settings. We address the high false positive rate (FDR) issue in large experimental settings where numerous interventions have varied and dependent effects. To curb the explosion of FDR, we explore the concept of "intervention effect identification," which comprises two objectives: first, strongly controlling FDR to pinpoint the most influential intervention effects; second, efficiently and accurately identifying the effects of interventions with lower power requirements. To achieve these goals, we establish a regulated FDR procedure drawing upon strong convexification and multivariate Benjamini-Hochberg procedures. We demonstrate that the proposed method's FDR control maintains a factor of $\sqrt{S}/\gamma$ lower, where $S$ represents the number of interventions, compared to the standard Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at a cost of $\frac{1}{\gamma}$ factors of additional bias in the intervention effect point estimates. To minimize the bias factor $\gamma$, we introduce a novel "confidence set" strategy for intervention effect identification, which significantly reduces its value. Finally, our numerical analysis substantiates our theoretical findings. The proposed techniques are validated through real-world application to a fundamental application - medication eligibility assessment in hospital databases - where we successfully identify the most impactful factors contributing to free medication programs for patients. Moreover, our approach is successfully applied in a company's large-scale logistics and supply chain dataset to identify key factors determining customer satisfaction based on sales promotion interventions. The results reveal a notable difference between the two datasets, with the former exhibiting more dependence among interventions and the latter characterizing customer satisfaction interventions. For various convolutional neural network-based deep neural networks (DNNs), speech features like Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients or vector flow features are typically used for speaker recognition tasks. In the context of conversational speech, the task of synchronizing speech features becomes significant in addition to identifying the speaker. Since the existing approaches focus mainly on speaker recognition, incorporating synch features becomes essential. By incorporating the synchronization information in a supervised distance metric, the performance of the DNN is expected to improve significantly. Utilizing unsupervised methods for synchronizing speech could enhance the efficiency in data preparation, thus making it a worthwhile approach. In this study, the feasibility of using two unsupervised metrics - dynamic time warping and local alignment with constraints - on a pre-trained, speaker-identifying DNN is evaluated. By applying these metrics to speech from two different talking individuals, the performance of the DNN in a mixed corpus is found to decrease compared to when speaker and synch are in alignment. Furthermore, the investigation reveals that the DNN is more sensitive to synch misalignment than speaker misalignment, and that the increase in errors occurs more readily with greater speaker misalignment than synch misalignment. As a result, the incorporation of synch information appears to have minimal effect on the DNN performance, and thus further research is necessary to devise a more effective synchronization distance. In order to improve speaker recognition using DNNs on conversational speech, the recommendation is to pre-align speech features based on a time-aligned annotation of the spoken text or utilise a separate DNN optimized for conversational speech that naturally incorporates synch features. Moreover, the proposal suggests using a time-warping response as a more effective metric in keeping the speaker's frame in alignment during speech feature extraction. Most existing research on action segmentation is based on supervised learning, but this requires precise annotations, a time-consuming process, especially for long videos. To overcome this issue, our work introduces SSCAP (Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing), a method for unsupervised action segmentation. SSCAP is built upon two key modules: a non-linear feature extractor and a coherent activity parser. The former module takes raw video data as input, while the latter module uses self-supervised learning to produce coarse-grained actions. SSCAP utilizes co-occurrence statistics and multi-path distribution learning to prevent situations where ambiguous scenes are mapped to specific actions. Furthermore, we incorporate multi-level temporal information to enhance robustness and integrate a coherent activity parser for discovering fine-grained actions. SSCAP is distinguished by its efficient use of video data, including physics-based transformations and sampling strategies, to reduce computational complexity. Experimental results demonstrate SSCAP's superiority over other co-occurrence-based methods, with notable improvements in performance on Kinetics-Segmentation and Breakdance datasets in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. The associated code and models can be accessed at a publicly available GitHub repository. The paper also includes a pilot domain adaptation study. SSCAP achieved promising results on dataset Dataset-SegB, a recently developed dataset for video action segmentation, unknown to us at the time of submission. The conventional approach to assessing students' coding abilities in professional settings is fine-grained review. However, this method has been shown to be effective in specific contexts, such as testing, when students are provided with clear expectations and evaluation criteria. Given the potential for inquiry-based assessments to promote deeper understanding, we conducted a study that combines a traditional approach with explicit feedback to determine which method, conceptual or detailed, is more effective in testing education. Our study compared two groups of students - one receiving conceptual feedback and another receiving technical feedback - to assess their performance in a subsequent project. We analyzed the results of this comparison using a Bayesian mixed-effects model. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like image classification and natural language processing. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns or regulatory restrictions, this approach becomes impractical. We evaluate our method on three different datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness across different distribution shift scenarios. Moreover, we successfully applied our method to a state-of-the-art language model, and our results show that it outperforms concurrent domain adaptation techniques in cross-dataset experiments. Notably, our method exhibits more consistent performance and is more resilient to overfitting. To facilitate future research, we are open-sourcing our code and make it available on our GitHub repository. Our empirical findings contribute valuable insights towards understanding the behavior of domain adaptation models. Ultimately, we hope that our study contributes to developing generalizable language models that can generalize across different distribution shifts effectively. Scientists have observed a spectacular solar eruption resulting from a shock triggered by a jet interacting with a sunspot's edge.  The extraordinary event was recorded at high cadence by GREGOR/1.6-m telescope in Boulder and simultaneously by LOFAR in the lo-w frequency range.  The event displays distinct phases: initial oscillations, an over-pressurized sunspot, a shock wave, and a post-shock phase.  The event was studied using both spectral and spatial LOFAR data, resulting in a 90-180 min timescale for the shock wave.  The estimated pressure and temperature within the post-shock region indicate that the event took place about 5-7 times higher than the average coronal height.  The study demonstrates the potential for using low-frequency observations to inform high-resolution optical observations, and reveals through 3D simulations that the event likely resulted from the interaction of a jet with a sunspot's edge, or the following the high-speed moving magnetic feature that triggered the shock.  The study shows the value in combining these different wavelength observations in order to further solar research.  The study further highlights the potential for using LOFAR in studying various solar phenomena. In a recent experiment, the CERN's Muon Collide project aimed to measure the muon's magnetic moment with unprecedented precision. The results showed a substantial discrepancy from the standard model's prediction, highlighting a 4.2 standard deviation inconsistency. Simultaneously, experiments studying flavour changing neutral currents found anomalies in the data, connecting it to new physics' potential implications. To explore this in the two Higgs doublet model, we have calculated key parameters including a type III see-saw model's Yukawa Lagrangian, and obtained constraints on $\lambda_{33}^{l}$ and $\lambda_{33}^{q}$ parameters at a 90% confidence level. The results indicate that solution spaces exist for both the g-2 anomaly and flavour changing neutral currents problems without requiring fine-tuning. Furthermore, we have introduced probability assessments for observed anomalies' explanations. The results show that while the two Higgs doublet model can address both discrepancies, the g-2 anomaly is more closely related to the model's requirements. Finally, we have established the model's potential to predict the muon's magnetic moment with standard model benchmark values. The results enable a future Muon Collide experiment to determine whether the two Higgs doublet model can be conclusively verified. Finally, we start exploring the utility of functional probabilistic differential equations and their adaptation in the study of turbulent dynamics. Moreover, we initiate an interdisciplinary conversation involving mathematicians working with measure-valued Markov processes, physicists studying turbulence, and geologists analyzing rock formation processes within fractures. The idea behind boson sampling suggests that measuring photons in order to learn about them is effective. However, if we consider the power of multiple measurements to reach a thorough comprehension, then non-classical effects may surface even in scenarios previously thought to exhibit no distinct advantages over classical models. To evaluate this notion, we calculated entanglement present in the entire state vector of boson sampling in both ideal and non-ideal conditions. Surprisingly, our results show that in both cases, a quantity measuring entanglement equals zero, indicating that multiple measurements do not uncover non-classical properties in boson sampling. Furthermore, we derived a criterion to assess whether a multi-partite state contains non-classical properties across any possible measurement. In accordance with this definition, our analysis found that non-classical effects can be exhibited by boson sampling, but only when certain post-selection measurements are involved. Importantly, some of these measurements are feasible in current experimental settings, thereby highlighting the need to revise the existing perception of boson sampling as a protocol lacking distinct advantages over classical models through a single measurement. Additionally, we applied the concept of boson sampling to a broader theoretical framework involving Markov processes, which may have practical applications in understanding rate processes in chemistry. The relevant code for our work can be accessed at https://github.com/MateuszKus/Entanglement-in-boson-sampling. A supplementary material for this paper can be found at https://link.springer.com/cn/article/10.11884/APSPhysicalReviewB.2022.5.435025.2/Supplementary.

Deep neural network training depends on large amounts of unorganized data, yet in life science research, analysts typically need to interpret complex, high-dimensional time-based sequences, often exceeding hundreds of parameters to accurately reach a verdict. Though feeding enormous datasets into a deep neural network would yield optimal results, such an approach isn't practical due to the immense computational requirements and the presence of inaccuracies within the training data. Therefore, a novel deep neural network, called the 'former-x', has been developed to quickly identify meaningful patterns within high-dimensional time-based sequences, even in very short datasets. Former-x utilizes a 'guided learning' technique to focus the deep neural network's training on specific time-based sequences, enhancing its capacity to identify relevant connections. Former-x integrates an optimized combination of a temporal attention mechanism and a recurrent structure, allowing it to process very high-dimensional datasets at very high speed. Experimental results show that former-x outperforms other techniques, including 'ilastik', across various dimensions of time-based sequences, even in very small datasets of just three samples. When used to identify frozen changes in cell development, former-x successfully detected shifts in 43k out of 62k possible dimensions. Reinforcement learning models with partially observable environments predict that neural networks will develop complex and entangled learning strategies.  Such environments can hide key state information from even the most informed agents.  Due to the intricacy of partially observable conditions, researchers have employed simplified models, like POMDPs, to better understand these complex situations.  A specific type of POMDP called a 'budgetized' POMDP is particularly useful for analyzing complex tasks, as it limits information exchange between the agent and its external environment.  A simple experiment with a specific type of partially observable task demonstrates how POMDPs, in conjunction with a factorized value estimation technique, facilitate faster discovery of hidden states and, most importantly, more efficient use of information.  Our proposed method outperforms conventional approaches, such as max-margin reinforcement learning and Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), in real-world neural networks.  Moreover, the factorized value estimation approach also optimizes the speed of task discovery in cases where POMDPs limit this process.  A specific type of recurrent neural network, in combination with our factorized value estimation approach, enables direct learning of key environmental states and demonstrates the potential for optimized discovery of hidden states and, most critically, more efficient use of information from even the most informed agents.  In a more challenging test of this concept, we employed the POMDP of an intelligent robotic manipulation task to separate its hidden key states, such as whether an object would be grasped or moved, from its observable properties.  A factorized value estimation model, in combination with a recurrent neural network and expert-labeled data, efficiently identified these key environmental states and discovered a strategy for optimized task reward.  Such models can be particularly useful in cases where the key environmental states and agents' motivations are naturally ambiguous and open to different possible interpretations, such as the content of a large online news article or a specific image. We conduct extensive experiments on SGD-120 and TRECVID Surveillant Task datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, achieving performance on par with strongly guided methods in both speed and accuracy. A virtual competition, the Image Similarity Challenge, was hosted in 2021 and brought together researchers to develop and showcase novel image acquisition and processing techniques utilizing data from the Zooniverse platform.  By analyzing the submitted entries, which consisted of over 300, they were able to gather insight into the experiences of individuals participating in crowdsourcing efforts and the outcomes of combined human and automated systems.  It was discovered that the main obstacles faced by participants were dealing with imperfect input data and dealing with high dimensional images.  By comparing different approaches to handle these issues, it was found that the configuration of the camera captured images of approximately 60x60 degrees on the sky map. Data processing techniques such as rotation detection and color filtering were found to be highly effective in reducing noise and misalignments, which further refined the image focus to approximately 20x20 arcminutes in diameter. Moreover, the FDR threshold was found to be set at 0.01 in order to filter out noisy images. It was also discovered that the key to success lay in strike a balance between the number of images processed in a batch, which affected the inter-rater reliability and the faintness of the processed images. Lastly, it was found that the key output of the pipeline was consisting of three types of classes: stars, galaxies, or unknowns, with an accuracy of 90%, 60%, and 10% respectively. It was discovered that the pipeline only reached 100% accuracy on images classified as stars. By analyzing the known galaxy class, it was found that the accuracy reached 60%. Lastly, it was discovered that the unknown class had the highest accuracy at 10%. It was also found that the pipeline failed to capture images of planets, nebulae, or other astrophysical objects other than galaxies or stars. In terms of implementation failures, it was discovered that the most common issue was a failure to process images at all. Conversely, the most common completion failure was a failure to classify the image. In terms of implementation timing failures, it was discovered that the most common issue was a failure to compute output within a reasonable timeframe. Conversely, the most common completion timing failure was a failure to start processing the image in a timely manner. Recurrent neural networks are highly effective at processing sequential data such as speech, but training them in a distributed manner is challenging due to the extensive communication requirements. In the context of cross-site privacy protection, standard approaches either sacrifice cross-site homogeneity or result in excessively large communication burdens. We introduce DP-REC, an efficient recursive technique that achieves reliable cross-site privacy protection through gradual parameter narrowing, allowing for faster, more efficient model updates and reduced communication overhead. DP-REC maintains compatibility between model updates, enabling seamless deployment in practice. In performance tests, DP-REC consistently surpasses its PRECISE counterpart while also outshining other privacy-protecting methods. Notably, on the Kaldi dataset, DP-REC's 97% accuracy matches the non-privacy model's performance, whereas previous approaches could only achieve 83%. We measured the column density of molecular gas by observing its absorption of far-ultraviolet light and compared it to the column density of young stars. We found that areas with high-density molecular gas have a lower rate of star formation. We measured the ratios of different atomic species within the molecular gas and found them consistent with recent surveys from ALMA and Herschel. We observed no correlation between the molecular gas and the locations of recent star-forming regions, which indicates that the gas is preventing new star formation. We found that the molecular gas is primarily composed of small, individual molecular clouds rather than large, continuous regions. We compared our data to simulations of star-forming regions, which suggested that the molecular gas is a result of the collapse of a self-gravitating disk. However, the simulated column density of this disk was too high to match our observations. One possible explanation for this disparity is that the molecular gas is not the primary component in the initial collapse. This paper investigates multi-phase games with incomplete information by defining a hierarchical structure of cognitive models. We examine the completeness of cognitive layers and derive a criterion for their optimization. Furthermore, we introduce intermediate cognitive models and demonstrate that they form a fully ordered sequence. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between intermediate cognoscenti and identify conditions under which they correspond to specific stages of incomplete information. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our findings to a multi-phase mixed martial arts contest. A fundamental property of cognitive layer models is that they are interdependent, with each stage assuming the knowledge of previous layers. This leads to the concept of equivalence of cognitive models, where two models are considered equivalent if one assumes the knowledge of the other. Furthermore, we define the completeness of a cognitive layer model, where the knowledge of the previous layer is sufficient for the current layer's assessment. We show that only two types of complete models exist - Markov equilibrium and Bayes equilibrium. We demonstrate that a sequence of cognitive layer models forms a fully ordered sequence, meaning that for any two models, there exists an intermediate model where the prior knowledge of the previous model leads to the equivalence with the latter model. Long-term changes in population dynamics, urbanization, and migration patterns are crucial indicators of essential development metrics, including GDP per capita, health, and education. Conducting accurate and thorough surveys to estimate populations in developing countries like Mozambique is complex and often costly. Sending teams to these areas can be hazardous due to security risks. Utilizing drone technology to generate population models and estimate necessary development metrics, while initially expensive, could be more cost-effective in the long run. Although drone surveys have previously been employed for similar purposes, they have typically been limited by the following critical considerations: the suitability of their algorithms for estimating populations and adapting to local conditions, the speed at which they can complete surveys, and the quality of the data collection process. Evaluating Quality of Experience (QoE) for TPSs poses a significant challenge, especially in interactive scenarios, due to users navigating complex virtual environments. User studies were conducted with 100 participants, who operated the TPS under different conditions representing real-world, wireless, and fiber optic connections. The results were obtained using a mixed effects regression approach. Non-linear effects of wait times on QoE were observed, with a moderate degree of variability in regression results across participants. The findings indicate that TPS QoE is sensitive to wait times, especially when users encounter obstacles or complex interactions. User-generated delay has a significant impact on QoE, with a 5-second threshold affecting its perception. Relative to wireless connections, fiber optic connections reduce QoE distortions by 64%. To make TPSs more robust to network conditions, recommendations are provided for their implementation. The data and analysis tools from these studies have been made publicly available for replication and potential application in the TPS community. The study's findings illuminate the complex factors influencing TPS QoE and provide a stronger foundation for quality evaluation in interactive scenarios. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that TPS QoE is shaped by interactive principles and user experience, emphasizing the necessity of incorporating these considerations in QoE assessments. The study's implications for TPS development and researchification are examined. The study's conclusions are drawn, highlighting its contributions and future research directions. In many scientific fields and data mining applications, clustering is a crucial task for processing and categorizing unclassified data. Various clustering techniques have been developed and are widely used in both theoretical and practical contexts. Theoretically, most clustering methods can be categorized into two fundamental types: model-based and hierarchical clustering. Model-based clustering methods utilize a common probabilistic framework and are linked to multivariate mixture modeling. On the other hand, partition-based clustering methods are characterized by dividing data into distinct, separate groups using a distance metric. From a practical perspective, the main clustering methods are hierarchical and non-hierarchical types, with hierarchical clustering employing a bottom-up approach to connect related groups and non-hierarchical clustering relying on statistical measures to determine dense data regions. The Dial-a-Ride Problem is a key problem in Distributed Routing. It involves multiple vehicles picking up and dropping off passengers with minimal overall travel cost. This problem has a solution paradigm in which viable passenger routes are continuously reduced. However, such solutions typically take a long time to compute and are usually simplified. In this research, a new algorithm is proposed to solve the problem to a metropolitan level of detail, extending a previous version of the dial-a-ride problem and incorporating time deadlines for pickup and dropoff. The proposed solution involves an algorithm to trim unviable routes and speed up the solution process. It was tested on various scenarios and showed improved computational time when compared to a more complete solution algorithm. Furthermore, a new variant of the dial-a-ride problem and its associated graph model is proposed to suit urban routing better. It was observed that solutions generated from this new version and the original problem matched in most cases but that the new version allows for faster and more computationally manageable solutions and allows for various types of cost functions to be implemented. It was also suggested that future research involve the integration of this version of the dial-a-ride problem with other distribution and routing challenges. Finally, an open source version of the algorithm was released and the potential applications of the proposed solutions were discussed. It is suggested that such dial-a-ride problems and their associated algorithms could be used to create harder problems for testing in the metaheuristic community. Furthermore, due to the requirements of the dial-a-ride problem, it could be implemented as a benchmarking problem in the Optimization community. In order to promote scientific progress in the dial-a-ride problem, an open source repository with the algorithm's code and the associated datasets used in the experiments has been shared at the link below. Additionally, we suggest that future research involve the integration of the proposed Dial-a-Ride problem with other Distribution and Routing Challenges and propose the development of a Special Issue in a prestigious Journal on this matter. This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing the lack of relevant methods in current literature. Existing approaches primarily focus on general vision and language tasks, neglecting the distinctive characteristics of E-commerce product images and customer reviews. In our work, we develop a novel E-commerce specific multi-modal pretraining framework, tailored to capture knowledge from product images and customer reviews that complement each other. A designed knowledge recognition module is introduced to extract recognizable knowledge from domain-specific dictionaries, guiding the learning of deep features from product images and reviews. Importantly, our method is unsupervised, addressing the problem of scarce labeled resources in E-commerce. We establish a dataset, called DS-CRC, which compiles five crocodile related categories from Amazon-Comp (Abdul-Rhman et al., 2021). We evaluate our method against multiple baselines with both single-modal and multi-modal tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and unsupervised superiority. Our method's weakly supervised pretraining capability is further verified through strong gains in E-commerce specific E-commerceSearch and EVAccRank tasks. The E-commerce multi-modal pretraining framework we proposed can be widely applied to enhance E-commerce product image and review classification models. The framework, as well as our proposed knowledge recognition technique, can be an efficient tool in E-commerce for text and vision data processing. The framework, known as E-CRMT, is made available on my GitHub repository. Moreover, we release our proposed framework and related code for reproduction, alongside the DS-CRC dataset and its related data on my repository. 

Overall, in this research we accomplish the following key outcomes:

Alzheimer's disease, characterized by progressive memory loss and cognitive decline, is largely a biological condition with supporting evidence from biomarkers and family histories. Current research uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans to measure changes in brain anatomy. However, traditional machine learning methods have been shown to be ineffective in identifying early Alzheimer's patients. This study demonstrates how Deep InfoMax, a self-supervised deep learning approach, can improve the accuracy of sparse and limited-scanner MRI data in diagnosing Alzheimer's disease. Using the Alzheimer's Disease Corpus, a dataset with detailed labels, we trained a model that achieves a 65% accuracy score, representing a 6% improvement over previous work with a two-sample t-test significance of p<0.001. Additionally, our findings highlight the potential value of self-supervised deep learning in processing under-collected medical data. Natural Language Understanding has reached a critical point where deep learning techniques predict semantic meaning, but these predictions often fail to align with human understanding. The main reason for this discrepancy is that computational models are isolated from the world they aim to interpret: they do not have the ability to interact with their surroundings. The semantic representation generated by these models is based solely on statistical patterns extracted from large text collections, which do not accurately capture context-dependent meanings. In this paper, a novel approach to language interpretation is presented that employs a type of recurrent neural network designed to capture implicit semantic connections through systematic and structured interactions. The proposed method is successfully applied to uncover hidden meanings in paradoxical ancient Greek texts, while a theoretical framework integrating interaction and meaning is also introduced. The research demonstrates the potential for a more effective, interpretive semantic approach, and a crucial next step for AI systems would be to bridge the gap between the internal state of these models and the external world. By achieving this integration, language understanding models can potentially become part of a two-way communication system, and in the longer term, language generation capabilities could emerge. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/sb2015/IRNN. The findings described in this paper were presented at the International Conference on Computational Semantics (ICS 2020). In systems with strong spin-orbit interaction and correlation, a crucial factor is understanding how interactions affect spin-orbit interaction. This is particularly important in materials like PtBi2, where strong correlation exists, led to developing a first-principles method called "rotationally dependent interaction". This approach enhances the calculation of spin-orbit interaction by considering an infinite series of terms. Through this method, it was verified that spin-orbit interaction's direction dependence has a substantial impact and that it is influenced by the structural asymmetry in materials like PtBi2 and PtBi2Hg, even in cases where hexagonal layers are stacked differently. Additionally, this method's results can also describe the self-energy and the hybridization, making it usable to compute the low-energy model parameters of SrPtO3 and potential superconductor SrPt2Ge2S6 via the "rotationally dependent interaction" scheme. As a result, this method's wide applicability to various materials with strong correlation and spin-orbit interaction has been demonstrated. We also introduce a module to adjust for uneven class distributions in target datasets, alongside a proposed metric that captures a model's reliability across different datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method and divergence metrics on both synthetic and real-world medical image datasets. In particular, the proposed approach leads to a significant improvement of over 15% for a breast cancer diagnosis model. We have openly contributed our code to the community. The approximate number system (ANS) plays a crucial role in human mathematics and is found across various species. Its widespread presence has led researchers to investigate its fundamental nature. We previously proposed the ANS Effective Compression (ANSec) hypothesis, suggesting that the most efficient coding methods for probabilities should be preferred. Theoretical and simulation results show that humans' subjective numeration experience aligns with the predictions of the most effective codes. The findings support the ANSec hypothesis. The proposed framework can generate predictions on the numerical sequence based on the most efficient codes and may serve as a basis for future cognitive models. The models and guidelines provided can facilitate the design of more better (machine) number sequence generators. Moreover, the most efficient codes have implications for the development of probability learning and perception. The study demonstrates that taking into account the most effective codes under different assumptions can improve their performance. The methods and techniques developed in this study show promise in tackling a range of challenges in the field of numerical cognition. The study offers a number of theoretical, experimental and application avenues for exploration. The study's code and data are available at https://github.com/antonzagorulko/ans-decoder-hypothesis. The development of high-resolution X-ray computed tomography (XCT) technology has shown its utility in the area of cement and concrete research. Current research has utilized XCT to examine cement and concrete samples at various stages of simulation, testing and construction, resulting in a wealth of informative micro-structural and pore-related data. However, a critical aspect of analyzing XCCT data remains overlooked - the impact of the pore fluid. Studies in materials science and engineering have highlighted the complex electrical properties of liquids, emphasizing the need to account for these factors when interpreting results. This investigation aims to explore and understand the electrical properties of pore fluids in cement-based materials through comparison of experimental and modeling outcomes. A particular emphasis is placed on the Dielectric Spectroscopy technique and the development of a dielectric model for analysis. This research aims to provide a comprehensive foundation for interpreting XCT data, facilitating a deeper evaluation of cement and concrete structures. As such, this thesis is divided into two primary components. The first section involves conducting dielectric property measurements and establishing a comprehensive dielectric model for systems comprising cement paste, mortars and concretes. A second section demonstrates the application of these findings in analyzing XCCT data of cement and concrete samples. A dielectric model was developed to simulate various cement-based materials with different porosity levels. Observations revealed that as the porosity of these materials increased, the dielectric constant decreased, aligning with the geometric mean rule. This geometric mean was found to be inversely related to the volume fraction of the pore fluid within the material. Using this model, XCCT data of different cement-based materials was converted into dielectric property images. Upon comparison, these images correlated well with traditional epsilon-matrix models and confirmed that XCCT can be employed for non-destructive evaluations of dielectric properties. Moreover, XCCT data facilitated a comparison of dielectric properties of different cement-based materials. Notably, concrete was found to possess dielectric properties intermediate to those of mortar and cement paste. Using XCCT, it is feasible to determine the dielectric properties of layered and composite materials such as mortars and concretes. A numerical investigation revealed that XCT detected the central binder liquid in a mortar sample and computed its dielectric properties in tandem with traditional methods. Consequently, XCCT has the potential to yield novel insights into liquid-free and multi-component materials while offering dielectric property images of separate components. Overall, XCCT has proven useful for analyzing dielectric properties of complex cement and concrete structures, thereby providing a viable alternative to conventional techniques for dielectric property

The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest at distant galaxies within our Universe allows scientists to make precise measurements of the subtle changes in the cosmic structure as it evolves over time, providing valuable insights into dark energy. These measurements are challenging due to the complex interactions between ionizing radiation and neutral hydrogen, which affect the forest's shape, making its data analysis intricate. By simulated studies, researchers discovered a novel approach for measuring the cosmic structure's evolution, focusing solely on the three-dimensional distribution of the forest's most highly ionized state. This distribution is influenced by two key factors: the intergalactic medium's redshift power and the mean transmitted flux. By controlling for these variables, scientists can isolate primary indicators of the cosmic structure's evolution, such as its density and the overall scale. This new method exhibits reduced uncertainties and greater stability than existing techniques and can be applied to current observational data, potentially yielding more accurate results. Notably, it is best suited for datasets with a size of three times that of existing datasets, which would yield significant improvements. Furthermore, researchers expect that three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ data analysis will become even more effective with the release of upcoming large-scale surveys, potentially yielding precise measurements of the Hubble constant, the growth of structure, and dark energy's properties. A groundbreaking experiment was conducted to observe the transfer of transverse and longitudinal beam emittances between two beams of different energies at the Fermilab Accelerator. Data showed clear signs of emittance exchange in both directions between the low-energy and high-energy beams through a $q\rightarrow q'$ recirculation magnetic insertion. The observed emittance coupling strengths were found to be in line with the expected values from the insertion magnet, with the measured splittings and comings together matching the predicted ratios. The results confirm that emittance exchange can be a reliable method for making precise energy adjustments, and potentially serves as a means to perform high-precision beam measurements of emittances. A detailed description of the experiment and its implications has been presented, with the goal of contributing to future beam-based energy measurement experiments. Emittance exchange could play a pivotal role in these experiments, potentially enabling fine-scale tuning to verify the desired beam energy, while simultaneous measurements of emittances could reveal dE/dx measurements and beta function values. For example, a similar approach could be employed at the Electron Ion Collider to measure the beta function at the vertex, and at the future Electron Collider Collaboratory, where accurate beam energy measurements will be essential. Moreover, emittance exchange could facilitate fast extraction in proton synchrotrons and may aid in resolution of anomalies during the process. Further research is necessary to fully harness the potential of emittance exchange for these applications. The observed effects were, however, not influenced by the formation of chirp-like structures in the beams, indicating a lack of connection between emittance exchange and these phenomena. Further investigations are needed to understand these particles and their relationship to emittance exchange. Similar experiments have been successfully conducted many times in the low-energy beam lines at SLAC, using the NIM line. Based on the results presented, similar experiments are proposed for testing, with the goal of verifying that emittance exchange can be a reliable method for energy adjustments and beam measurements. A detailed description of these proposed experiments has been provided. One such experiment has already been implemented at SLAC in 2021, demonstrating the feasibility of emittance exchange for energy adjustments and beam measurements. Results from this experiment have been presented, showcasing the potential of emittance exchange in these applications. This research aims to enable precise energy corrections and beam measurements at accelerator facilities, with the goal of a prominent application in future experiments. More specifically, these goals are for the Fermilab proton accelerator, the PIP II superconducting proton accelerator, and the Electron Ion Collider

Deep learning's rapid advancements in computer vision and image processing have now significantly impacted the broader geospatial sciences, incorporating tasks like routing, location prediction, and traffic forecasting. Traffic forecasting in particular demands precise temporal and spatial understanding, not least because of the inherent safety considerations. Current approaches to predicting the paths of moving objects, whether vehicles or pedestrians, tend to overlook two crucial factors - recurring patterns in behavior and the potential for other agents to change our predictions. Our proposed model, Sliding Sequential CVAE, is designed to tackle these two limitations by using recurring patterns in behavior to inform our predictions and taking into account the potential for interactions with other agents. Our model demonstrates excellent performance across a range of traffic prediction benchmarks. Our experiments using the TrajectoryNet dataset have shown that the potential rewards from considering the complex interactions of multiple agents on a road are very substantial. Our findings also confirm that the social aspect of our model plays a vital role in informing our predictions and helps us to mitigate the potential risks of our predictions. In various scientific fields, measuring complexity is a major challenge due to the lack of an universally accepted definition. As a result, different approaches to complexity analysis have been suggested in statistical physics, all attempting to capture the essence of this concept. Two widely used measures of complexity in this context are the average entangled entropy and the linear complexity, which have been applied to Boltzmann machines. Our research explores the contrasting behavior of these metrics as machines transition from simple to complex configurations. Our objective is to illustrate the differing nature of these complexity metrics and highlight their potential for concurrent yet distinct information on the characteristics of the systems being studied. Additionally, we observe that the average entangled entropy is more sensitive to detecting potential transitions between various system states, while the linear complexity provides insights into the static properties of the systems under investigation. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of complexity can be achieved by considering multiple, contrasting metric criteria. Our research also discusses the implications of combining multiple metrics and proposes that a deeper understanding of complexity in Boltzmann machines can be obtained by exploring the geometrical structure of the space of valid configurations in a way that is dependent on the chosen metric criteria. Ultimately, we believe that the contrasting nature of these complexity metrics offers valuable insights for further investigation into the intricate nature of this concept. As such, this work may serve as an inspiration for future research endeavors focused on analyzing and quantifying complexity in diverse systems. Additionally, we have included an appendix containing a new metric criteria of complexity that takes into account the geometrical structure of the space of valid configurations, as well as an analysis of the underlying relationships between the differing metric criteria presented in this thesis. Specifically, we demonstrate that the average entangled entropy is closely related to the information of mutual dependence between distinct elements, and that it shares a connection to the concept of free energy commonly employed in thermodynamics. Moreover, through geometric interpretation of the contrasting metric criteria, we have established a bounded relationship between the differences of the metrics in the case of metrics that report negative values, such as mutual dependence information, as well as an unbounded relationship in the case of metrics that report positive values, such as Boltzmann machine metrics. Consequently, a more comprehensive analysis of complexity can be achieved by considering multiple, distinct metric criteria in a unified manner. Furthermore, in the Geometric Data Analysis approach, the space of valid configurations is divided into neighborhoods, and the resulting geometric structure of the space of valid configurations is analyzed. A fundamental principle in quantum control is counterdiabatic driving, which requires no adjustments once a target state is achieved. We developed a method that produces CD-driven Hamiltonians for complex many-body systems without needing complicated model descriptions. We applied this approach to the Hubbard model and generated CD Hamiltonians for any interaction strength, based solely on the final quantum state. We also demonstrated that these CD Hamiltonians remain optimal even in the presence of extraneous terms. Furthermore, we showed that local steering is feasible in systems with interacting fermions and that assemblies of spin-symmetric fermions can be controlled using a simplified single-parameter family of Hamiltonians. Our findings provide a framework for effortlessly creating customized quantum control strategies adapted to any many-body system without the need for a detailed Hamiltonian description. They also open the door for utilizing machine learning to improve quantum control strategies. As a practical application, we investigated the use of gate-variable strategies for assembling a spin-singlet state in a hole-doped cuprate material, taking into account experimentally relevant variables such as the jump rate and interaction strength. We found that, while variable strategies may be necessary for achieving the target state, the CD Hamiltonians remain stable even when these strategies are varied. Ultimately, our work highlights the viability of ground-state assembly through adjustable Hamiltonians driven by simple, low-energy operations. We believe that such a paradigm could serve as a foundation for efficiently realizing quantum states and computing algorithms. We also explored the connection between our many-body control model and a thermodynamic cycle, which uses the quantum analog of the Otto cycle to achieve maximum efficiency at any interaction strength. We identified two key conditions that minimize entropy generation during this process: using a fast oscillator as a compressor and assembling a model where particle and spin excitations are coupled. Our findings provide experimental opportunities in materials with these characteristics, as well as theoretical insights into efficiently realizing quantum states and computing algorithms. We conclude by providing an algorithm for generating adjustable Hamiltonians that efficiently change the interaction strength of any model whose dynamics can be described using a narrow class of models with a simple, universal parameterization. We open-endedly open the door for machine learning to improve quantum control strategies, even for applications that cannot be described using such a model description scheme. We anticipate that our findings will inspire experimental investigations into the adjustable Hamiltonians that efficiently change the interaction strength of any model, as well as quantum control strategies. Under certain conditions, the harmonic hyperbolic metric on S can be related to the Green's function of a specific Euclidean domain, and this provides an alternative characterization of when a surface can be conformally embedded into the Riemann sphere. This in turn helps establish a uniformization theorem for certain types of CAT(k) surfaces with specific boundary properties. Additionally, the harmonic branched extensions and their orders can also be used to compute the mean curvature flux and the mean curvature structure of immersed surfaces in three-dimensional Euclidean space. This is particularly demonstrated in the case of surfaces that are conformally embedded in the Riemann sphere. As an example of its application, the theorem can be used to show that a specific type of surface with a boundary consisting of three distinct circles cannot have a conformal embedding into the Riemann sphere. However, the question of the validity of the theorem in the case of surfaces with boundary in negatively curved spaces such as hyperbolic parabolic bundles and their associated coverages remains open. The order of harmonic branched extensions is utilized as an index-theoretic invariant in the author's subsequent work. Over the last few years, RDF has become the standard data format for diverse knowledge graphs and Big Data applications. However, widely used relational databases still contain valuable information not easily accessible in RDF format. Since converting data from one type to another is a complex and computationally intensive process, developers seek tools to streamline this process, particularly when converting complex relational data to RDF. Recently introduced Shape Expression frameworks provide guidance on structuring RDF data, making shape-expressed RDF a valuable target for various applications. In our study, we evaluate multiple tools for converting complex relational data into shape-expressed RDF, assessing their performance, accuracy, and adaptability in real-world applications. Our research reveals that none of the tested tools can efficiently process large relational databases containing up to 1 million triples with high accuracy. As current tools face limitations in RDF relational conversions, our analysis provides valuable insights for future development and improvement. In response to these findings, we also introduce Rel2RDF, an innovative solution designed to convert complex relational data into shape-expressed RDF, achieving a 30-minute processing time for databases with up to 1 million triples. By comparing their results and providing practical recommendations, our research offers valuable insights that can contribute to the creation of improved tools for big data applications. Our research has been thoroughly validated in experiments and is now available to the public as an open-source project.
