Among these, 17 were selected for more precise observations. The effective temperature, surface brightness, and reddening of these stars were calculated using independent methods. The resulting values showed that all of these stars have very similar temperatures and surface brightness levels but different levels of reddening. The Be-type stars' properties were compared with those of isolated stars and found to have lower temperatures and reddening levels but similar surface brightness levels. The predicted luminosities, masses, and evolutionary stages of these stars were also calculated. The cluster's parameters were estimated based on the 30 Doradne stars' data. To apply machine learning algorithms in text analysis, it's necessary to standardize text formats such as sentence splitting and title case use. While data augmentation can simplify this process, its practical application in text is complicated by the varied distribution of sentences. As a result, inverse text augmentation has emerged as a proposed method, but it hasn't been effectively utilized. Our research focuses on developing data augmentation techniques tailored to the specific needs of text standardization. We employed two machine learning models, including a transformer and a BERT model, to our approach. In our experiment, we examined the effectiveness of our method by comparing the results with existing inverse text augmentation methods. Our experiment covered three types of text standardization - sentence splitting, title case use, and word capitalization. Our experiment showed that our method performed better than existing methods in two out of three tasks and performed similarly to existing methods in the third task. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/sudharshan5/ITA_Daemon. Additionally, we demonstrated the beneficial effect of our method on downstream text analysis tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis. In particular, it led to a significant improvement of 4 and 6 points in F1 score in text classification and sentiment analysis respectively when applied to existing models. Therefore, it showcases the potential of our method to enhance the performance of machine learning models in text domain. Our qualitative analysis of our method also revealed that our models produced title case predictions that aligned more closely with human standards of grammar and syntax. Also our capitalization model learned to capitalize proper nouns and disregarding the case of other words, therefore performing better than existing methods. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/sudharshan5/ITA_Daemon. Although our method was found to be successful in text standardization and enhancement of downstream text analysis models, it didn't completely eliminate the errors made by existing models. Therefore further improvements are needed to fully correct the errors made by existing models. One such potential improvement could be the effective integration of rules of grammar and syntax in our method to further enhance its performance and accuracy. Our paper was accepted at WkspAI'22. This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs. Additionally, related inequalities involving 
isoperimetric quantities are explored. 

Let $\mathbb{H}^{n}$ be Euclidean space and consider the first eigenvalue 
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{H}^{n})$ of the Robin Hermite operator with boundary condition 
$\beta$, defined as the solution to

$\lambda_1(\mathbb{H}^{n}) = \sup \left\{ \int_{\mathbb{H}^{n}} (1 -
\Delta_{\mathbb{H}^{n}} u) \left( |u|^2 \mathrm{d} x \right) ^2 \mathrm{d} x :
u \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb{H}^{n}), \mathcal{R}(u, x) \equiv \beta \right\}.$

We show that for $0 < r < \infty$, and $R > 0$, the ball $B^{\mathbb{H}^{n}}(r)$ 
is an isoperimetric set for the first eigenvalue when subject to Robin boundary 
conditions if and only if the following condition is met:

$\frac{r}{R} \leq \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi e \left( 1 + \frac{\sqrt{n}}{R}
\right) ^2 \left( 1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{2} \pi^{1/2} n^{1/2} R} \right) ^2 }}.$ 

Furthermore, when subject to Robin boundary conditions, we establish that a 
half-space (the positive half of the $x_n$-axis in $\mathbb{H}^{n}$) is 
the solution to an isoperimetric problem, and we investigate the conditions 
under which equality holds in the Isoperimetric Inequality. 

The results we present can be seen as an extension and generalization of 
previous results, and our method of proof is entirely different from the 
existing ones.

We introduce a novel framework, capable of handling non-exchangeable random variables generated by normalizing flows, allowing us to train and test on independent, non-identically distributed samples. Our proposed framework subsumes both real-valued functions and energy-based models within a unified structure and provides a versatile learning approach. We apply this framework to various complex datasets and show significant improvements. Our findings indicate that models immune to exponential tails are particularly beneficial for datasets with subexponential noise or outliers. We also investigate the implications of our approach on minimizing the Wasserstein-1 distance between different distributions. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in several real-world scenarios, encompassing image generation, 3D reconstruction, and colorization tasks. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations among particles remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that intracavity electron-electron interactions and other forms of correlations significantly impact non-Hermitian topological systems. We examine a one-dimensional chain of intracavity quantum dots connected by the tunneling amplitude J and coupled to fermionic baths in a non-Hermitian setting. Using the numerical perturbation method for attractively interacting fermions, we establish a correlated topological phase structure for attractively interacting fermions in the presence of a non-Hermitian environment. Notably, we uncover an extensive topological phase structure that extends across all non-zero tunneling amplitudes J, in contrast to the Hermitian single-channel case where correlations led to phase reduction. Furthermore, we investigate the dynamics of topological current in the system and reveal that correlations can trigger counterintuitive time-reversal violation. Our research reveals that correlations can enrich non-Hermitian topological systems and contribute to a comprehensive understanding of topological phenomena in these systems. The origin of this phenomenon can be explored through a two-channel model with attractively interacting fermions. Please see the related paper for more details. Previous studies have shown that characteristics of synthetic speech, such as vocal traits, can influence human perceptions of a speaker's personality, yet investigations into their combined effect are rare in the field. This study examines the impact of integrating social speaker traits on perceived comfort levels, as opposed to focusing on individual traits. To achieve this, a vocal attribute modulation system was developed and an online study was conducted, presenting participants with a variety of vocal characteristics and trait combinations. Results indicate that high-similarity vocal traits can enhance user comfort, especially when combined with attributes of warmth, friendliness, and playfulness. Conversely, dissimilar vocal characteristics can slightly decrease comfort. Moreover, certain combinations of social speaker traits and attributes can lead to enhanced comfort, exemplified by a combination of a warm and playful voice. Results also reveal a minor decline in comfort with certain combinations, such as a combination of a warm and pleasant voice. Results suggest that the interpretation of social speaker traits and vocal attributes is complex and robust, and that their integration poses a challenge in the field of synthetic speech. Ultimately, this study contributes to understanding the combined effect of social speaker traits and vocal attributes and provides insight into developing more nuanced synthetic voices that reflect a speaker's unique personality. Results of this study suggest various avenues for future research to create voices that accurately reflect a speaker's personality and traits. Firstly, differentiating between attributes and social speaker traits is vital in creating a distinct voice. For instance, attributes like playfulness can be characterized by significant, dynamic vocal changes, in contrast, a warm voice could be characterized by subtle, gentle nuances. Additionally, developing voices that combine multiple traits and attributes in a more nuanced manner can lead to a more detailed representation, such as crafting a voice that is both warm and playful but distinct from a voice that is only warm. Finally, developing a more extensive set of voices that accurately represent a speaker's personality could lead to a more remarkable synthetic speech experience. Comprehensive online studies that incorporate various trait combinations and attribute combinations could help scientists better understand the complex relationship between these factors and human perceptions, ultimately advancing the development of synthetic voices that reflect a speaker's unique personality. Significant alterations in land usage and environmental conditions can be detected using high-resolution hyperspectral imaging, which utilizes various spectral frequencies to reveal intricate environmental changes. Two key benefits of this imaging technique include its capacity for accurate object identification and detailed tissue analysis. As a result, numerous researchers have been leveraging hyperspectral imaging to great effect. Notably, many previous studies have relied on supervised methods to identify alterations within images, requiring vast datasets annotated by experts. However, this limitation greatly impedes practical applications. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative framework that relies on a novel combination of deep convolutional autoencoders. Our approach can learn alteration feature detection without relying on extensive annotated datasets, utilizing a dual network architecture that combines pixel-wise and image-level supervision. Our experimental findings demonstrate the efficacy of this method in detecting alterations across diverse datasets. Moreover, due to its end-to-end design, our approach allows for seamless generalization to new datasets, even those with various dimensions. Finally, we have made our source code available to the public, facilitating future research and development. Our paper showcases its usability via a live demo. Overall, our approach has far-reaching implications for multiple fields. We analyze the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in model potentials and their corresponding atomic and molecular counterparts. Specifically, using pairs of pairwise and supercell simulation results, we compute viscosities and residual entropies for 11 different gases and liquid phases. These residual entropies are then used to predict viscosities across various temperatures and pressures through Hildebrand's equation. We find that this predictive approach is generally accurate for pure gases but produces less reliable estimates for liquid phases. A comparison with visitation entropy, which accounts for all possible molecular visitation sites, reveals that visitation entropy offers improved predictions for liquid phases. This study provides insight into the efficacy and limitations of Hildebrand's equation for predicting viscosities in materials science and chemistry. Moreover, it sheds light on the connections and differences between entropy-based and viscosity models, especially the relationship between configurational entropy and supercell-derived viscosity. Ultimately, this research points to the potential of Hildebrand's equation as a practical tool for obtaining reliable viscosities across various matter states through the use of molecular models. Our model combines the Lambda Cold Dark Matter cosmogony with a cyclic universe theory, incorporating an inverse tangent function to describe the universe's evolution in a cycle where the scale factor periodically approaches and is repelled from 1. The proposed equation of state, with values ranging from -1 to 1, indicates that dark energy is not constant, with its possible emergence only after the scale factor exceeds 1. We've determined that matter dominates both dark energy and radiation, with both dark energy and the universe exhibiting similar energy densities, when the scale factor exceeds approximately 0.8. Furthermore, we've found that dark energy density reaches a maximum at a scale factor exceeding approximately 1.05. The scale factor then repels towards 1, with all matter having disappeared when the scale factor exceeds approximately 1.2, until it minimizes at a scale factor exceeding approximately 0.8 again. This cycle repeats indefinitely, with our analysis focusing on the behavior of the scale factor, dark energy density, and deceleration parameter within a single cycle. We've also determined that our model's deceleration parameter minimizes at a scale factor exceeding approximately 0.8 and maximizes at a scale factor exceeding approximately 1. Cycles of the universe, characterized by growing values of Lambda, become less frequent over time, resulting in less frequent occurrences of the scale factor exceeding 1. We've also found that our model differs from the standard Lambda Cold Dark Matter cosmogony in that its deceleration parameter never reaches zero and its deceleration parameters' signs match those of matter when the scale factor exceeds approximately 1. Consequently, our model suggests that Lambda is not a constant. The results of our model match real-time LIGO observations of gravitational waves, and we've calculated a universe age of approximately 8 times 10^11 years. Given an estimated number of cycles constituting the universe, we've found that its age constitutes approximately the 8th cycle and the universe is approximately 1.04 times 10^11 years old. Analyzing Big Bang theory data, we've estimated that our universe constitutes approximately the 3rd cycle and the universe is approximately 2.67 times 10^11 years old. Analyzing another set of estimated data, we've found that our universe constitutes approximately the 4th cycle and the universe is approximately 3.33 times 10^11 years old. We also provide an alternate explanation for why there has been no observed radiation excess in the real-time cosmic background

This work focuses on pure gauge fields in two dimensions, which are naturally lacking in local degree of freedom. We aim to demonstrate that 2D fermions in such a pure gauge field environment exhibit a critical point characterized by an infinite number of degenerate vacuum states, thereby distinguishing it from the case of interacting bosons in a dimer arrangement. In various fields, including medical science, DNA research, and radiotherapy, data is often collected in categorical forms known as nominal data. Many studies have focused on developing techniques for analyzing high-dimensional categorical data. This paper aims to achieve two objectives. Firstly, it examines the statistical performance of the Group Lasso model in a high-dimensional setting and establishes joint asymptotic results for the model's coefficients. Secondly, the paper proposes an enhanced Group Lasso method called SpGroup Lasso, incorporating an innovative substitution technique for evaluating the Lasso term. The research demonstrates that the new approach, SpGroup Lasso, yields superior outcomes in comparison to the original Group Lasso method and competing enhanced Lasso methods. The between-group methods, particularly Group Lasso and SpGroup Lasso, are shown to exhibit favorable performance across 100 simulated trials. The method's efficacy is further evaluated using real-world datasets, specifically in a study examining the effect of radiotherapy on local tumour recurrence. The between-group methods proved effective here as well. The method can be accessed through the author's personal GitHub account. When two equal groups, each with its own oscillatory system, are coupled, a special type of synchronization known as chimeric synchronization can occur. The oscillations within each group are randomly dispersed but uniform across each group. This study examines how various parameters affect this type of synchronization in two different scenarios. Firstly, as the strength of the within-group connections change while keeping the inter-group connections weak, a complex pattern of chimeric synchronization occurs. As the strength of the inter-group connections increase, this pattern shifts and eventually changes into complete synchronization, unless a specific parameter known as the bifurcation parameter varies in a particular way. Secondly, when the within-group connections are extremely strong and uniform, chimeric synchronization can occur in a completely different manner, requiring relatively weaker inter-group connections, and can also transition into complete synchronization in a similar manner to the previous scenario. Chimeric synchronization is known to offer various benefits, including improved network stability and resilience, and can be found in numerous applications across various fields including biology, medicine and neuroscience. This study may lead to the development of new methods for controlling complex oscillations and could have implications for understanding complex systems in biology. This study aims to lay the foundation for further research into chimeric synchronization and its application in biology, physics and medicine. It examines the phase transitions and states of chimeric synchronization that occur as the strength of the within and between groups of coupled units change. This study considers the possibility of controlling chimeric synchronization by manipulating the within and between groups of coupled units and may lead to new therapies for diseases that result from oscillations, including epilepsy. It examines the related concept of partial synchronization, including anti-phase and in-phase synchronization, and demonstrates that these phenomena may be used to control chimeric synchronization in the future. Automated learning and control techniques have become the preferred choice for controller design due to their potential to overcome traditional pitfalls, such as the requirement for human expertise. Despite post-design resilience being a critical concern for already-deployed systems, it has received relatively little attention in the literature. This study focuses on developing a controller that can adapt to internal and external disruptions after deployment, using model-based policy search methods. We introduce a search direction calculation technique that leverages stochastic models and temporal logic specifications. This approach aims to discover control strategies that maintain performance and satisfy specification requirements under various disturbance scenarios. We derive the direction using a reinforcement learning-based evaluation of model reachability, which can be computed from high-level logical formulas via existing reduction methods. We apply this technique to a web application's controller, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding robust and resilient control strategies through model-based policy search. Moreover, we showcase the controller's ability to successfully operate the application even in the presence of unforeseen external disruptions. Although this technique is presented in the context of temporal logic specifications, it is essential to note that other types of performance measures, such as mean square error or receding horizon optimizers, could potentially be used in its place. Additionally, our proposed method has been validated using actual model code for the web application, as well as through a model checking and verification approach with the use of Z3 solver for analyzing specification constraints and reachability. Both of these were found to be effective methods for our introduced problem. We suggest that both of these can be used depending on the type of problem, programming model, and performance metrics used. We further extend this technique to account for parameter uncertainty in addition to external disruptions. We also recognize that one of the main challenges for policy search methods is the requirement for an initial viable control strategy before search. To overcome this limitation for already-deployed systems, we provide a method for synthesizing a parameter-free temporal logic controller using model checking. This allows the generation of a controller from any stochastic model, without requiring any system knowledge or human intervention. We test the effectiveness of these techniques on the web application, demonstrating their ability to tolerate parameter uncertainty and disruptions. We also compare their performance with other controller synthesis methods. In summary, we have introduced a model-based policy search approach for designing and adapting controllers that can overcome internal and external disruptions after deployment. We have also provided an efficient technique for synthesizing temporal logic controllers from high-level specifications, using model reachability and reinforcement learning-based evaluation of model reachability. We have applied these methods to a web application

The choice of Refracted Entropy is motivated by its compatibility with the convex sum property and its ability to characterize chaotic behaviors in random tensor programs. The relationship we observe holds true even in the presence of infinite interaction distance and, statistically speaking, remains valid for any number of tensor layers. Furthermore, our findings align with the underlying physics of 1D holographic tensor networks, suggesting that Refracted Entropy serves as a reliable indicator of chaos in random tensor programs. The refinement of Refracted Entropy enables us to pinpoint the threshold for quantum computational complexity in tensor networks. The entropy growth rate, for instance, remains linear in the interaction distance for the Haar optimized holographic tensor network, indicating a quantum algorithm's potential for speedup, whereas the maximum violation of the sum rule in tripartite Refracted Entropy indicates the onset of classical associativity chaos, which occurs at a higher interaction distance than the maximum violation of the tripartite area principle and, in certain scenarios, the halting problem. Our numerical investigations suggest that achieving optimal algorithms and efficient computations in complex tensor programs may require a delicate balance between chaos and order. The structure of this matrix can potentially be utilized to develop new algorithms and computational tools that exceed the limitations of the quantum computational complexity as initially defined by the tensor networks. The work presented here marks a significant advancement in the study of quantum complexity and may have significant implications for future research in quantum computing and related numerical algorithms. Structural Neural Networks have garnered interest for their ability to represent complex hierarchical relationships within data. However, existing implementations have primarily focused on static data environments, neglecting the potential benefits of adapting to changing conditions over time. In order to develop an adaptable framework capable of ongoing learning and handling dynamic data patterns, we propose introducing multiple smallest receptive fields early in the network to facilitate detection of evolving temporal and spatial patterns. The main body of the network can then explore and identify more complex features based on the insights gathered from smaller receptive fields, while an adjustable part allows for seamless incorporation of new features or insights in real-time. We demonstrate through experiments on both artificial and real-world ensemble forecasting problems that our approach, named NEO-ensemble, effectively enhances ensemble performance throughout an online ongoing learning process. The associated code is available online for public access at https://github.com/haidget/neo_ensemble. With this advanced neural structure, we aim to provide a fundamental model that can be broadly applied in various online learning scenarios. The findings of this study can contribute to the advancement of structural neural networks capable of adapting to changing conditions over time. Furthermore, we present a novel method known as Moving Averager Ensemble (MAE) that aims to improve the accuracy of real-world ensemble forecasting models, while comparing it with the state-of-the-art method, Mean Averager Ensemble. Through MAE, we achieve significant enhancements in prediction accuracy for wind speed, with minimal decrease in computation due to the simplicity of the added GAN component. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) employs a sophisticated trigger system that reduces the data processing load in the CERN's Experiment 0 area, prioritizing only the most relevant events for in-depth analysis by complex computing systems and digital facilities. Among these computing systems and facilities, the CMS SiPixel Detector utilizes advanced readout methods and precise calculation algorithms for determining the location of silicon sensor edges during system commissioning at CERN's LHC. This paper details the development and validation of a novel algorithm, known as Pixel Pilot Edge Algo, for calculating pixel sensor edge positions. It also includes the evaluation of the chosen algorithm based on data derived from the CMS SiPixel Detector during Type-C, Type-E, and Type-H module readings recorded across 18 planes from four different modules spanning five different rings. Furthermore, a comparison of the chosen algorithm's results against those obtained from Type-C module edge finds using the Mean Current method is provided using Type-C, Type-E, and Type-H find data. In addition, the chosen algorithm's parameter values were examined for consistency across different modules. Ultimately, the chosen algorithm was shown to produce reliable and precise calculated edge positions, with most reading noise spires positioned near sensor edges, across all investigated modules. It is worth noting that although this algorithm was initially developed and tested with edge positions from pilot modules, it is anticipated that similar algorithms could be applied to full-clustering methods for calculating pixel sensor edge positions in the CMS SiPixel Detector. This algorithm could potentially be adopted for calendar year 2021.

This study introduces a novel learning method, employing complex numbers as its core operation, for complex-valued deep learning. Our approach is motivated by the finding that learning complex-weighted neural networks can be transformed into the equivalent task of learning four real-valued neural networks. However, the standard complex-to-real coordinate transformation is susceptible to catabasis (neural network degeneration), which necessitates an alternative coordinate system to prevent it. A new domain equality theorem is formulated and proven, providing insights into the optimal coordinate system. The results show that the proposed method, using the optimal coordinate system, can alleviate catabasis and yield superior performance. Experimental validation on multiple datasets supports the effectiveness of this approach. Compared to the standard method, it can achieve a significant reduction of $3.5\%$ in test accuracy decline and $5.0\%$ in training loss increase on the specific dataset 'cnn_3' of the CSDL. Additionally, it can achieve performance gains of up to $7.0\%$ in test accuracy and $10.0\%$ in training loss improvement in the best-performing neural network from the CSDL. This method is applicable to a wide range of applications, as demonstrated by its successful adaptation in the fields of image processing and data classification. The proposed clustering approach uses the Pleplet metric to measure the density of case data and apply clustering techniques to detect genuine outbreaks. Through simulation tests and case studies involving COVID-19 data in Scotland, we have validated the effectiveness and applicability of this method. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map analysis suffers from a data reduction effect denoted by $x$, which is due to the loss of one degree of freedom when creating circular maps and considering azimuth and polar angles. This effect causes subtle, but highly correlated artifacts in CMB maps, specifically around map origins, which have been misinterpreted as residual dust or Planck Noise Level (PNIL) residuals in previous studies. To eliminate this effect in CMB maps, we investigate two practical methods. Firstly, we explore the consequences of suppressing the $x$ term in the azimuth and polar angle expansion, similar to the approach used by Bicep/Keck. Secondly, we develop a technique of shifting the origin of the maps by piecing together adjacent quarters, which does not alter map two-dimensional power spectra. Through simulations and practical application, we assess the efficacy of these methods in removing the data reduction effect and assess the remaining achievable accuracy in CMB sky polarization data restoration, achieved through these techniques. Although these techniques do not restore perfect noise level correlation properties in CMB maps, they successfully remove or greatly diminish several identifiable $x$-induced anomalies and enhance CMB map usability in deep polarization data sets such as BICEP/Keck 150. This includes the restoration of plausible gradient variations in signal bias across CMB map radial directions, which can further contribute to CMB map signal graduation verification and potential gradient-induced spatial dipole removal. Overall, applying these techniques allows for the creation of CMB maps that are susceptible to gradualization and dipole removal processes. Additionally, under assumption of white noise across CMB map quadrants, the origin shift technique preserves natural gradient variation properties, thus allowing for the creation of CMB maps that are independent of external factors, in addition to restoring the correct CMB map pixelization effect and power spectrum dominance. This originates from the statistical character of CMB map quadratic power spectra generated by unrelated statistical $E$- and $B$-mode noise factors. Utilizing these techniques may facilitate the successful extraction of CMB principle angle or rotation angle across CMB map quadrants, a crucial factor for assessing non-Gibbs rotations effectiveness, e.g. $E$-mode enhancement, across CMB map datasets such as Planck, BICEP/Keck 150 or Planck/MILCA. This could also involve quantitative estimation of remaining non-Gibbs effects and noise levels across CMB map quadrants, a crucial step for assessing deep polarization CMB team achievements in noise

In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, supervisors typically demonstrate optimal actions in response to specific targets or accomplishments, with the goal of training an agent to replicate these policies. This learning process is complicated when multiple targets or actions share the same description, a problem known as referential ambiguity. This paper's primary contribution is the design of a supervisor protocol and efficient learning algorithms capable of overcoming referential ambiguity. We develop natural language indices to track the progression of learning and incorporate distributional reward functions that condition the agent's policies based on multiple distinct outcomes. Our experiments confirm that the proposed methods can indeed learn versatile policies when referential ambiguity exists. Compared to existing protocols, our approach is characterized by increased data efficiency and more robust performance in practical settings. We validate these results through a range of empirical studies, including a series of practical tasks drawn from the game of chess. Additional information, including open-source code and supplementary materials, is available online at https://sites.google.com/view/ldl-projects/cspolicy. An extended version of this research is also published on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05257. Moreover, a related demonstration is featured at https://dl.allenai.org/cscrl.

We develop a novel shadow, or state-independent, approach to tomography for quantum channels. This method does not rely on knowledge of the channel's characteristic operator. By analyzing input and output measurements from a quantum channel, we can determine its effectual representation on an operator level. This effective operator serves as the channel's representation. Furthermore, we derive bounds on the error in this effective representation based on the channel's trace distance and demonstrate its applicability to specific quantum channels, such as unital channels and Pauli channels. Notably, we show that precise effective representations can be achieved for these channels with significantly reduced measurements, namely, $O(N^2)$ rather than $O(N^3)$ for unital channels and $O(9/2k^2)$ for Pauli channels, where $N$ is the system size. This represents a substantial improvement in both sample complexity and classical processing. Additionally, we employ the shadow formalism to describe a new method for determining a full CPMP channel representation through post-selecting measurements, where we define a specific set of optimal measurement operators. We illustrate, however, that this optimal scheme is difficult to implement, so we instead propose a more practical, less efficient (but easier to execute) scheme for obtaining a CPMP representation. We conclude by applying our developed techniques to the specific case of a quantum depolarizing channel. Furthermore, we provide bounds on representativity and error of effectual operators for general quantum channels. Fixed-time periodic missions for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) necessitate completion within a predetermined timeframe. This research investigates how to plan the UAV's path to accomplish these missions in the most expedient manner while maintaining the highest level of route efficiency. To achieve this, we propose an algorithm that integrates the generation of trajectories and velocity profiles. This approach is based on a two-layer model comprising an outer layer for route efficiency and an inner layer for velocity. The inner layer employs a linear controller to regulate the desired velocity, and both algorithms have been proven to converge asymptotically in a multi-agent scenario to an optimal trajectory and velocity profile. Furthermore, a simulation is presented to demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency and convergence to the optimal velocity and route. This research utilizes the direct transcription method, a non-convex technique to formulate the optimization as a non-convex problem with the advantage of easily transferring the algorithm from one scenario to another and accommodating various constraints as required. The advantage of this approach is the simplicity of implementation and the ability to obtain a feasible solution at a minimal computational cost. The algorithm is shown in simulation to easily adapt to different scenarios with a minimal increase in the computational cost. This research is published in a paper titled 'UAV path optimization using velocity limitations and efficient route models'. Through a renormalization group analysis, the interaction between layers in bilayer graphene is investigated with both intralayer and interlayer couplings undergoing critical examination. Starting with the weak coupling regime and expanding to strong coupling by utilizing an interacting Schrödinger equation, the renormalization group method allows for the calculation of interaction strength. It is found that the interlayer coupling runs to infinity, causing the system to transition into the strong coupling regime. Once within this regime, further application of the renormalization group method reveals the subdominant correction to interaction strength exhibits divergent behavior at a specific critical point. Beyond this critical point, the system experiences an increase in correction, indicating a strong-layer density variation in the strong coupling regime. Consequently, the system can be considered in a state of quantum instability. Moreover, the system possesses a sequence of Landau parameters, enabling the transition from a state of quantum instability to a state of conventional instability. We have also established a generalization of these findings, applicable to multilayer graphene with an arbitrary number of layers. Furthermore, the system shows resemblance to the properties of the Hubbard model when layers interact in a parallel fashion, and it is also similar to the Coulomb collapse of one-dimensional systems, albeit with an interaction strength of a different nature. A significant difference between this system and traditional instabilities lies in the presence of N symmetries where N represents the number of layers in the graphene structure. Consequently, the system anticipates a significant transition from a state of density variation to superfluidity upon reaching the critical point. However, the possibility of achieving superfluidity in this system is hindered by the parallel interaction and one-dimensional nature of layer interactions. Consequently, the system anticipates a transition into a state of quasi one-dimensional Coulomb collapse in the strong coupling regime and is devoid of superfluidity. A new concept of quasi one-dimensional Coulomb collapse is introduced in this system and it is notable for being stable against density variations. Furthermore, it is observed that the system can be transitioned into a state of charge density waves where the charge density is perpendicular to the layers and exhibits a periodicity of π. Upon reaching the critical point of the renormalization group method, the system shows resemblance to the collective excitations of charge density waves. In addition to these findings, the system also exhibits a state of quasi one-dimensional 1D state of Coulomb collapse where the density of layers is strongly coupled and is devoid of quasi two-dimensional character. The next phase of the Internet is focused on incorporating the Internet of Things (IoT), which equates to constructing a vast network of low energy devices. In order to construct this network, we must use efficient cryptographic methods that require minimal computations and energy consumption. In this research, we will introduce Nid, a lightweight encryption protocol designed for devices with low energy capabilities, utilizing a state-of-the-art tool to evaluate and compare its security and energy efficiency against established protocols like AES and lightweight alternatives like LightHash. The results indicate that Nid surpasses its counterparts in efficiency while maintaining robust security properties. Due to its strong security properties along with efficient computational and energy footprints, Nid is ideally suited for application in secure IoT environments. The implementation source codes of Nid and LightHash have been made available to ensure reproducibility of results and to facilitate adoption of the protocol in low energy devices. Performance metrics reveal that Nid consumes 35% fewer resources than LightHash and enables the use of both faster and more power-efficient hardware and software implementations. The research contributes towards building secure IoT systems through novel cryptographic methods like Nid that are both secure and energy efficient. The study also highlights crucial factors that impact security and energy efficiency across different IoT platforms and reveals critical performance metrics that should be considered during design to ensure trustworthy design of IoT systems. The result of this research aims to motivate the community to develop secure IoT systems through novel cryptographic methods like Nid that are both secure and energy efficient. A novel statistical model is introduced, enabling the formulation of adaptive Bayesian trials in Ramsey interferometry experiments. This research develops a Bayesian approach to infer the average length of carbon-13 spins in paraffin wax samples provided by a manufacturer. Following a preliminary analysis, each sample is analyzed under Ramsey conditions, with a Bayesian inference method choosing the optimal sequence parameters, such as phase advancement, $\Delta$, for detection and/or frequency measurement. A key aspect of this research involves establishing a likelihood function capable of describing complex spin-spin interactions in bulk samples, despite their non-Gaussian frequency distribution. A simulation reveals the model's potential in detecting unknown variations in its underlying frequency distribution, while a real-world application is demonstrated in measuring the average bond length of carbon-13 in paraffin wax samples against the literature value. Azimuthally symmetric solutions in the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravity (ASTG) are explored. The general equations for this theory and their relationship with Einstein's general theory of relativity are examined. Specific conditions under which the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravity and the Einstein's theory converge are identified. The constants for the ASTG are defined in terms of the Einstein's constants. The magnetic-type metric in the ASTG is derived from the Einstein's 1915 metric. The behavior of the gravitational force in the presence of a scalar gravitational potential within the ASTG is also investigated. The principles of conservation in the ASTG are discussed. An analysis of the energy spectrum in the azimuthally symmetric potential of the Schrödinger equation is provided. The behavior of a Dirac particle in a cylindrical wave guide with an azimuthally symmetric potential is also investigated. The properties of electromagnetic and electromagnetic-gravity equations in the azimuthally symmetric formalism are examined. The proposed equations are consistent with the principles of symmetry and duality. The admissibility of these equations is discussed. The relationship between gravitational and electromagnetic fields in the presence of a magnetic-type metric is investigated. The proposed theory is applicable to objects that are spherically symmetric. The presence of both gravitational and electromagnetic fields is detected in the supermassive black hole M87 through imaging and spectroscopy. A novel neural network architecture, tailored for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations, has been developed. Designed to solve both hyperbolic and parabolic equations, this method employs a step-wise approach where the neural network is trained in sequential stages. We prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution for each stage, leveraging the maximum principle to preclude ill-conditioning in the middle stages. Furthermore, extensive numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficacy and scalability of this approach. Notably, our results suggest that the optimal convergence rate is achieved when using the L2 loss function for stage-one and the adjoint operator for stage-two. We showcase this method's capability to solve the 2D and 3D heat equations with various initial and boundary conditions. Our study also investigates the impact of dimensionality on the network size and efficiency, revealing a beneficial trade-off. Finally, a demonstration is provided on how this method can be adapted for the high-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations using the CNN-RNN architecture. We found that particles are continuously ejected from the disk at all phases, with ejection rates heavily dependent on the magnetorotational parkway efficiency within the hybrid region. In our earlier study [arXiv:2109.14885], we introduced the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) as a theoretical model capable of explaining polar ejection through a disk-shaping force. We have now derived the post-Newtonian form of this theory and applied it to an analysis of the disk-shaping phenomenon. Our analysis reveals that the disk-shaping force is comprised of two distinct components - one acting in tandem with and the other opposing the gravitational force. We present a diagram illustrating the gravitational landscape of a star with 1.6 solar masses, and highlight the existence of 'funnel zones' in which orbital paths become increasingly irregular over time. Moreover, our calculations indicate that the disk-shaping phenomenon is capable of generating a disk-pressure of approximately 3.7 x 10^4 bar/m^3 and a stress of approximately 4.8 x 10^4 dyn/cm^2, thus furnishing a driving force for the maintenance of the disk's physical configuration. We have also derived the equations of motion in the post-Newtonian form and identified the disk-shaping orbital path as an elliptical orbit with a highly eccentric (e ~ 0.996) and highly inclined (theta ~ 68.5 degrees) orbital plane, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the observed polar ejection phenomenon reported in various stars. Lastly, our analysis also reveals the theoretical possibility of a novel binary formation mechanism grounded in our theoretical model. A comprehensive video illustrating the motion of a star governed by our theoretical model has been made available at the specified URL. The theoretical model is capable of producing a range of behaviors governed by the general parameter combination, with the gravitational constant (G), light speed (c), the star's mass (M), the angular velocity (omega), and the disk-shaping parameter (gamma). Furthermore, our analysis also demonstrates that the disk-shaping phenomenon is capable of generating a repulsive force, thereby preventing the star from shrinking and producing a repulsive force on small particles located close to the star. Consequently, our theoretical model offers an original and innovative explanation for the observed polar ejection phenomenon reported in various stars. Although the underlying physical mechanism remains unclear at present, we have identified a range of essential parameters required to generate the observed polar ejection phenomenon and have made a significant theoretical contribution by introducing a novel gravitational theory capable of explaining polar ejection through a disk-shaping force. In contexts where FRBs emit in optically active regions, their emission can be categorized into two types: concurrent (occurring immediately after the radio pulse) and deferred (occurring after the radio pulse). By examining data from FRBs 200216B, 200306B, and 20190207A, we used their distinctive spectral patterns to bound their concurrent and deferred optical emission in various models, including both synchrotron and inverse Compton mechanisms. Our findings reveal tight constraints on the optical emission in the synchrotron model, but leave room for significant emission in the inverse Compton mechanism. Furthermore, consistent with optical emission from FRBs, our analysis shows that for FRB 20190207A using the inverse Compton mechanism, its optical flux is sufficient to explain the observed fraction of scattered optical photons when compared to the derived brightness temperature. The analytical approach presented in this work can be expediently applied to any given FRB, but with the necessity of possibly numerically resolving the radiative transfer equation to derive the optical flux. The mean flux threshold is ultimately found to be at least 10 times higher than the observed optical flux in the specific FRBs studied. This technique has the potential to be particularly valuable in the future for analyzing a larger sample of FRBs, ultimately leading to the detection of optical emission. Lastly, our findings also reinforce the possibility that following FRBs there should be an optical "afterglow" period, and we suggest FRB 200216B could possibly be such an instance. The significance of this is that FRBs could potentially be part of distinct classes where active FRBs exhibit "bright eruption" events via the inverse Compton mechanism, and "afterglow" events via the synchrotron mechanism. The forthcoming CHIME FRB catalog is anticipated to offer adequate data to confidently establish the existence of such an "afterglow" period. The theoretical framework presented in this work encompasses not only FRBs but also other radiation-magnetized plasmas including neutron stars and blazars, highlighting novel optical emission phenomena. The present study includes a publicly accessible Julia code which can be swiftly applied to any given favorable source to derive the optical emission. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two different signature schemes, along with a separate verification process.
Our research indicates that Delegated RingCT yields approximately 10 to 30 times faster transaction processing times when transmitting multiple inputs or outputs, as compared to Standard RingCT.
In particular, Delegated RingCT excels at transactions with a high ratio of inputs to outputs, such as payment processing services, as it optimizes performance by streamlining the mixed signatures verification process through the use of one-to-one relationships and publicly disclosing the sender list while concealing the receiver information. Moreover, Delegated RingCT adopts the same differential privacy mechanism as RingCT to safeguard user anonymity, ensuring that distinct users cannot be identified from a combined transaction hash.

Efficient deployment of deep neural networks on resource-restricted devices necessitates quantization.  Network quantization condenses heavy neural networks into lighter, portable models while retaining their performance. The key challenge in quantized neural networks lies in maintaining their accuracy without significant loss after being converted from a floating-point format to an integer format with limited bit allocation. Existing techniques attempt to optimize quantized neural networks through retraining, but the cost of remaking the neural network has become a major concern during the execution stage. The objective of our paper is to address this concern by developing a pioneering optimization strategy, AskewSGD, which iteratively refines the quantized neural networks. The method is inspired by Stochastic Gradient Descent, incorporating a unique askew kernel for distinguishing direction and magnitude of gradients. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of AskewSGD in achieving improved results for self-supervised learning and retraining of quantized neural networks, yielding a significant enhancement of at least 0.495 points in CIFAR10, 2.39 points in CIFAR100, 2.15 points in ALBERT, 8.85 points in MobileNetV2, 6.24 points in ResNet50 when measured against conventional SGD on CNNSERT, allowing the creation of lighter neural networks while maintaining their accuracy. The output of AskewSGD also exhibits a notable decline in training energy consumption and memory consumption on various platforms including GPU, A64, and Mobile. The technique's efficiency has also been found to surpass traditional SGD by a factor of 5 when applied to Mobile. The effect of critical parameters, including askew factor and step size, was thoroughly investigated and explained throughly. AskewSGD showcases its superiority over cutting-edge optimizers such as SGD, LARS, ADAGRAD, ADAM, RAdam, RMGD. Our technique allows the creation of smaller quantized neural networks with lower memory requirements, thus enabling deployment on platforms with stricter resource constraints. In recent years, the need for robots that can safely interact with people has become more pronounced due to an aging global population. To effectively support healthcare and quality of life enhancements for older people, robots must be able to adapt to diverse environments and functionalities. Soft robotic technology offers a promising solution by allowing the manufacturing of highly flexible and inexpensive robots. However, these robots typically undergo a complex process from design to final product, which involves multiple materials and intricately interconnected components within the robot's structure. As a result, accurately predicting and controlling the behavior of these robots in various situations can be extremely challenging. To overcome these limitations, researchers have focused on developing advanced modeling and control techniques. Notably, incorporating AI capabilities such as machine learning and expert systems has greatly simplified the design process and interaction strategies for these robots. This review provides an in-depth analysis of the key aspects of modeling and control in soft robotics, with a particular emphasis on artificial intelligence systems and their corresponding applications. Furthermore, this paper highlights the main advantages and disadvantages of the different models and control methods mentioned in the literature, with the ultimate goal of serving as a valuable resource for researchers interested in understanding and navigating the numerous models and control approaches established to date. Ultimately, this review seeks to identify the primary obstacles and propose potential avenues for future research in modeling and control for soft robotics. One of the main hurdles is the current absence of an authoritative guide on design methods and control strategies for soft robotic systems. To address this, this review offers a comprehensive overview of the various models and control methods in the literature and provides some general recommendations and suggestions for future research in this field. Specifically, future studies could explore the development of more unified frameworks or integration of existing models, with the goal of accurately assessing and predicting the behavior of soft robotic systems across different design models and control approaches. Additionally, future studies could focus on developing expert systems that can automatically adapt to new uncharted territories, with the ultimate goal of ensuring that these robots remain safe and reliable in all situations. Or, as an example of application-driven research, future studies could focus on developing models and control strategies for specific soft robotic applications such as surgical procedures. With the ability to create a virtual replica of the robot and incorporate haptic feedback, future studies could focus on developing models and control approaches that integrate force and position feedback systems in a more holistic manner. Or, as example of technology driven research, future studies could focus on developing more sophisticated and user-friendly AI tools to assist with the design process and interaction strategies for these robots. In multi-armed bandit problems, the optimal outcome is typically determined both statistically and economically. However, in real-world applications, the interconnection of these two aspects is often complicated. Nonrandomized bandit strategies, which make decisions without probability, are typically capable of achieving economic optimality, whereas the opposite applies to randomized methods. This distinction arises from the different capacities to respond to individual arms, with randomized approaches generally granted more flexibility, and nonrandomized methods able to tailor their responses to each arm more effectively in certain scenarios. The distinction can also be seen with the incorporation of delays: whereas nonrandomized methods are able to combine delays and responses in a way that maximizes performance, randomized approaches are limited in this capacity. Diverging from the conventional non-stationary bandit model, in which each arm's state is independent, we investigated a more general model in our research. This new approach, known as the $p$-non-stationary bandit model, is characterized by arms with an independent distribution but with arm-dependent parameters. In our research, we demonstrated the existence of a nonrandomized algorithm, referred to as the 'combined-with-delay' (CwD) algorithm, which is capable of achieving optimal performance in the $p$-non-stationary bandit model. The effectiveness of the CwD algorithm relies on an explicit expression derived from the ideal speed-error curve, which is obtained via analysis of a nonrandomized speed-error cone. In our research, we incorporated geometric tools to provide sharp lower bounds for nonrandomized algorithms in models incorporating delays, while exceeding current state-of-the-art results with the derived bounds in single-machine minimize-average-latency (ML) and online-test-paper (OTP) bandit problems. The implemented methods in our research are shown to be purely deterministic, as they originate from a broader family of cactus diagrams in hyperbolic geometry, which is known to have a rich set of solutions to classic optimization problems. The research provides a theoretical link between statistical and economic optimality in bandit problems and offers a theoretical explanation for the success of the Choose-Choose algorithm, a well-known nonrandomized method, in achieving optimal performance in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the research offers a theoretical justification for the effectiveness of the rank-based nonrandomized speed-error cone in non-stationary and non-orthogonal models. Naturalistic driving studies have been found beneficial for numerous automated driving objectives, such as motion planning and decision-making. However, gathering data from cameras poses a significant challenge due to the high storage requirements. To overcome this barrier, we suggest a data reduction strategy centered around key entities like vehicles and road signs, to create situations reflecting everyday driving scenarios. Utilizing a 3-layer neural network, we apply instance segmentation to identify essential camera objects, and then use a decision filter to prioritize situations based on frequency and amplitude. A dataset comprising 42,515 minutes of driving data was collected from 26 drivers, containing 7 million frames, to test the effectiveness of our situation extraction method. As a result, we present the SceNDD dataset - a collection of non-binary situations recorded from diverse driving environments. Evaluations revealed that our dataset contains 82.5% relevant situations, with a majority (63.7%) holding high amplitude. Our research delves into how regular and avid users of the encrypted messaging app Signal understand and use PINs. We surveyed 20 enthusiastic users who utilize Signal's built-in attribute system to share PINs and discovered that, contrary to expectations, they may not entirely comprehend the purpose of these PINs. We found that while users may create PINs for aesthetic reasons, they are also uncertain about which PINs they've shared and receive. Our findings, based on qualitative user comments, reveal possible explanations for this confusion: the inherent complexity of the Signal features that facilitate PIN sharing and the need for enhanced visual cues in the user interface to facilitate discovery of shared PINs. We also observed that users who engage in Signal's community are better informed than casual users about the app's features, including PIN sharing. We offer several recommendations to improve accessibility of Signal features, including incorporating notification features and simplifying user onboarding to enhance comprehension of PINs and other similar Signal features. The recommendations were presented to Signal developers through a heuristic evaluation, drawing on human-computer interaction principles. The Signal team found them plausible and may consider implementing them. Our research contributes to our understanding of how Signal's unique features, like PIN sharing, are comprehended by users and how to support them in using these features effectively. We aim to begin a new research line in the area of end-user security, focusing on feature comprehension. We've made our study available in three languages - English and Signals supporting Spanish and Russian - to increase diversity in our research subjects. Signal developed a new feature, 'Profile Pins', in December 2020, which showcases a user's public pins without needing to click on them, which addresses some of the concerns we uncovered in our research. Unfortunately, our copy of Signal doesn't support this feature yet and we plan to further research how it affects enthusiastic and casual users once we can view PINs without needing to click on them. The feature, although improving, still requires users to click on a public account to see the shared PINs of the contact profile, which doesn't resolve our concerns about PINs discovery. The feature also makes profile attributes visible on the contact profile, which may make enthusiastic users feel uncomfortable, as a result of which some of our research subjects didn't know about the PIN sharing feature. Our research subjects didn't know about the feature either, which highlights how the feature is not effective in guiding users into using PIN sharing. The feature also doesn't provide notification when a PIN is shared, which is the second concern we identified in our research.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its Gauss-Newton extension is highly valued for optimizing performance, but it is also extremely computationally intensive. Recent innovations in neural network training, such as the inverse frequency matrix and its equivalents, offer more efficient ways to incorporate curvature. Despite their potential, these matrices are often overlooked due to simplicity from the outer layer and the lack of a comprehensive understanding. In this paper, we explore the diminished structure of the Gauss-Newton matrix and demonstrate its equivalence to a specific ViViT structure, which encompasses more complex inner layers and simpler outer layers. We show that this structure can efficiently yield an approximate Hessian or its rank-one approximation without the substantial computational costs associated with traditional methods. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence that highlighting the inner layers in ViViT can improve model performance and accuracy when compared to conventional techniques. In languages that indicate grammatical gender through noun morphology, the link between a noun's form and its gender influences how we perceive the word. This connection impacts how humans and computational models like neural networks interpret nouns, with varying effects depending on the language. We investigated how the gender indicators in Spanish and Hebrew affect the representation of nouns in the brain and through predictive models, focusing on whether these languages' distinct grammatical gender systems yield different outcomes. We found that in Spanish, but not in Hebrew, the gender indicators strongly influence the neural processing of nouns and the accuracy of predictive models. We considered several factors that might contribute to this difference: the prominent distinction between masculine and feminine forms, varied morphological forms, limited word datasets, and the complexity of noun root structures in Hebrew. Our study indicates that taking into account a language's unique grammatical gender system is crucial when designing and evaluating neural language models. We hope that our work sparks further research in this area. The code for our analysis and results can be found at https://github.com/alexandrayoo/nlgender. We discuss potential mechanisms behind the observed effects, suggesting that future research explore the cognitive and neurological underpinnings of grammatical gender in language processing. In addition, our findings motivate the development of more robust and efficient neural language models that incorporate the complexities of natural languages as they are naturally processed. Estimating the pose of individual objects within images is a complex issue,
compounded by the additional requirement to accurately predict both the object
and its orientation. Despite recent advancements that tackle pose and object
prediction simultaneously, there isn't yet a standard approach to apply various
object categories to pose estimation systems. This work explores the critical
aspects necessary to develop a system capable of predicting numerous, unseen
object classes. We introduce and release the Zero-Shot Object Pose dataset, a comprehensive set of images containing diverse objects with varying poses, along with a training dataset for independently training object and pose prediction models. By combining these models with class-specific bounding box estimates, we achieve notable zero-shot performance gains on datasets containing rare categories. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework outperforms baseline approaches in predicting poses for seen and unseen object classes on the PASCAL3D+ dataset. Predicting future traffic patterns is vital for urban cities. Yet, traffic conditions are highly irregular and often fail to adhere to assumptions made by current deep learning models. These traditional methods force pixel values into discrete categories, resulting in significant data loss. We diverge from these conventional approaches by developing a novel sparse traffic forecasting model called SpTF. This model consists of two parts: the Generator produces features by incorporating spatial correlation, while the Discriminator relies on the similarities between images to extract crucial information. Our extensive experimental findings reveal that SpTF significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. This paper presents VACA, a new model created with the purpose of learning interventional relationships in the context of causal graph learning. VACA stands out from other existing models such as PLC and structural CAUs, which can only predict based on observational data. In contrast, VACA is able to incorporate interventions into its training, allowing it to accurately model causal relationships. To demonstrate its capabilities, VACA was tested on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which confirmed its effectiveness. Notably, VACA was shown to accurately apply the causal Bayes net (CBN) algorithm by generating interventions, ultimately leading to accurate applications of the algorithm. Furthermore, VACA was utilized to create counterfactual queries, which were found to align with Causality's CGB predictions. The distribution of transient events like Fast Radio Bursts across the celestial sphere can reveal valuable information about hidden matter in the universe. Project REALTA is a project that runs in the background on the LOFAR radio telescope, constantly scanning for these intriguing phenomena. Between July 2021 and June 2022, REALTA detected 15 Fast Radio Bursts, which supported the localization of four of them. Real-time data analysis allowed REALTA to quickly identify the characteristics of the detected FRBs, including their positions, distances, and rotating radio bursts associated with pulsars. Furthermore, REALTA observed five repeating FRBs, indicating a promising potential for the project to increase its detection rate in the future. By automatically filtering out astrophysical signals and rejecting man-made noise, REALTA demonstrated its efficiency in identifying rare FRBs with minimal CPU costs. With approximately 10% of the LOFAR network's total observing time allocated to REALTA during this period, the project is expected to significantly contribute to finding more FRBs with greater frequency and efficiency. REALTA's algorithms and implementation have been successfully tested and are now ready to be used on other LOFAR stations, opening up opportunities for collaborations between institutions to share resources and maximize their detecting potential. Such partnerships will ultimately result in REALTA identifying a greater number of FRBs. REALTA is also set to be integrated into the LOFAR backend across all stations, which will further enhance its capabilities. REALTA's next stage aims to improve its technology to identify gamma-ray bursts and solar radio bursts while continuing its search for FRBs. Real-time data showing the performance of REALTA is found at https://realta.lofar.ie/real-time-data/. A full description of the project can be found at https://realta.lofar.ie/. Videos demonstrating the distribution of detected sources are found at https://realta.lofar.ie/dynamic-data/. REALTA is maintained by J.C., S.R., and C.B., and is overseered by M.J.M. Metaphotonics is a highly interdisciplinary field that explores unusual phenomena resulting from extremely long-wavelength light-matter interactions. This field focuses primarily on the detection of extremely weak light signals via superconducting detectors and highly sensitive measurement instruments. Researchers in metaphotonics are able to create innovative millimeter-scale light-matter systems, enabling the investigation of quantum mechanical principles that underpin various basic phenomena of light. Recently discovered metaphotonics advancements include temperature-independent light detection and localized demagnetization effects that have significant applications in technologies such as spintronics and nanoscale detection tools. Currently underway is a comprehensive analysis of the theoretical foundations of metaphotonics in the framework of quantum field theory, aimed at incorporating electrical current and designed to facilitate the development of a quantum computer based on millimeter-scale quantum mechanisms. Ongoing is a comparative study of the underlying principles of metaphotonics and photonic circuits, which has led to the proposal of a 'clever metaphotonics' concept as a means of boosting weak metaphotonic signals through machine learning methods. This development strategy is based on the idea of incorporating 'dirtiness' of a light wave into a light-matter system to yield a clean electrical output. This article aims to introduce the concept of 'clever metaphotonics' and showcase its capabilities in resolving metaphotonic signals into high-resolution images of superconducting band structures. The results will also be discussed in terms of their implications for the development of quantum computers based on quantum mechanisms. Furthermore, the article will explore the potential of metaphotonics to transform millimeter-scale electrical and magnetic property measurement tools into cutting-edge technologies for fundamental science research and nanotechnology applications. Finally, the article will examine the theoretical and experimental challenges in incorporating'machine intelligent metaphotonics,' an area which has promising avenues for future developments in quantum computing and nanotechnology. Key experimental and theoretical developments in this field are proposed to be presented along with an in-depth review of the existing literature. The main obstacles to incorporating metaphotonics are the need to develop light-matter systems with very weak and localized photon occupation, something currently within the scope of this field. The main challenges to incorporating machine intelligence are the need to design algorithms capable of leveraging the'medical condition' of a millimeter-scale quantum mechanical state, something that currently presents a significant obstacle to further developments in this area. The growing integration of renewable energy sources into modern power grids poses significant challenges to their operation and expansion. One major issue arises from the variability of distributed energy resources, which requires rapid geographic communication among grid managers to maintain voltage stability. Within the European grid, network operators have implemented an innovative strategy to address voltage management issues by utilizing regulated power capabilities of certain devices such as inverters and capacitors to provide localized support. To facilitate voltage control, network operators have divided the grid into smaller areas called balancing zones, enabling near-instant communication and fast-correcting mechanisms to maintain balance. To enable safe and efficient voltage management in balancing zones, over 90 frequency response services have been developed, including AFCs, which allow generators, storage systems, and other assets to provide energy within a specified geographical boundary and time frame. One of the leading AFC providers in Northern Europe is Norway's Agder Børs, a major grid operator, which has developed its own frequency response services, including AFC. This move reflects a significant step in AFCs moving from experimental to commercial application. This article draws on commercial data from Agder Børs to explore the characteristics of AFCs providing frequency regulation to maintain voltage stability. It examines the timeframes in which AFCs are most active, provides an overview of system behavior, and suggests possible adaptations to improve stability. Furthermore, the research aims to contribute valuable knowledge to the further development of AFCs by highlighting both technical and business requirements for their optimization. Similar knowledge gaps exist across the industry, and addressing them is essential for the widespread adoption of AFCs. This study is part of a larger project titled 'Stabilization Services for Voltage Stability', which is exploring frequency regulation to enhance voltage stability and discover new derivate services that can benefit grid operators, generators, and consumers, promoting more efficient energy markets. It shifts the focus from technological developments to the operational aspects of voltage management and the key characteristics of the leading commercial frequency response services. A novel approach to baryon creation is proposed within a novel quantum fragmentation concept, where a quantized fragmentation of a QCD filament takes place in a specific orientation. It is postulated that breaking the filament's chirality through the reverse process gives rise to baryons for the same reasons baryons are inherent in the Choquet-Bruhat quantized Yang-Mills theory, specifically in how initial state properties are encoded in the field's initial momenta. Utilizing this understanding, we determine the elementary units (quarks, gluons) within the broken filament and identify three fundamental constituents for baryons: three color charges, one isospin, and one spin operator. A key difference between this theory and the standard quantum fragmentation concept lies in the field's non-standard initial momenta distribution across the breaking surface, which necessitates distinct attribute allocations among the constituent quarks and gluons. We outline a potential measurement protocol for confirming the proposed model and discuss related work. Furthermore, we suggest a generalization of this concept to create various hadrons via a three-dimensional, spatial breaking process. In the study of the sun's internal rotation, helioseismology provides significant insights guided primarily by surface rotation velocity maps obtained through Doppler shift measurements. Despite their importance, widespread low-resolution mappings have overlooked important temporal changes and high-resolution observations of the sun's rotation across different latitudes. To fill this knowledge gap, this research investigates the impact of longitudinal movements near active regions on the helioseismic north-south rotation differential by using the MIT Helioseismic and Magnetic Infrared Surveyor (HMIPS) dataset. We developed a simulation-based method to evaluate travel-time observations in a linear model and found that incremental changes in average movement velocity across active regions influence travel-time measurements with coefficients that largely correlate with the corresponding coefficients in a differential rotation model. We observed that the coefficients related to movement velocities within specific latitude bands exhibit significant correlations with corresponding differential rotation values. However, the coefficients associated with active region-specific movements show weaker correlations. We found that the coefficients related to movement velocities outside active regions exhibit significant correlations with corresponding differential rotation values. To interpret these results, we analyzed the effect of longitudinal movements near active regions on the helioseismic travel-time measurements. We estimated that the contributions of movement velocities across active regions to measured north-south differential rotation are roughly half as large as those reported by Gilman, from an early study on the sun's rotation. In contrast, the coefficients related to movement velocities outside active regions exhibit negative signs, indicating an opposite effect when interpreted through the lens of differential rotation. The implications of these findings are significant, revealing that the measured north-south differential rotation may be subject to modification by movement-related terms. However, the high dimensionality of light field data hinders its efficient use in various fields, including robotics and virtual reality. To address this challenge, we suggest a new compression model that takes into account the relationships between distinct viewpoints as well as information from a pre-trained neural network that specializes in understanding images.
