Achieving cross-language information retrieval without human involvement can be challenging due to language differences. On the other hand, some cross-language retrieval tasks allow for some level of interaction, such as showcasing relevant images and asking users to rate them. In this study, we explore the potential benefits of combining both interactive and non-interactive approaches to further improve cross-language retrieval efficiency. To this end, we have created a new architecture that effectively utilizes multilingual vector representations, accompanied by an efficient algorithm for processing query-image pairs in an efficient manner. Our proposed method not only enhances retrieval efficiency but also minimizes computational requirements. Experimental outcomes have demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed strategy, as it achieves notable gains in terms of time and computation savings, with minimal loss in accuracy; these findings were validated through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, and observed using both human-based and automated evaluation methods. Lastly, we have made our method's source code available for public access.

Population health research and public health decision-making heavily rely on estimates of health outcomes in local communities. Large-scale surveys are commonly used to estimate population health, often produced in collaboration between governments and international agencies. The two primary methods for estimating population health are the empirical and design-based approaches. The growing use of administrative databases in health research has intensified the debate around the relative strengths of these methods. This debate is crucial in developing low- and middle-income nations, where estimates of health outcomes are essential for health interventions and policies. The objective of this study is to compare different estimation techniques with a focus on spatial estimation, using a sample of Canadian seniors from the 10/18 survey, the Quebec health insurance database, and combining this with a spatial weighting model. The findings suggest that the most effective approach is a two-step procedure involving a spatial post-stratification. The estimated rates were similar across different techniques but a step further showed the importance of taking into account the clustering of data. The use of secondary data for adjusting estimates was found to be unremarkable. The study's results can guide future research in estimating population health in low- and middle-income nations and contribute to the ongoing methods assessment initiated by the MEASURE Evaluation project. In this study, we present the design and implementation of a model that generates atmospheric representations and identifies spatial and temporal patterns in atmospheric perturbations. As these conditions and their changes are unique to each observation site, our tool is intended to support observers in making the necessary representations and predictions on a case-by-case basis. In this paper, we focus on characterizing the common features of atmospheric representations, regardless of the specific site being considered. These features include specific parameters and the types of functional representations used to model them. Moreover, we present examples of the distinct models that can be employed to describe different parameters and the significance of identifying the appropriate model for a given application. Lastly, we demonstrate the capability of our system to generate atmospheric representations on a large scale. These capabilities are utilized in a companion paper, which focuses on the application of these models to the specific conditions observed at the Large Binocular Telescope. A new reinforcement learning method has been developed that efficiently controls complex dynamical systems with vast state and action spaces, utilizing large graphs. This algorithm simplifies the complex control problem into smaller, manageable sub-control tasks and leverages the structure of the graph to minimize the complexity of the control tasks. The sub-control tasks are then solved using a novel extension of the off-policy matrix completion algorithm, which efficiently utilizes a dataset of sampled trajectories. The method does not require simulation environments and relies on the presence of a rich dataset or valuable side information represented as a graph. We tested this method in three practical scenarios: (1) a simplified version of the Mars Curiosity Rover's peak power trajectory for acting variables with limited authority, (2) a control signal for a simple actuator with a temperature controller, and (3) generating effective swimming motions for a highly complex underwater robot using limited actuator forces. These successful applications demonstrate the potential of this method for controlling complex systems with large, high-dimensional action and state spaces. The method's efficiency was evaluated in terms of its performance and learning efficiency. The resulting control signals obtained from this method produced the highest reward among all other sub-control tasks. Our approach significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning methods in terms of learning and efficiency. One crucial factor driving research in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is identifying why certain architectures yield better performance than others, which in turn facilitates NAS's practical application in real-world scenarios. Another key element is ensuring NAS can be carried out within a reasonable time frame. In order to address these issues, this study focuses on investigating the interference occurring when NAS experiments are concurrently conducted, and subsequently introduces methods to mitigate it. By employing design of experiments and in-depth analysis, the findings reveal that NAS' performance variability is largely attributed to architecture similarity rather than the impact of introduced interference. Moreover, the introduction of naive and random strategies appears to diminish the impact of interference on architecture search. Ultimately, the integration of noise into the NAS process enables the training of diverse models, which in turn unlocks the potential for ensemble learning and large-scale generalization. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/mind-georgetown/nas_interference. The dataset used in this study is publicly available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/1s5e0xnpwv3t3et/nas_dataset.zip. The dataset's documentation, including problem definitions and labels, is provided in https://www.dropbox.com/s/7m5c5yf6oc0wvz/nas_labels.txt. The architecture performance data, originally obtained from https://github.com/forestrs/contrastive_nas, is incorporated into the dataset. The dataset's size has been expanded through augmentation using different techniques. The purpose of this study is to shed light on the underlying principles of NAS and inspire the exploration of novel methods to mitigate the impact of introduced noise. The empirical analysis conducted here lays the groundwork for future research. The calculation of Val Acc for 3,456 different architectures, employing a 40-design and 40 train epochs, yields a noise level of 10%. Consequently, a 20-design, 20 train epochs, and 5 noise level noise search yields 98.7% Val Acc. Ultimately, a 20-design, 40 train epochs, and 50 noise level noise search yields 98.3% Val Acc. The architecture "nn_153" (formerly known as "nn152") is defined in https://www.dropbox.com/s/1667ar4gr4.ew4/nn_153.txt. The accompanying video is accessible at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6CwMiIRcS9g. The final model is currently being utilized in ongoing research at Mind-GE

Trustworthiness of a translator can be measured by the correlation between the translator's input and output, with variables adjusted for extraneous factors. A proposed Bayesian approach evaluates a translator's dependability by estimating this correlation and incorporating prior knowledge, extra validation data, or both. Theoretical foundations of this method are discussed, along with a step-by-step implementation guideline using a commonly used metric called Reliable Machine Translation Score (RMTS). Furthermore, a practical application of this method is demonstrated using a multilingual Wikipedia dataset in English, German, and Russian languages. The study showcases the effectiveness of the proposed Bayesian approach in assessing a translator's trustworthiness and how reliable the RMTS metric is in this context. Upper limits of a translator's dependability are also explored along with suggestions for more reliable evaluation methods. Moreover, a comprehensive comparison between the proposed Bayesian approach and traditional evaluation metrics highlights their differences and suggest that the Bayesian method offers more accurate and trustworthy evaluations. Implementation details of the method, including the RMTS calculation, are available at https://github.com/darpr/Dependent-Translators. Experimental findings indicate that extra validation data significantly enhances a translator's dependability evaluation, while incorporating prior knowledge remains crucial even with the presence of such data. Moreover, the experiments reveal that the RMTS score and the Bayesian approach are correlated, indicating that RMTS score may serve as a reliable proxy for assessing a translator's dependability using the proposed Bayesian method. Finally, the study reveals that human evaluations are redundant with the proposed Bayesian approach and the RMTS score, suggesting that these metrics provide sufficient insights into a translator's dependability. In summary, the proposed Bayesian method enables reliable assessment of a translator's dependability by estimating the correlation between its input and output through the RMTS score. In addition, the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach by confirming that extra validation data and prior knowledge are crucial in a translator's dependability evaluation. Moreover, the experiment findings suggest that the RMTS score and the Bayesian approach offer accurate and trustworthy evaluation of a translator's dependability. Consequently, these scores provide significant and reliable insights into a translator's trustworthiness in translating texts from one language to another. Ultimately, the proposed evaluation using the Bayesian approach enables and improves multilingual communication among people who speak different languages by identifying and verifying a translator's dependability through the RMTS score. In doing so, the proposed method facilitates and promotes the use of reliable translators in translating important contents, thereby promoting their trustworthiness

In various areas, a major concept has been the Mott or Anderson localization transition, which has been notoriously difficult to understand. A different method to approach this challenge involves examining energy absorption in systems that scatter and studying the sums of specific values related to energy absorption in different configurations. However, the utility of these methods was unclear due to inconsistent results from multiple studies. In a breakthrough, our team developed a mathematical expression describing the relationship between energy absorption sums and the critical point in scattering systems. Critically, our expression is valid for systems of any complexity and at all energy levels. By applying this approach, we were able to consistently determine the critical point in three distinct scattering systems and to derive a set of summation equations that hold across all energy levels. The equations we derived are particularly useful as they do not require a thorough comprehension of the system's dynamics or whether it is disordered or not. In fact, our ability to analyze three-dimensional systems using a technique called numerical diagonalization suggests that the principal contribution to energy absorption comes from parts of these systems that border on regions of total reflection. In the future, our expression and the equations we derived for energy absorption sums can be applied to a wide range of scattering systems, allowing us to gain a deeper, consistent understanding of the mysterious Anderson-Mott localization transition. Ultimately, our work marks significant progress in this area and brings the theoretical and experimental study of localization one step closer to a satisfying resolution. The equations we developed are not only confined to statistics on localization but can actually be applied to various fields where scattering systems are used for applications such as noise suppression, protection against interference or to discover new methods to absorb light. In order to further advance our understanding of the Anderson-Mott transition, our team suggests the study of one-dimensional systems where the theoretical and experimental investigation can be conducted in detail. Additionally, our expression and the equations we derived for energy absorption sums could be applied to other systems, such as quantum systems that use bosons or two-dimensional chiral systems. The work reported here signifies an important step in the study of quantum behavior in scattering systems and brings us closer to high-precision experimental validation of one of quantum mechanics' most elusive components. In terms of applications, our expression and the equations we derived for energy absorption sums can be utilized for systems of neutrons, electrons, light, neutrinos or generally systems involving fermions. By doing so, our work at the interfaces between physics and related fields advances the existing knowledge and pushes the theoretical and experimental limits of the study of the Anderson-Mott localization

t-SNE is a widely employed method for creating low-dimensional visualizations in high-dimensional data. Its core component is a probabilistic model that maps points within a high-dimensional Euclidean space to a lower-dimensional space. In its original form, this model assumes points follow a Gaussian distribution. In our work, we develop a version of t-SNE tailored for data that lies on or close to a hypersphere. To accomplish this, we replace the standard Gaussian distribution with a probabilistic model based on the von M\"{o}isperter distribution. Our proposed method, VMF-SNE, maintains the same computational complexity as its original counterpart. Through simulation tests and visualization experiments, we demonstrate that VMF-SNE is more effective in handling spherical data. Additionally, we apply VMF-SNE to a classification task involving hate speech detection on a highly spherical distribution of text data. Our results indicate that VMF-SNE yields significantly better performance in visualizing and classifying such data. In order to understand the impact of network instability on IoT upgrades, we carried out extensive experiments within a large mesh network. Participants, comprising conventional IoT devices, were given three choices: initiating updates through the network or relying on a backup plan. The results revealed that in cases of network instability, a significant proportion of devices (nearly 40%) were unable to successfully complete upgrades in two out of five test environments. Furthermore, we found that mesh network topology contributed to these issues more so than energy efficiency. The cause of these problems was identified as hardware limitations inherent in many low-cost IoT devices. Given the widespread presence of such devices in numerous networks, we believe our findings have considerable practical implications. Consequently, we have developed a novel adaptation of the Flappy Bird game, "Flaky Bird," to serve as a reliable upgradable application that alerts users to potential network hazards and helps in mitigating these problems. A critical aspect of this upgradability mechanism involves the "Flaky Bird's" ability to efficiently reboot the device and resume the game at the point of failure. Following thorough testing, we have proved its robustness and effectiveness through a comprehensive evaluation process. This research focuses on exploring the interaction between classical and quantum neural networks, particularly in understanding how classical adversarial examples can impact quantum-based classifiers. Colloidally assembled gels offer a simple and cost-effective alternative to synthetic materials, allowing easy modifications through external stimuli such as shear forces, electric fields, and ultrasonic vibrations.  Specifically, this study analyzes the effect of ultrasonic vibrations at varying intensities on the properties of gels formed from a suspension of silica particles in a carrier liquid and common industrial polymers.  Results indicate that increasing the vibration intensity decreases the yield stress and shear modulus of the gel, and accelerates gel collapse under gravity by nearly doubling the gelation time in a vertical environment compared to a horizontal setup.  Moreover, ultrasonic vibrations at higher intensities facilitate flow through narrow tubes, reducing flow resistance by nearly half, and enable gels to flow out of containers, unlike their static counterparts.  Yet, despite these advancements, increased vibration intensities hinder the flow characteristics of these materials, prolonging flow times through channels and increasing flow instability in response to perturbations in the channel wall.  Notably, this study provides empirical insights that can inform industrial applications, and sets the stage for optimizing industrial workflows using ultrasonic vibrations to modify gel properties and behavior.  In particular, this technology may be applied to create sophisticated biomedical devices such as sophisticated lab-on-a-chip platforms, and to develop sophisticated pharmaceutical delivery systems.  Ultimately, this study contributes to a more complete understanding of industrial materials and lays the groundwork for utilizing ultrasonic vibrations to enhance and transform gel-based materials and devices.  Additional information regarding experimental setup and testing, as well as potential industrial applications, can be found in the accompanying video supplement. Although often attributed to nonlinear scattering processes, we uncover that these patterns can arise solely from laser-induced heat distribution within the liquid. We visualize the thermal field generated by the laser within the liquid in exquisite detail, thereby accurately quantifying the time-dependent liquid refractive index. We demonstrate that these thermal and refractive index modifications can give rise to scattering patterns identical to those generated by self-induced small scattering sites. Furthermore, we devise a universal approach for calculating general $m$-order scattering patterns and apply this method to explain various previously reported scattering phenomena, including those of first, second, third and fourth order. Our findings provide a definitive explanation of higher-order scattering patterns and reveal that these are inherently produced by the interaction of laser parameters and liquid properties. These results will facilitate a deeper understanding of scattering processes in both liquids and gases, and may also shed new light on recent experiments utilizing liquid-based nonlinear scattering facilities. Utilizing our approach, researchers can effectively interpret existing experimental results and design custom scattering setups. To tackle this problem, we developed a system that frames design dialogue mining as a natural language-based conclusion drawing task. Utilizing a model trained on design discussion forums, we successfully extracted hidden design values from user conversations. Experiments revealed that our model's insights were highly consistent with human judgments, demonstrating a mere 2% difference in requirements overlap with human generated conclusions. Additionally, our model demonstrated impressive ability to generalize across various design fields, achieving successful performance on a newly introduced design dialogue mining dataset. Furthermore, our findings show that by integrating multiple design dialogue sources, our model can uncover more comprehensive design values compared to using a single source. Ultimately, we hope that through this study, we can shift design dialogue mining towards a more automated and less labor-intensive process that leverages natural language processing capabilities. The growing demands of data analysis and applications on streaming data require robust systems that can seamlessly integrate with data management systems and support the sophisticated analytics typically found in data warehouses. To address these needs, our proposed stream processing framework, H-STREAM, was designed with the capability to not only process streaming data, but also to access a fully featured data warehouse with support for complex queries, scalable data aggregation, and efficient data caching. By combining these features, H-STREAM enables users to create custom pipeline designs that cater to real-time data streaming and historical data querying across diverse scenarios such as single-signon authentication, device tracking, game statistics, cognitive computing, scientific research, and more. With its extensive feature set, H-STREAM enables users to build sophisticated query pipelines that leverage data caching for enhanced performance, while its modular architecture allows for seamless integration of new functions and query types to meet evolving data analysis needs. Furthermore, our system uses a query optimization technique to ensure that the resulting query execution plans from the combined streaming and historical data are efficient and cost-effective. Our in-depth evaluation has demonstrated the capabilities of H-STREAM through various case studies and real-world applications, showcasing its potential to build innovative data analysis solutions. As part of our research, we have made publicly available the source code of H-STREAM, which aims to inspire software systems and applications that combine streaming data and historical data querying, ultimately enabling users to build more sophisticated data solutions to address real-world challenges. The source code of our project can be found at https://github.com/byuCSSE/H-STREAM. The related database schema and data can be found at https://github.com/byuCSSE/H-STREAM-data. In recent years, SPARQL machine translation has received significant attention from researchers due to its numerous applications. A key challenge in SPARQL machine translation involves leveraging knowledge bases to enhance translation processes, particularly for languages with limited resources. Building upon this concept, researchers introduced the idea of Duplicate Mechanism in Convolutional Neural Networks to improve English-to-French SPARQL translation by utilizing analogous sentences within the dataset. Our research presents an enhanced Duplicate Mechanism designed for use in Convolutional Neural Networks and Large Convolutional Neural Networks, specifically for SPARQL tasks. We evaluate the effectiveness of our mechanism with the EREC dataset, revealing that it produces equivalent results without exacerbating the problem of duplicate data overfitting. Furthermore, we analyze the efficacy of our mechanism by investigating the characteristics of sentences that facilitate translation improvements. Through this analysis, we conclude that our mechanism successfully harvests valuable information for improving SPARQL translation from the duplicate sentences in the dataset. Additionally, we have made our code and dataset pre-processing techniques available for public use, aiming to facilitate future research. Experimental findings indicate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in SPARQL machine translation by achieving an average improvement of +3.64 or 21.53% in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. The results of our experiments are presented in Tables 7 and 8 in Section 4.2. The presented research and its code are expected to inspire future studies on SPARQL machine translation. The code can be accessed via the link provided at the end of this document. The Duplicate Mechanism's ability to leverage dataset duplicates for SPARQL machine translation serves as a model that researchers and practitioners can adapt for other machine translation tasks, promoting more efficient data utilization and accurate translation. To address this, we developed Venue Insights, a set of quantitative measures capable of capturing the collective impact of venues across different disciplines. Our framework initially calculates a set of basic metrics, including the frequency and distribution of appearances, co-occurrence, and collaborations between authors who collaborate across multiple venues. Furthermore, we employ dimensionality reduction techniques to visualize the impact of each venue. Through the application of our method to a large database of over 180 million published papers between 1950 and 2015, we present qualitative results regarding venue characteristics, encompassing a wide range of characteristics, including interdisciplinary venues, international venues, and research hotspots. To demonstrate the practical value of our approach, we show how our method can facilitate strategic decisions in research evaluation, including evaluation of individual researchers, evaluation of departmental efficiency, and evaluation of departmental comparison, ultimately leading to a more informed, evidence-based evaluation process. Moreover, by extracting semantic and topical information from the main titles of papers, we successfully illustrate the link between venue and content. Our comprehensive analysis of the data highlights the significance of research venues in influencing the overall research output and suggests the necessity for new evaluation criteria to complement existing metrics. Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in numerous complex tasks within the fields of vision and acoustic analysis, as well as in plays and games. However, its applications in control theory remain relatively unexplored. This research investigates the use of neural networks in control and addresses a key question: what underlying characteristics of a task enable its implementation using a neural network? In order to pose this question, we first define the essential elements: a neural network that maps an input to a desired output, and a measure of error between the two; and a method to validate whether a neural network control approach is equivalent to the original in a continuous-time framework. This is achieved through a new concept called Input Output Continuous ReReachability, and corresponding tools for practical use. Our study uses a simple example - neural network controllers for a linear system - to illustrate the crucial role of task specificity and the measures of error and validation. Inspired by our findings, we introduce the idea of experimenting with various input designs to validate neural network control approaches, and verify that specific network architectures can learn such inputs when trained with corresponding datasets. Finally, we consider the complexities of using neural networks to mimic complex nonlinear behaviors. Like many tasks whether in control or outside it, what something can learn is dependent on what something is taught. And what something is taught is related to but not the same as what something is validated. This is equally true for both control and outside it. For instance if you consider 'what something is taught' as driving on the left side of the road and 'what something is validated' as actually driving on the right side of the road then while many things can learn both and validate both, many tasks actually exist where either left or right validation poses significant difficulties. Further study is required to explore and establish interfaces between neural networks and control theory concepts. And this requires a major rewrite of the paper for clarity and precision. And the key to this is that while neural networks can map inputs to outputs, measures of error between neural network outputs and desired outputs are what actually validate the neural network control approach. And such error measures are not part of the neural network optimization process. And this is where deep connections between neural networks and control theory occur. And this is where further study is required. And the key to this is that while neural networks can learn task specific inputs when trained with corresponding datasets, what actually validates the neural network control approach is what actually makes the neural network control approach equivalent to the original in a continuous-time framework. And this is not the same thing as what something can learn.

Clustering is a common technique used to extract natural structures from data sets that are represented by vectors in a high-dimensional space. In this paper, we propose a functorial clustering method that is based on a functorial hierarchy, enabling us to obtain consistent results regardless of the approach used to construct the hierarchy. We also provide evidence suggesting that functorial clustering is capable of overcoming the challenges associated with overlapping substructures. We conduct rigorous analyses of the method's performance across a range of simulated and real-world data sets, demonstrating its effectiveness and benefits. The source code for this approach has been made available on the GitHub platform under the repository 'functorial-clustering'. Additionally, we contribute to the development of groupoid functor calculus by generalizing a key theorem known as the 'categorical correspondence of transport and homotopy'. This advancement has the potential to expand the scope of transport-based methods in machine learning and data clustering. Furthermore, our findings provide a mathematical framework for understanding the concept of overlap through the lens of category theory. We also discuss the connection between functorial clustering and both multilevel sets, semigroups of maps, and the k-systolic ratio. As a result of the semigroup of maps approach, we are able to develop a novel version of functorial grouping with minimal overlap restrictions. We perform evaluations using real-world data sets in the fields of chemistry and computer vision. The corresponding source code is available on the GitHub platform under the repository'semigroups-of-maps-clustering'. The primary objective of this research is to facilitate the use of mathematical ideas as inputs to deep learning networks, similar to the method employed in mathGAN. Our work highlights the potential for meaningful collaborations between mathematical theories and machine learning approaches. We also provide recommendations for future research directions. The main technical contributions of this approach can be found in a companion paper where we establish the foundation of mathematical theory, while the present paper focuses on applying this concept to develop a practical algorithm using practical examples and evaluations. We anticipate that the practical contributions outlined in this research will serve as a starting point for implementing the theoretical concepts presented in the companion paper. We encourage readers to review the companion theory by solving the practical challenges first. The source code for the practical contributions has been made available on the GitHub platform under the repository 'practical-functorial-clustering'. We gratefully acknowledge the support provided by the numerical science fellowship at the University of Geneva. We also would like to express deep gratitude to Prof. Masashi Tatsuya Saito for providing valuable suggestions

High-dimensional data like video, audio and MRI scans can be transformed into tensor-like structures and represented as streaming tensor rings when partitioned into segments. To recover damaged video, audio or MRI images, the tensor structure must be maintained. Current methods like tensor completion often require entire tensors, leading to inefficiencies in scenarios with limited data or streaming inputs. To address these limitations, a proposed solution, Patch Monitoring-based Streaming Tensor Ring Restoration, employs patch monitoring to update tensor rings and restore damaged components. By using monitoring patches and predicting errors in tensor rings, the method effectively updates and recovers damaged content. To optimize performance, various techniques such as sparse and greedy optimization for patch selection, tensor ring reconstruction and preserving critical data points along tensor rings have been employed. Moreover, the method allows parallel updates of tensor rings and incorporates optimal solutions for fixed and learnable bias adjustment. Experimental results demonstrate that the method successfully updates and recovers damaged content and even improves upon supplementary approaches by reducing reconstruction errors and increasing restoration rates. The code and detailed implementation guidelines are now available online. Our method ultimately achieves superior performance in repairing damaged content across various fields. To validate its practical applications, a series of user studies were also conducted. The method successfully improves visual content and maintains user experience and preferences in different contexts. Ultimately, the approach allows seamless streaming and preservation of high-dimensional data. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/fintech123/PSTRR. It is demonstrated that a Nichols algebra over a traditional Weyl group $W$ with rank greater than one has the same U-greedy property if and only if it is isomorphic to the classical Nichols algebra $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{K}_{\text{reg}}(W))$. Consequently, the classification of infinite series of Nichols algebras over Weyl groups of rank 5 is completed. Examples of derived Poisson structures on Weyl groups of rank 3 and 5 are given. Additionally, it is shown that the U-greedy property does not hold for the classical Nichols algebra $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{K}_{\text{reg}}(B_{6})$. Furthermore, it is found that $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{K}_{\text{reg}}(A_{3}\times A_{2}\times A_{2}))$ and $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{K}_{\text{reg}}(A_{4}))$ are simple as Leibniz algebras. We also introduce a useful tool for determining if a finite group $G$ has an easy-to-interpret character $\chi_{\rho}$ for any irreducible representation $\rho$ of $G$. This characterization enables us to identify that $A_{3}\times A_{2}\times A_{2}$ is the only example of a group with a rank 3 quadratic character that does not have the U-greedy property. Lastly, it is demonstrated that generic extensions of quadratic Lie algebras or quadratic deformation of Lie algebras cannot result in a subalgebra with the U-greedy property. Furthermore, it is observed that certain extensions or deformations yield algebras isomorphic to classical Nichols algebras or provide new examples of infinite series of Nichols algebras. We also employ similar methods to show that certain cohomology rings do not have the U-greedy property. In particular, it is discovered that generic extensions of orthogonal Lie algebras or quadratic deformation of symplectic Lie algebras cannot have the U-greedy property. In contrast, generic extensions of classical Lie algebras or Lie algebras related to classical Lie algebras do result in algebras isomorphic to classical cohomology rings or provide new examples of infinite series of cohomology rings. The last section involves the analysis of the U-greedy property for specific algebras

This research confirms the spectrum predicted by the Zakharov-Kolmogorov theory through simulations of inertial wave turbulence in rotating, contained geometric shapes. By adjusting the intensity of external forces and observing the resulting spectra, we verified the theory's validity across a range of anisotropic configurations. In addition to these findings, we noted that the ZK spectrum accurately described the spectra seen in our simulations for low-to-mid wavenumbers, while high-wavenumber spectra tended to be influenced by viscous effects, leading to a potential third kinetic energy component. Furthermore, we clarified the behavior of isotropic IG turbulence by showing that the theory's applications are somewhat restricted. These discoveries contribute to our understanding of turbulent inertial waves, and their implications are particularly important in hydrodynamic dynamics research related to rotating fluids. An accompanying video demonstrates the anisotropic distribution of energy across inertial waves in our simulated supergiant Taylor-Couette flow. By visualizing these wave behaviors, we can better comprehend the complex processes at play in rotating fluid turbulence. Anisotropic energy distributions, seen in our time-varying snapshots, are rooted in the preservation of angular momentum in rotating systems. In rotating geometries like the Taylor-Couette flow, the topological properties of the flow's supporting equations can generate such anisotropies; similarly, in vortex dynamics, these anisotropies arise from its inherent properties. It is hoped that these simulation results, supplemented by analytical models, will enhance our understanding of the intricate phenomena characterizing turbulent inertial waves. The problem of determining a graph's standardization was initially defined as finding a graph where tau star is equal to tau star prime, which has been proven to be solvable in linear time for graphs that are well-formed and have at most two sizes. By applying these principles, researchers derived equations to describe the relationships between various graphene properties and temperature. These relationships were found to be similar to those of a doped semiconductor. Furthermore, the theory's predictions about the dependence of electrical resistance on temperature align with experimental findings. The introduction also outlines the historical context and previous studies related to the thermodynamic properties of graphene. The related literature highlights inconsistencies and problematic aspects in previous theories, which motivated the development of a new thermodynamic approach for the thermodynamics of graphene. This approach considers the electron-hole system as a combined entity consisting of two interacting subsystems, which is essential for understanding the thermodynamic properties of graphene. This approach has also led to the revision of traditional semiconductor concepts, which was necessary for the thermodynamic analysis of graphene. The new thermodynamic model was derived by considering the electron and hole subsystems as interconnected components of a combined electron-hole system, which is characterized by combined parameters such as electrical conductivity, capacitance, and polarization. These combined parameters play a crucial role in the thermodynamic analysis of graphene. The models describe the relationships between various properties, such as electrical conductivity, capacitance, and dielectric permeability, in terms of temperature and chemical potential. These relationships were derived from the corresponding averages of electron and hole properties. The text also explores the thermal equations of state for the electron and hole subsystems, which demonstrate significant differences in their behavior. The theoretical models were developed for the monolayer graphene with internally generated heat sources and were applied to derive equations for the dependence of electrical resistance on temperature and chemical potential. Recent observations of the low-frequency periodic radio emissions from the binary system CR Draconis have revealed a low-frequency radio spectrum. Obtained with a low frequency radio telescope at 18 meters, the observations covered a frequency range of 10-80 MHz and lasted for about 789 days. In total, there were 83 periods of radio emission detected during the monitoring period. The radio spectra were often found single-peaked, occasionally showing a double-peaked structure. The peak frequencies varied significantly, ranging from 35 to 75 MHz in single-peaked spectra and having frequencies of 45-85 MHz in double-peaked cases. The frequency of the single-peaked spectra ranged from 10-60 MHz and the frequency separation between the peaks in double-peaked spectra ranged from 20-50 MHz. The intensity of the radio spectra varied significantly, the upper limits of which ranged from 30 to 80 Jy. The period of the radio emissions matched the orbital period of the binary system, lasting for about 3.285 days. The amplitude of the radio emissions varied, the upper limits of which ranged from 0% to 0.2% of the primary star's flux. The radio emissions were often detected during the phases of the secondary star's perihelion. Furthermore, the frequency at which the radio emissions showed a low frequency drift rate of -0.2 kHz/s. A circularly polarized emission was also detected during the monitoring period, the occurrence of which ranged from 20% to 50%. Based on the properties of the radio component, it has been suggested that it originates from incoherent electron-cyclotron maser radiation. A comparative study has revealed that in CR Draconis, the radio emissions show both distinct and similar properties in comparison to other known electron-cyclotron maser radiation sources. Ultimately, it has been suggested that the origin of the periodic radio emissions in the binary system CR Draconis involves a magnetic loop structure. The study has also highlighted that the periodic radio emissions do not affect the stellar atmosphere of the primary star. Moreover, it has been suggested that a similar magnetic loop structure may exist in other flare star binaries, the non-detection of which in CR Draconis shows that it may not have a large volume. A future observation of the radio emissions in other binaries and the low-frequency spectrum of the system is required to confirm this hypothesis. Information on the magnetic loop structure and the periodic radio emissions can provide valuable insights into the magnetic field configuration of the binary system

There is consensus among researchers that computers and humans respond differently to nuanced image changes, ranging from subtle variations in color and pattern configuration to the presence of common objects. However, the impact of drastic alterations to image content, particularly those that result in extreme and unusual contexts, remains poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the effect of intense modifications on perception and classification, focusing on images that have been heavily distorted, such as those with severed limbs or excessive text overlay. Our analysis reveals that computer vision models are consistently hindered by these changes, whereas human observers are more adaptable and capable of accurately identifying objects even in highly altered states. These observations hint at the existence of disparate visual processing strategies adopted by humans and machines. In an effort to better understand these differences, we outline potential areas for further exploration and suggest that fusion of human-machine vision, incorporating elements like human-annotated image datasets and visual explanation tools, may be key to unlocking more resilient and adaptable vision systems in the future. Our research is accompanied by publicly accessible code and the modified dataset, referred to as the ImageShock dataset, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ExplainableML-inferml/ImageShock. That repository also contains the code for the ExplainableML inferml library, which allows for the integration of human and machine vision. For related inquiries, please feel free to reach out to us at [ml.inferml@nasa.gov]. Our goal is to spark further investigation into these intriguing visual adaptation phenomena and foster collaboration between the two vision communities to ultimately develop more robust vision systems at the intersection of human and machine vision. Kerr-lens mode-locking in ultrashort-pulse lasers is evaluated using a combination of theoretical and computational approaches, including steady-state simulations and time-domain calculations. We examine the ability of a Kerr-lens mode-locking broadened Gaussian pulse to pass through an amplifier without significant loss, coupled with the time-domain behavior of the pulse as it interacts with the amplifier's gain region. We explore strategies to enhance the sustainability of Kerr-lens mode locking, including the incorporation of frequency nonlinearity and the utilization of a curved lens. We determine that frequency nonlinearity can support a higher number of transverse modes in a smaller curved lens while maintaining low loss. We also recognize that these solutions to Kerr-lens mode locking face practical limitations in actual ultrashort-pulse laser construction. We decide not to publish the associated Python code due to its complicated nature but instead encourage researchers to create their own variants as an exercise. We hope this research to contribute to the development of high-power ultrashort-pulse lasers. Using a particular parameterization of the tetration function, specifically $t(t)\to e$ as $t\to\infty$, we re-examine the primary branch of the tetration function, denoted $\to$, given the equation $t(t)^a=e^a$ with the base $a$ in the interval $[1,\infty]$ and the variable $t$ initially defined as the iterated exponential function $\to(t);a$. By changing the variable $x$ and expressing $a$ in terms of $x$, we obtain the equation $$to(x)=e^{a(x)}$$ where the function $to(x)$ is obtained by taking the tetration of the function $t(x)$, with the function $t(x)$ being the solution to the first-order ordinary differential equation $$t'''-3t^2t''+2t'=0$$ with given initial conditions $t(0)=e$, $t'(0)=0$, and $t''(0)=1$. This equation is known to be the van der Monde equation, and as a result, we obtain a particular asymptotic solution for the obtained differential equation that is equivalent to the tetration function, allowing us to find the necessary derivatives of the tetration function in a closed and convenient form. Additionally, by using the obtained solution, we are able to derive important estimates for the values of the tetration function, specifically for the values of $t$ in the interval $[0,3]$, as well as derive important inequalities for the derivatives of the tetration function, allowing us to access the information from an arbitrary number of iterations of the tetration function with the given initial values. Ultimately, the derived asymptotic solution is shown to be highly reliable, specifically for the values of $t$ in the interval $[0,3]$ or even farther from $0$ if the value of $to(x)$ is decreased. Moreover, the derived solution is shown to be highly accurate when compared to the existing methods of solving the tetration equation, specifically for the values of $t$ in the interval $[0,3]$. Interestingly, the derived solution is shown to be equivalent to the superexponential tetration function, specifically for the values of $t$ in the interval $[0,3]$. Moreover, the derived solution is shown to be highly accurate when applied to the complex numbers, specifically for the values of $t$ in the interval $[-1.5,3]$.

We present a new method of constructing high dimensional metric expander graphs, which is based on a combinatorial concept called covers. Typically, high dimensional metric expanders are constructed using hyperbolic methods. In this study, we demonstrate that certain hyperbolic structures (specifically thickened sphere covers and Cayley complex covers) can be expressed as finite bipartite subgraphs of the complete graph on a finite set, which adheres to the properties of high dimensional metric expanders. Additionally, this method allows us to establish the existence of large sets of isometric mappings between high dimensional metric expanders, which have minimal distance from the identity mapping greater than a fixed constant. The latter result has implications for coding theory and the theory of operator algebras, particularly in the study of distance problems in operator algebras. Distinct examples of high dimensional metric expanders are constructed using this new method, which differ from previously known examples based on hyperbolic structures. Moreover, one of the constructed examples achieves better bounds on high dimensional metric expanders than any previously known example based on hyperbolic structures. Finally, the study begins by introducing the concept of covers and formalisms for working with them, which has independent value in discrete geometry. Several open problems related to high dimensional metric expanders and distance problems in operator algebras are also proposed at the end of the paper. The study is supervised by Yoni Zion Ravid. Large social networks grow exponentially, enabling personal connections with billions. However, individual network sizes are often much smaller, typically ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands of nodes. Current methods for predicting links in social networks rely on graph and node embeddings but are inefficient and unsuitable for sparse networks, where a majority of nodes have no direct connections. To address this, we've developed SSNE, a computationally efficient algorithm creating node embeddings in sparse networks, leveraging their inherent structural characteristics. SSNE performs exceptionally well on various sparse network datasets and outperforms existing link prediction methods. SSNE is open-source and available on GitHub at https://github.com/djgiser/SSNE. The silicon frame establishes an extremely narrow gap - just 5.6 micrometers - between the silicon substrates, and is incredibly stable with an internal pressure of around 0.5 Pa. The deep silicon gap is ideal for applications requiring a broader cross-section for light absorption and scattering. However, the deep silicon gap is associated with some drawbacks such as reduced visibility during vision-based feedback and an increased sensitivity to minor vibrations due to the silicon thickness of 200 micrometers. Despite these limitations, the developed device showcases exceptional stability, making it an ideal choice for complex multi-component systems, deep silicon gap-based experiments, and various optical atomic physics research applications. We evaluate the susceptibility of dual-polarization 4D transmission formats to nonlinear disturbances and analyze various factors that influence this vulnerability. Notably, when connecting with a single-mode fiber, the format degradation is significantly heightened by coupling between polarization modes and the propagation of self-phase modulation-induced nonlinear impairments. To facilitate design and optimization of 4D formats, a comprehensive mathematical framework for nonlinear disturbance power is introduced, complementing an existing study that explored impulse response modeling in polarization-space. Building upon the nonlinear disturbance power concept, a method for defining effective nonlinearity coefficients is proposed and demonstrated in a case study involving coherent 4D quadruplex transmission over up to 320 km single-mode fiber. This approach enables the simultaneous optimization of various 4D formats, including quadruplex, sextuplex, and octuplex formats, to boost transmission reach. Notably, with optimized coefficients, 4D sextuplex formats can achieve comparable performance to 4D quadruplex formats with up to 80% reduced PM-XPOL interference and selectivity. Furthermore, by leveraging decoded sextuplex format data, 3D spatial data can be extracted with superior signal quality compared to that of 4D quadruplex formats. Our work facilitates the design and optimization of high-order 4D formats for diverse applications. Wildfires pose a significant threat to global ecosystems and human infrastructure, necessitating innovative image fusion methods to enhance wildfire detection and visualization. Existing techniques, such as pixel-wise methods employing convolutional neural networks, are limited by their reliance on predefined rules in the feature extraction process. As visual analysis of wildfires is crucial for emergency response and rescue operations, there is a need for a more effective procedure to improve the quality of wildfire-related visual data. To address this challenge, we propose the FIRe-GAN, a novel approach using a unique cooperative training process for infrared and visible image fusion. By merging pixel and feature mapping techniques, FIRe-GAN produces high-quality fused images, outperforming contemporary pixel-wise image fusion methods in both subjective and objective evaluations. Moreover, FIRe-GAN exhibits exceptional adaptability and can be applied to other image fusion applications. Given its open-source nature, this proposed method offers vast potential for applications in various image fusion domains. Experiments and performance metrics validate the efficacy of the FIRe-GAN approach. Further investigation is recommended to analyze the underlying causes of mode collapse, which may negatively affect the overall performance. Such an exploration could lead to improvements in the image quality, with potential extensions to other applications like medical image processing. Ultimately, the FIRe-GAN technique holds promise for future developments. The source code for the FIRe-GAN is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ihatmounir/FIRe-GAN. The dataset employed in the study can be accessed at https://github.com/ihatmounir/Not-Conventional-Visible-Infrared-Image-Fusion. This paper's primary objective is to establish a practical technique for identifying individuals likely to be struggling with depression based on their social media updates and everyday smartphone usage data. To accomplish this goal, we gathered and analyzed a dataset consisting of voluntary input from mental health professionals, comprising related social media posts and general device data such as location history and aggregated device usage statistics. Subsequently, we trained a BERT-based model using the collected social media posts to predict depression, and also developed a mobile app incorporating Android FABs to streamline data collection and further refine our model's predictions. Furthermore, we successfully deployed our model in a binary classification scenario, where press-related inputs can trigger a depression detection analysis. Notably, our results reveal that the integration of all device sensors enhances model performance above standalone social media or clinical data, yielding results comparable to existing depression screening tools. The combined analysis of social media and clinical data has the potential to yield an accuracy of 70%, significantly higher (25%) than using clinical inputs alone. Similarly, aggregating all device data contributes 8% to the accuracy score compared to solely social media updates. Ultimately, we intend for this system to provide valuable insights to mental health professionals, enabling them to make more informed decisions during therapy sessions. The model formulation mirrors typical epidemiological patterns observed during the global health crisis. Two-dimensional contour plots help highlight interplay mechanisms between transmission and mortality rates. Furthermore, our framework is extended to investigate the impact of distributed transmission and mortality rates. Additionally, we utilize our model to approximate COVID-19 data from both national and global levels, and then use the estimated parameter values to forecast COVID-19 outcomes under varying vaccination scenarios. Lastly, an uncertainty analysis is conducted to assess variability in parameters. This research provides a mathematical representation of the complex COVID-19 epidemic and sheds light on its underlying dynamics. Conversely, the growth in total cases is mainly contributed by cities with higher transmission rates. The vaccine scenarios simulated in this study all result in reduced total cases and/deaths, with the exception of the scenario involving 'no vaccine'. Moreover, our model's predictions show that the outcomes under the 'vaccine' scenario vastly outnumber those of the 'no vaccine' scenario. The software package and model offer a synergistic combination for tackling the daunting COVID-19 challenge. The descriptions and explanations provided in the software package help explain the underlying mathematical concepts of the model. A study is conducted on the dynamic behavior of systems governed by a Coulomb friction model, where the friction coefficient undergoes both exponential and power-law decay in response to an actuated motion. This research explores the long-term behavior and steady-state convergence of such a system near its desired equilibrium state. It is revealed that the exponential decay of the friction coefficient leads to system convergence, while a power-law decay with certain system parameters can result in an oscillatory "stick-slip" behavior and eventual convergence is only achievable at a singular point. The importance of understanding friction models in the design of stable control systems is also discussed. It is observed that the adoption of a Coulomb friction model may be sufficient for certain small-scale robotic applications, where the friction coefficient is linearly related to various factors including robot mass, length of articulation, and actuation force. For instance, a simplified friction model for a two-jointed robotic arm reveals that the friction coefficients are correlated with specific system parameters, allowing the formulation of a relationship that effectively replicates the behavior of a Coulomb friction model. Therefore, this study presents guidelines on how to choose Coulomb friction parameters based on system characteristics and uses numerical simulations to validate these findings. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the adoption of a Coulomb friction model with linearly related friction coefficients can accurately capture the complex behavior of a multi-degree-of-freedom system. The proposed methodology can be applied to various mechanical systems, where the friction model is crucial in the design of stable control systems. Specifically, this study has implications for soft robotic systems, where actuation forces may be insufficient to overcome frictional forces and therefore understanding the behavior of systems governed by Coulomb friction is essential for both system analysis and design. The study is further expanded to understand the behavior of multiple degree-of-freedom systems, where the friction coefficients are correlated with various system parameters. Based on this, a method is developed to choose friction coefficients of a Coulomb friction model such that it accurately captures the behavior of a physical system. The study is demonstrated using a two-jointed soft robotic arm, where the multiple degree-of-freedom system has several key parameters that influence its motion and therefore understanding how friction coefficients vary with these parameters can accurately capture the behavior of the system. The study effectively showcases the importance of understanding multiple degree-of-freedom systems governed by Coulomb friction through dynamic modeling and system design. A novel method has been devised for instructing neural networks to produce valid hedging strategies in terms of stochastic differential equations, thereby facilitating the derivation of closed-form solutions and uncertainty quantification via Monte Carlo simulations. This approach is distinguished by its capacity to specify the stochastic characteristics of the underlying price processes and to impose rigorous mathematical constraints on the generated hedging mechanisms. Furthermore, it is theoretically demonstrated that the neural network-generated hedging strategies are indeed viable, and an analysis of its sample-wise accuracy is provided along with an estimation of the corresponding error rate. This method has been successfully tested with both straightforward and complex examples. For instance, a challenge was set for the neural network to develop a no-cost hedging strategy for a given option, with the result being a strategy that not only met the challenge but also allowed for a straightforward derivation of its feasibility through algebraic calculations. Additionally, a more sophisticated example involving the hedging of a double-option outcome was selected in order to evaluate the approach's ability to generate hedging strategies for complex financial instruments. As an added layer of certainty, both the neural network-generated hedging strategies and the analytical calculations were grounded in Monte Carlo simulations, enabling the determination of approximately 95% confidence intervals for the estimated hedging costs. According to the test outcomes, there appears to be little discrepancy between the neural network-generated hedging strategies and the analytical calculations, suggesting the method to be reliable and accurate in its current form. A comprehensive software package for reproducing the method's outcomes is available for public access at https://github.com/grundemann/lie-groups-for-neural-networks. The method of obtaining Bessel functions through confining potentials is well established, yet the mechanism by which their properties are inherited from the original potential remains understudied. This study explores a specific unfolding mechanism associated with the Fokas-Whitney map and reveals that Bessel functions can be derived from a transformed double confluent Heun equation serving as a universal unfolding of a central, symmetric zero of the original potential. An illustrative case involves the unfolding of a Gaussian potential, and corresponding eigenfunctions and singularities are computed for both the unfolding equation and its associated Bessel equation. Additionally, the research considers a specific non-standard normalization for Bessel functions, denoted $J_{\kappa}(z)$, and shows that these functions, along with their first and second derivatives, exhibit quadratic convergence to $1$,$\kappa$, and $-\frac{1}{2}$ respectively, as $z\to\infty$. A particular solution to the unfolded equation is found, and its asymptotic behavior is compared with the corresponding asymptotic behavior of the Bessel functions $J_{\kappa}(z)$. Finally, the research revisits a prior result: the Gutzwiller formula for the semiclassical sum - a spectral series for $J_{\kappa}(z)$, and demonstrates that this result can be reinterpreted as a consequence of the properties of the unfolding mechanism. Additionally, the research considers a specific case - the unfolding of a $|x|^\gamma$ potential for even $\gamma$ odd in the range $3\leq\gamma <5$, and shows that for this potential, the Gutzwiller formula for the relevant potential can be reinterpreted as a consequence of the properties of the one-dimensional harmonic map. In statistical modeling, heterogeneous data often pose a challenge due to differences in variance or other characteristics across distinct groups. When dealing with data in matrix form, a common goal involves approximating a high-dimensional matrix that represents various groups, each with its own unique characteristics. While existing methods like PCA focus solely on the entire data structure, they fail to account for these disparate groups, leading to inconsistencies. In order to capture these differences, PCA is often combined with other techniques, such as partition-based methods, which apply PCA to each group separately. However, these approaches simply combine separate low-rank projections, overlooking the fact that projected groups may vary and failing to address variations in variance levels across groups. Utilizing low-rank projection with a specific focus on individual groups, this study introduces a novel approach for matrix approximation, one that is robust to heterogeneous data. Furthermore, this work derives the critical or essential projection limits for this method by analyzing convex optimization problems. Additionally, numerical experiments are conducted to verify the effectiveness of this method and compare its performance against other techniques. The proposed method is also applied to the analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing data. The methodology and findings are further substantiated through theoretical analysis and simulation-based validation. A related MATLAB project can be accessed at https://github.com/tiangkinis/Matrix-Approximation-with-groupwise-heterogeneity. The provided code enables the execution of the methodology and facilitates the generation of the low-rank projection with groupwise heterogeneity. By applying this method, it is demonstrated that it is possible to achieve low-rank projection with improved fidelity for matrix approximation, particularly in the presence of heterogeneous data. Moreover, the effectiveness of the proposed method is illustrated through its application in the identification of low-rank structures in seismograms. The proposed method successfully recovers a well-known seismogram matrix, further validating its performance in matrix approximation with groupwise heterogeneity. Finally, a related Python project at https://github.com/tiangkinis/Convex-optimization-for-matrix-approximation enables the simulation and presentation of the methodology and findings. The provided code facilitates the replication of the experiments and analysis, and showcases the effectiveness of the proposed method in matrix approximation. One key advantage of the proposed implementation is its intermingling of matrix factorization and convex optimization techniques. By doing so, it is possible to achieve efficient and accurate low-rank matrix approximation with groupwise heterogeneity. The speed at which traits and genes change over time in responding to shifting environmental conditions can be described using various mathematical frameworks, some of which we outline in this paper. These models, rooted in evolutionary theory, suggest that the rate and complexity of ecological and evolutionary changes are interconnected. While the standard model is linear, with changes occurring at consistent rates in both space and time, we also examine two modified models that take into account varying rates of change and how they affect predictions in different scenarios. Our analysis shows that these extended models better anticipate the pace of change in real-world situations than the standard model, revealing that the rate of change can accelerate over time. By increasing the rate of genetic change, for example, we can speed up the evolution of traits, whether we're talking about complex genetic modifications or simple ones. These findings suggest that the influence of genetics on evolution can be effective for a long time. On the other hand, accelerating ecological dynamics generally leads to accelerated evolution, but only if the ecological changes are relatively slow and brief in comparison to the timescales over which genetic changes occur. If there is too much rapid ecological change, then there is an optimal point beyond which accelerating ecological change actually slows down evolutionary change. Our study indicates that the rate of change in evolution is influenced by factors such as genetic variation, temperature, and whether we're looking at complex or simple characteristics. These factors can often make a big difference, but only under specific, perhaps more uncommon, circumstances. These complex interactions between ecological and evolutionary changes can't be grasped by looking at either field in isolation, but rather require an integrated analysis that takes into consideration the interconnectedness of these changes. One of the predicted outcomes of such integration is that the rate of change in ecology and evolution can be correlated, but also independently influenced by genetic variations, temperature, and complexity of the traits being considered. Furthermore, our theoretical framework precludes the possibility that the standard model could ever be universally applicable, but rather depends on the actual dynamics being harnessed in real-world situations. By incorporating various rate modifiers, we've been able to predict evolutionary change with greater precision, but these types of dynamic processes can also make predictive challenges due to their versatility and potential applications in diverse ecological and evolutionary settings. Therefore, it's crucial that the rate modifiers are carefully considered and integrated within the predictive framework, but they can also be strategically manipulated to achieve desired outcomes, for instance, accelerated evolution, that may not be naturally occurring in real-world conditions. Research into self-supervised learning for speech tasks has gained significant interest due to its potential for cost-effective model development and adaptation across various domains. However, using SSL models in contexts with different emotional profiles or acoustics can be challenging due to their susceptibility to certain types of stimuli. In this paper, we investigate the propensity of speech SSL models to be hostile towards certain groups using two prototypical examples. We demonstrate that SSL models are more inclined to misbehave in subpopulations characterized by distinct emotional patterns or unique recording environments. Furthermore, we highlight the counterintuitive notion that certain popular SSL approaches, though achieving excellent performance in mainstream datasets, may be more prone to errors in alternative settings. Our analysis underscores the importance of a thorough examination of a model's emotional hostility during speech SSL learning. Such an examination can help guarantee that speech-based SSL models are used with empathy and sensitivity in diverse applications. To facilitate this, we introduce a straightforward, yet effective method for measuring emotional hostility and provide a metric system to facilitate comparisons between SSL approaches. Ultimately, we advocate for the incorporation of emotional consideration in speech SSL learning and develop a strategy for the design of more compassionate models. Our proposal enables the creation of SSL models that not only demonstrate outstanding performance but are also more receptive and respectful of varying emotional contexts. The research highlights the significance of emotional awareness in speech SSL learning and suggests a pathway for the development of SSL models that not only achieve excellent performance but are also emotionally considerate and susceptible to hostile environments. In many cases, statistical analysis relies on incomplete data, and our inability to observe the missing information can distort conclusions. There is currently a lack of comprehensive tools to assess the impact of missing data, and associated analysis becomes an essential but often neglected step in research. We suggest a novel approach centered around the E-value, a comprehensive measure of uncertainty, to examine the effect of missing data under various assumptions. By applying Bayesian analysis, our approach allows for smooth updates after receiving new data, thereby incorporating prior knowledge. To illustrate the efficacy of this method, we utilize simulated datasets to investigate different patterns of missing data and reveal that traditional methods often fall short. Conversely, our approach proves capable of accurately estimating parameters in all scenarios examined. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of this method to a real-world example involving AIDS studies. By using the E-value to assess uncertainty, our approach provides insight into parameters such as the AIDS latent period and the natural progression rate. As an added benefit, our approach can be used to estimate parameters for diverse models, including logistic, mixed, shared-frailty, and Gaussian processes, making it a versatile tool for a wide range of research areas. Furthermore, our approach can be used for various missing data types, including up to 30% missing in some scenarios, illustrating its potential for application to complex datasets. Overall, our approach enables researchers to incorporate critical information regarding missing data and is a valuable tool for assessing such data and making informed conclusions. Utilizing the E-value allows for quantifiable and numerical assessments of the impact and reliability of missing data, and is a useful metric in many different contexts. To further promote usage and understanding of this concept, we have created both basic and advanced software packages in R to facilitate their use, as well as making the related data and codes available for public access through our website. The software is also compatible with other widely-used packages, including EM algorithms and is easily implemented in a variety of contexts. The provided code is available for reference at the specified URL. To sum up, our approach provides a useful numerical tool to assess and account for the impact of missing data, and is particularly adaptable for diverse applications. The primary goal of this study is to thoroughly categorize symmetries associated with the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for the multivariate Laurent series $q^{z_1 A + z_2 B}$ where A and B are generators in the algebra, and elements A and B belong to the generators of the algebra, and the multiplicative operation is defined by the quantum group's action. The text also presents a general definition of these symmetries in terms of the quasi-polynomials based on the highest weight vector in the Gelfand--Zak representation $V_{[m,n]}$ of the algebra for integers $m\geq 1$ and $n\geq 0$. The elements of this representation can be identified using the one-to-one correspondence induced by the algebra's action on the standard basis vectors in the representation space of $V_{[m,n]}$. The study also explores examples in the single-variable Laurent series $q^{zA}$ and discusses their connections to the elliptic Skymorphism introduced by L. Chekhov and A. Yakimenko in arXiv:math/0605248 in 2006. The work presented in this dissertation has led to the development of a new, comprehensive mathematical concept which is denoted by $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)\times U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, the direct product of the quantum group algebras for two copies of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Lie algebra with the algebra having a highest weight vector $v$ as its element, which displays symmetry properties similar to a quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ acting on a finite-dimensional representation of the algebra. The newly formed concept serves to express the Laurent Series $q^{z_1A+ z_2B}$ for elements A and B in the algebra in terms of the basis associated with the representation $V_{[1,1]}$ of the algebra for integers $z_1\geq 1$ and $z_2\geq 0$. The study demonstrates that this expression remains uniform across various fields to complex numbers. Furthermore, the text presents an analysis revealing that $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)\times U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is not unitary with respect to any action of the algebra

Due to the current scarcity of studies in this domain, this literature review hopes to stimulate research interest and motivate scholars to invest time and resources in the development of novel BFL-based systems. For the first time, the data also led to E measurements in both rapidity and transverse momentum for both ground and excited ($^1S^1P^0$) b meson states. In contrast, this paper explores a distinct research question by focusing on abuse detection in software, specifically by analyzing instances of Python's crypto API misuse. Our research revealed that improper use of crypto APIs in Python applications contributes significantly to abuse occurrence. However, upon closer inspection, it became apparent that the majority of such instances could be attributed to a limited number of common errors repeated across various applications. These findings have significant implications, as they suggest the potential to mitigate tech support burdens and security exploits by addressing these underlying issues through pro-active intervention. To date, there has been a lack of research aimed at detecting and preventing such instances of code abuse. In order to comprehensively address the topic, this paper outlines a novel machine learning framework for detecting code abuse, incorporating a specific model designed to identify crypto API misuse, as well as a detailed dataset collection and preprocessing procedure. Our research indicates that the technical constraints of the current models limit their ability to detect abuse on large scales, yet they demonstrate promising performance in smaller-scale testing. Ultimately, these models have the potential to contribute towards preventing crypto password exposure by raising red flags during review processes. Our research sets out a framework for detecting a broad range of software abuse, with the specific abuse variant being crypto API misuse in this particular investigation. Most current methods for creating detailed 3D urban environment models face
the same challenge: a severe scarcity of high-quality point cloud data. Denser
data capture is key to creating precise models but present methods fall short
of this goal. We expand on previous research in urban environment modeling by
introducing an innovative two-stage method that leverages user feedback through
a collaborative voting process among ground-based agents. By incorporating this
voting process, our approach ensures that dense 3D models can be generated from
sparse point cloud data. We showcase our technique's efficacy with recent
unmanned aerial vehicle data collection methods in various urban settings. 
Our approach successfully generates detailed models with accurate geometry in
real-world settings as shown in the experimental results provided. Furthermore,
our method adheres to a fully distributed paradigm, allowing it to scale up for
the more complex urban environments found in capital cities. This scalability
enables our technique to create reusable 3D models suitable for a broad array of
applications including emergency response, urban planning, and the creation of
virtual environments. Our method is now available for further development on
GitHub at https://github.com/mayj4/jc-urban-annotation. An interactive demo can
be accessed at https://value-jc.github.io.

Seismic imaging plays a crucial role in exploring subsurface earth structures, and inversion is a key method for determining the earth's reflection coefficients from recorded data. Currently, conventional sparsity-promoting inversion methods are widely employed due to their sparse-structure-promoting characteristics. In order to address these issues, we propose a novel neural network-based inversion approach called non-uniform sparse pattern network, or NuSPAN, which learns the non-uniform sparse pattern of reflectivity directly from data instead of pre-defining it.
