Our approach also identifies a distinct state created by the subalgebra and determines its reduced density matrix. By establishing an overlap with a finite-size vector, we can compute the subalgebra's properties in a system of size $L$. Our method is particularly useful because it allows us to bypass eigenvalue calculations associated with the subalgebra's commuting squad. In linguistics, part-of-speech (POS) analysis is a fundamental task for understanding the nuances of language, where different words can take on varying contexts based on rhetorical goals. While machine learning has been the standard approach since the 1990s, it is vulnerable to errors in the face of ambiguous words, where a single word can be assigned multiple classes based on its ambiguity. This challenge is particularly pronounced in ancient languages, where a lack of contemporary resources hinders efforts to develop effective models. To address this issue, we propose a new model called SPARCS, which is designed to capture multiple plausible classes for ambiguous words, relying on the pairwise relationships between words in the corpus. Utilizing a novel algorithm based on the ideas of von Mises-Fisher and Brown clustering, we are the first to apply the combination of these techniques to the task of set-valued POS tagging, where we are able to achieve accurate results through the use of transfer learning, even in the face of small and historical corpora. Further details are available at: https://github.com/alexkobalewsky/spars. This research forms part of a larger project aimed at developing automatic grammatical analysis for ancient Sumerian, a language with no contemporary grammatical framework and a small available corpus. As such, we are able to achieve highly accurate results, often exceeding 90%, even in the face of corpus limitations. This research aims to contribute to the broader field of historical language POS analysis and to create a new and robust framework for this task. Furthermore, in line with reproducibility principles, we are able to make both the code and data used in this research openly available. Ultimately, through the application of set-valued POS tagging, we are able to achieve more accurate results, moving towards a more robust and reliable analysis of ancient Sumerian language structure. This research is presented in partnership with the Sumerian Automated Parsing Project (SAPP). Both authors contributed to this research, with ultimate responsibility assigned to the submitting author. Our findings suggest that set-valued POS tagging may offer a superior performance over conventional sequence-based models, potentially serving as a reliable fallback in situations characterized by low resource environments. This hypothesis is further supported by our open-source release of the code and data. This work is made possible through the financial support of the numerical analysis research fund provided by the University of Montreal and the support of the SAPP. Both authors confirmed the integrity of this research upon its initial submission for publication. This work did not involve any animal testing or sampling

Recent research into variational inequalities and fluid dynamics issues has necessitated the development of a new approach to non-uniform integrability theory. This has led to the creation of a theoretical framework for a broad class of operators, encompassing x-bounded, non-uniformly Lipschitz, and multivalued operators. The proposed framework is based on the lower semicontinuity of non-uniformly Lipschitz integrals and offers flexible applications in diverse settings. The proposed method is illustrated by establishing a non-uniform integrability theorem for a broad class of operators and demonstrating its utility in tackling fluid dynamics and Hamilton-Jacobi equations-related challenges. Furthermore, it is shown that the developed theory can be reduced to the classical integrability theorem for uniformly Lipschitz functions under more conventional conditions. The developed theory is then applied to tackle the issue of existence and differentiability in various contexts, including a model for polyconvex functions, the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, and fluid dynamics models such as Euler and Navier-Stokes. The new approach is shown to be capable of addressing these complex problems in a unified and elegant manner. The developed theory is found to be reducible to the Carath\'{e}odory existence theorem for Euler and Navier-Stokes equations, while the issue of differentiability can be investigated more deeply in the context of polyconvex functions and the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, where the primary challenge lies in tackling equations defined by Lipschitz or non-differentiable integrals. Wherever possible, the developed theory is aligned with classical concepts and terminology, with original contributions marked in italics. The paper is divided into three parts, dealing respectively with 1) non-uniform integrability theory, 2) applications in variational inequalities, Hamilton-Jacobi equations, and fluid dynamics, and 3) illustrative examples. Furthermore, two appendices are provided, dealing with the issue of a new approach to lower semicontinuity theory for non-uniformly Lipschitz integrals and the relationship between the developed theory and various existing methods and theories in the field. The paper is intended to provide an in-depth review of non-uniform integrability theory and offer new perspectives and insights into this area of research. Wherever possible, the developed theory is illustrated by concrete examples, with an emphasis on promoting theoretical understanding and clarity. The paper is written in a style suitable for publication in the Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications. The graphical elements in the paper have been created using TikZ

The growth of a city is heavily influenced by its physical environment, let's call it Urban Setting. Cities need to adapt this setting to cater their needs, whether it's the layout of roads, buildings, or green spaces. However, managing such a vast setting is complex and requires precise planning, but cities struggle to translate their needs into detailed specifications due to limited expertise in specification languages. To bridge this gap, we've developed an innovative, user-friendly system that helps cities convert their requirements into formal and precise specifications with ease. This system is built on two key components: an intuitive interface that assists users in selecting appropriate features for transformation, and a machine learning-based module that expertly applies these features to generate a detailed specification. Our approach is demonstrated through a concrete example, showcasing its effectiveness in transforming an informal city requirement into a formal specification. Additionally, we've conducted a thorough evaluation by running a series of experiments and gathered feedback from city officials, both local and international, which has led to the improvement of our system's performance and usability. Our study highlights the potential benefits and drawbacks of using this system, including potential application areas for its deployed versions. Our system is publicly available on our website in its current deployed version. With our system, cities can now efficiently produce high-quality specifications that can be utilized in various urban projects, such as competitions, workshops, and educational activities. Our research aims to contribute positively to cities and city planners by translating their needs into precise specifications with minimal effort. Our system's website is accessible at https://smartassistant.to-models.xyz. A preceding version of this paper was presented at ICMT'22. Our system's resources are hosted on https://github.com/To-Models/SmartAssistant_URB. Our previous work is documented at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13421. Our original training corpora used for the machine learning approach are available at https://github.com/To-Models/UrbanSetting_URB. Our training data for the system is available at https://github.com/To-Models/UrbanSetting_URB/tree/main/urbs/setting. Our system was evaluated following the advice provided by Fox et al at https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.13365. Our international distribution of the system to city officials was facilitated by the CityPlanner.org community. Our study's feedback from city officials is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.68852. Our related work regarding modeling cities is available at https://arxiv

In modern quantum computing, errors caused by its fragile nature are tackled using quantum error correction. A widely employed approach, the encoded inverse method, involves encoding a single logical qubit across multiple physical qubits to enable error correction. However, this method has a significant drawback; it restricts the scaling of quantum computers. In our research, we propose an innovative noise suppression technique using concealed inverses, an idea derived from classical mathematics. This method does not necessitate encoding and instead harnesses the inherent qubit connections in superconducting circuits to automatically eliminate errors. A theoretical basis for our method is established, and it is substantiated by experimental validation across six different error types. Compared to traditional error correction, our technique, despite requiring no encoding, can correct up to three times more errors, thereby rendering it an essential error correction approach for complex quantum computing applications. Furthermore, our findings also highlight the significance of accounting for cross-capacitance in superconducting quantum circuits. A recently published study discussed the application of concealed inverses in multi-control gates; however, our research provides the first experimental verification of this concept. Its application in quantum error correction presents numerous opportunities for accelerated development and implementation. A demonstration of this approach in a 11-qubit superconducting quantum circuit is currently in progress. It is anticipated that successful deployment will render concealed inverses a vital component for efficient quantum computing. A pre-publication of our method can be found at arXiv:2111.15557. To safeguard structures in the marine industry from the intensity of severe atmospheric and oceanic forces, accurate estimation of spatially varying peak values of significant waves, wind, and wave-vector spectra is essential. We introduce a multivariate spatial density function for the peaks of these oceanic waves, incorporating the effects of location, wind direction, and the spectrum's frequency. This probabilistic model is applied to analyze a dependence between wave velocity and velocity of wind, characterized by a multivariate nonparametric regression coefficient with spatial complexity. We utilize a dataset from Typhoon Maemi (2006) to validate our model, providing estimated spatial densities and allowing for the prediction of locations of high wind, wave velocity, and wave characteristics. Recently, large-scale vision-language models have achieved impressive performance in correlating visual and linguistic inputs, but their practical applications are limited due to their reliance on massive dataset training. Specifically, models like CLIP struggle to learn general knowledge when trained on standard image-text pairs. To address these limitations, we introduce a new VT-CLIP framework that integrates visual-text cues to broaden their understanding of the world. By pre-processing the training data into visual-friendly forms, our method enables models to effectively generalize from these inputs. Through extensive evaluations on various benchmarks, we demonstrate that VT-CLIP significantly outperforms its counterparts, including metrics for visual recognition, semantic concept classification, and visual question answering tasks. Importantly, our method is adaptable to multiple visual encoders and can be applied to a range of visual-text datasets with minimal human intervention. By leveraging visual assistance to refine text representations, we show that visual expertise can notably enhance the quality of text representations. We test the effectiveness of our method in multiple scenarios, such as zero-shot learning and image-text matching tasks. Moreover, we successfully use the VT-CLIP models we trained on MS-COCO for a novel application: generating artistic fan art. Our proposed approach naturally extends to support multi-modal learning with three or more modalities. To facilitate further research, we provide detailed step-by-step guides and share the trained models, pre-trained visual guides, and visual-text datasets with visual assists at this https URL. This paper introduces a general approach to a matrix-inversion technique, flexible enough to accommodate various noisy matrix environments. By breaking down the noisy matrix S, our algorithm decomposes it into a smooth matrix A, with B as the background interference. Based on the characteristics of the interference matrix B, different applications of our algorithm can be defined, such as when B equals the zero matrix or has a specific, fixed form. To broaden our method's application scope, we suggest introducing adjustable parameters. By using our algorithm in the context of the Gaussian matrix, the results show that as the size of the Gaussian matrix increases, the probability of the algorithm's success converges to 1. What's more, our algorithm can not only restore the original matrix S but also recover the underlying data within the matrix, making it applicable in the field of source code stealing. According to our simulation results, our algorithm outperforms the existing numerical error correction methods in the noisy matrix environment. Moreover, our algorithm can not only correct numerical errors in the matrix environment but also detect whether there are interference items in the matrix and determine the background interference matrix under certain conditions. Therefore, our algorithm has wide-ranging applications. Lastly, our algorithm can be used in various types of matrices, such as integer matrices, matrices with special properties, etc. etc. without any modifications at all. Therefore, our algorithm is predictable and reliable. In addition, our algorithm can be used in many fields of study. For example, our algorithm can be used in the context of quantum computing. According to our simulation results, our algorithm outperforms the existing top ones in the superconducting circuit. Therefore, our algorithm is highly effective. In the future, our method can be used in the design of quantum algorithms.

A proposed solution, the Highdicom library, provides user-friendly, standard-compliant tools for encoding numerical image annotation and model output data in pathology and radiology. This includes support for widely used annotation schemes like QuIP and R-CNN, as well as traditional digitized pathology evaluations. By integrating with popular Python libraries like PyTf and Pytorch, and offering conversion tools for legacy data sets, Highdicom facilitates data exchange and zero-code data augmentation for research partners. The benefits and tools offered by Highdicom are illustrated through its application in a virtual pathology review workshop. The standard used by Highdicom, as detailed in the publication, can also be applied more broadly to other types of image annotation and model output data. In computational biology, researchers have focused heavily on identifying predictive models for individual DNA sequences, despite the recent revelation that sequence features are not the sole determinants of gene function. Consequently, there is now a growing need for uncovering broader insights into DNA function through the analysis of unguided patterns within the genomic content. We introduce an unsupervised method for extracting recurring patterns in the functional DNA content of organisms, and demonstrate its effectiveness on data from eukaryotic genomes. Notably, this approach yields meaningful geometric structures that align with biological principles, even when no relevant information is provided. We showcase the efficacy of this method using five selected eukaryotic genomes. Our results validate the hypothesis that unservised, sequence-based analysis can lead to significant new insights into the underlying DNA functional mechanisms. The presence of a surface termination consisting of a specific metal or oxygen atom has a profound impact on various properties of thin metal oxide films, notably in cases where these films exhibit insulating or metallic behavior. To illustrate this effect, our investigation focuses on V$_2$O$_3$ films, which display a metal-insulator transition and exist in two distinct surface termination configurations - metal or oxygen at the top - that can be achieved through varying growth conditions on Al$_2$O$_3$ substrates. Using a combination of x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and first-principles calculations to model different growth scenarios, we found that electron donation from metal to oxygen atoms at the surface is a key mechanism underlying the metal-insulating transition and can significantly influence electronic properties of these thin films. Moreover, our findings indicate that proper consideration of surface terminations is essential in theoretical models aiming to explain underlying driving forces of the metal-insulating transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films. This research provides valuable insights into the design and the intricate electronic structure of metal-insulating or metal-like thin films, which are crucial components of numerous nanoelectronics devices. For the metal-Insulator Transition in V$_2$O_3$ films, our investigation focuses on the impact of distinct surface terminations - metal or oxygen at the surface - which can be manipulated through varying growth conditions on Al$_2$O$_3$ substrates. A combination of x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and first-principles calculations were used to model and experiment the different systems, revealing a crucial role of charge transfer between the layers and the possibility of electron donation from metal to oxygen atoms at the surface. These findings emerged from a detailed analysis of experimental and theoretical results. Moreover, our investigation reveals that symmetry, phase coherence, and correlations play a vital role in driving the metal-insulating transition in these systems. A detailed comparison between various V$_2$O_3 and V$_2$O$_4$ systems was also performed to discuss distinct metal-insulating transitions. [Conclusion] Our investigation reveals that distinct metal-Insulator Transition in metal-oxide monolayers and multilayers, which exhibit either 2D or 3D density of states, are caused by different mechanisms. In contrast, a similar transition in trilayers exhibits topological properties, which are governed by Weyl semimetals. These distinct topological properties can be manipulated by changing the spin-orbit coupling or through an appropriate choice of layers.

Several machine learning algorithms have been evaluated and tested on the North Pole dataset, which includes essential meteorological information for accurate weather forecasting. These measurements are pivotal for the normal functioning of the NPL station, including the provision of basic weather information. Initially, a dataset with 13 features and 1592 samples was created for training and evaluation purposes. Various scoring methods and two types of models were employed: supervised and reinforcement learning. The performance of each model was evaluated using different metrics, ultimately yielding notable outcomes. Among the tested algorithms, Random Forest and Support Vector Machine scored the highest. By applying these models to the dataset, we achieved a 87% accuracy level. A subsequent analysis aimed to determine the significance of each feature using the SHAP values technique. Through this process, we identified vital meteorological parameters and their respective influence on model behavior. By validating the results and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms on the dataset, we established that Random Forest and Support Vector Machine deliver the most impressive outcomes in this context. This research aims to optimize and refine these models for the NPL station's dataset. Moreover, our results indicate that a deeper investigation into the influence of each feature on model decision-making is warranted, suggesting the use of more sophisticated techniques to assign weights to the original features based on their contribution to model performance. Ultimately, our study seeks to lay the groundwork for the development of accurate and robust machine learning models at the NPL station. However, further studies and discussions on the subject have revealed the need to modify some of the measurement variables, such as incorporating more relevant features for weather forecasting. With this goal in mind, our modification strategy will involve the selection of essential features from relevant domains, with the aim of ultimately producing a dataset that enhances model performance and advances the NPL station's weather forecasting capabilities. A demonstration presentation delivered at the conference IPNAS'2022 served as the initial outlet for these findings. All related code and data used in this research have been uploaded to the repository provided below the paper's DOI. By documenting and sharing these results, our study intends to contribute meaningfully to future research initiatives. The current development of these machine learning models is intended to foster collaboration and knowledge sharing. The ultimate objective of this research is to establish a strong foundation for data-driven decision making at the NPL station and other research institutions and institutions. Recently, a primary assignment for image representation has been orientation prediction paired with a convolutional network. This task is significant because image orientation influences the performance of subsequent tasks. While initial approaches were based on basic networks, subsequent research has proposed more advanced architectures. Our work indicates that a convoluted network is the optimal solution to both orientation prediction and image classification tasks. We support this conclusion with analytical proofs, extensive evaluations, and data analysis. Specifically, our findings confirm that a convoluted network outperforms other orientations prediction methods and is more efficient than others. Moreover, image classification models trained with data on convoluted networks exhibit superior performance compared to those trained with data on orientation-prediction networks. We also show that a convoluted network can be effectively trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised techniques. Our research is based on a analysis of the unique properties of circular prediction problems and the unique dynamics of these problems. The proposed method is designed to handle various types of circular prediction problems and is easily applicable to a wide range of tasks. We hope this method can inspire research in various fields. A novel metric called space utilization has been defined to represent the efficiency of use of a specific region in space over time, taking into account the diverse nature of space-based applications. This paper focuses on the space utilization in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO), 160-800km above the Earth's surface, where various technological and scientific applications reside. First, an overview of several initial design options is presented, then a more refined method to estimate space utilization in LEO is proposed. This refinement involves defining density functions for various sources: operational satellites, decommissioned satellites, artificial objects, and natural entities to illustrate the concept. Finally, some potential applications and future developments related to space utilization in LEO are discussed.

When model training occurs in a distributed setting, communication of model parameters between nodes is a bottleneck. To alleviate this, using local data and periodically sharing updated models between nodes is a common strategy. Nevertheless, when network issues arise, distributed training is hindered, and we seek to understand if using regional queries for robust learning could be beneficial. Essentially, regional queries involve asking the network for target data within a specified area at a given time, and we're investigating its potential to contribute to learning resiliency. Through a theoretical analysis on how regional queries impact learning speed and stability, we've developed an in-depth mathematical model and conducted computational experiments to verify our findings. Interestingly, our results show that regional queries are beneficial in environments with both specific and non-specific communication disruptions. Furthermore, our code has been made publicly available to facilitate future research. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to explore regional queries for resiliency in distributed machine learning. The outcome of our research could inspire others to incorporate regional queries as a part of learning resiliency strategies. Moreover, we've identified several avenues for further investigation. One such area is to extend our theoretical and empirical findings to scenarios where the source of disruption varies. Building upon that finding, we discovered a novel class of fast algorithms for solving the optimal transport problem. We developed a novel triangular matrix with a specific structural sequence that reduces to $O(n)$ the number of operations required to compute optimal transport between two probability distributions as per the OT2 method. This discovery, combined with our ability to compute the inverse of this matrix in $O(n)$ time and initialize it efficiently using $O(\log^2 n)$ operations, enables us to calculate optimal transport prices in $O(n)$ time. This new algorithm is just as scalable as our previous $O(n)$ algorithm for iteratively computing optimal transport. Nevertheless, under the OT2's closed-form formula for optimal transport, we observed a significant $O(n^2)$ decrease in computational complexity. To address this, we developed a new algorithm that computes optimal transport prices in $O(n)$ time using our newly derived matrix. This new algorithm is the first to achieve $O(n)$ complexity for computing optimal transport. This study expands upon the Birkhoff algorithm for solving Maxwell's equations in a medium with a linear relationship between electric current and electric field. We investigate how an isotropic and dissipative substance responds to radiation by calculating the energy absorbed, the momentum received, and the heat and momentum exchanged rates in relation to the incident radiation properties. We then use a numerical model to investigate the effects of different input parameters on the medium's response. We discover that the coefficient of dissipation significantly influences the amount of energy absorbed and momentum transferred, but the direction and rate of these properties are primarily determined by the radiation's polarization and angular distribution. A drag force arises when the dissipation coefficient is very high, causing a recoil effect that can alter the radiation's trajectory. We find that the direction and magnitude of this drag force are determined by the average frequency, angular distribution, and polarization of the radiation. However, the magnitude of the drag force can vary depending on the input parameters, and in some cases, the drag can even induce acceleration. We explore the potential uses of this model in scenarios where high-frequency electromagnetic waves interact with matter. We suggest that the dissipation properties of the medium and radiation properties of the Z boson could play a role in resolving inconsistencies in Birkhoff equations, which may lead to a new understanding of chirality in the Z boson. We propose that this model and concepts like radiation drag and energy-momentum trading could be key factors in explaining the apparent magnetic force experienced by charged particles traveling near compact, spinning objects like stars. Moreover, the presence of electromagnetic waves could significantly influence the dynamics of the particles, and the relationship between energy-momentum and electromagnetic waves might hold the key to explaining the empirical, weak Equivalence principle. We plan to further validate our model in various experiments and tests, and we expect that the experimental verification of our model could have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the physical universe. In particular, we expect that the presence of electromagnetic waves could substantially impact the dynamics of the particles, and the relationship between energy-momentum and electromagnetic waves might be crucial in explaining the Equivalence principle. We intend to extensively experiment and mathematically simulate our model to provide a more comprehensive explanation of the physical universe. Furthermore, the experimental validation of our model and our associated ideas could provide novel insights into the empirical Equivalence principle. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging can be more accurate and less invasive than traditional radiography, especially in asymptomatic patients. Determining the scoliosis curve topography and magnitude with ultrasound requires high-quality two-dimensional (2D) images and precise spatial localization. We assessed the reliability of robotic ultrasound imaging technology in evaluating scoliosis by comparing it to manual scanning. Twenty participants with scoliosis underwent ultrasound examinations by two different methods, following a standardized protocol. Curve topography and magnitude values were obtained for each method and from the robotic device alone after repositioning. Intraclass correlation coefficients, absolute and relative evaluation values, and measurement values of curvatures and apex angles showed no significant differences between the two scanning methods. We found high reliability and consistency in the robotic device's alone measurements. These results confirm the reliability and accuracy of robotic ultrasound technology in evaluating scoliosis, and demonstrate its potential as an alternative to conventional scoliosis assessment with improved reproducibility. Notably, this study achieved excellent correlations and reliability values, outperforming existing scoliosis ultrasound studies. Its results also surpass the minimum acceptable intratester reliability in orthopedic research set by the American Society for Testing and Materials. Future studies should prioritize maximizing patient participation to confirm these findings in a larger population. In addition, further research is needed to assess the clinical practicality and usability of this assessment approach. If successful, this assessment could expand scoliosis diagnosis to asymptomatic patients, utilizing robotic ultrasound technology. Such a development could also lead to its application in other spinal deformities and as a diagnostic tool in other fields, including radiology and physical therapy. Ultimately, further studies are necessary to assess its clinical feasibility and applicability. The inclusion of hate speech in social media platforms is linked to heightened hatred and hostility, which can also contribute to a decrease in mental health among users. Furthermore, social media platforms have also been linked to increased violence, particularly against specific groups. Our study focuses on detecting hate speech on Twitter by using a unique model based on characteristic extraction. This approach involves breaking down text into its core features and using those to classify the text as either hateful or not. Key aspects of this model include the use of word frequency, unique words, and a specific stopping word list to create distinct character sets for each text. These character sets are then used to train a model based on the XOR transfer learning neural network, which achieves good results across various datasets, outperforming some of the best existing models in the process. Our study showcases the effectiveness and simplicity of this characteristic extraction-based model. It's notable that the top models in this field, including deep learning models, often require large amounts of private data to train, creating a risk of data leakage. In contrast, our approach doesn't rely on such data. Moreover, the use of characteristic extraction allows for the annotation of unlabeled data through limited manual labeling, making the process more efficient. Finally, the decision boundaries produced by the XOR neural network offer better interpretability than existing neural models. Thus, our study highlights both the performance and the unique strengths of the characteristic extraction-based model for hate speech detection. The study demonstrates the success of this approach across three different datasets, and the results show no dependence on the size of the dataset. In addition, we have made our code available to other researchers. The study also explores the challenges of developing hate speech detection models from limited resources. Given the current lack of sufficient resources for this task, we have adopted a new strategy involving the use of transfer learning with distant supervision to improve model performance. In other words, we have taken advantage of pre-existing classification tasks to train hate speech models without requiring human-annotated data, a problem common in NLP but particularly critical in hate speech detection. Our study has achieved good results across various tests. The model trained on one task, distinct from hate speech detection, is surprisingly effective at detecting hate speech on Twitter. This outcome is particularly valuable given the difficulty of collecting hate speech data due to its private nature. Furthermore, our model is non-consequential, meaning it doesn't alter the labels of the data. Thus, our study has achieved good outcomes and expands the possibilities of transfer learning in NLP, particularly in contexts where datasets are limited

We present an assessment of current benchmark datasets containing images of historical significance. The document provides a comprehensive description of each dataset, accompanied by illustrative examples, with the aim of offering a unified entry point for researchers seeking to utilize these resources. Notably, we offer guidance on data acquisition, as well as access information, given that certain datasets are not publicly available for evaluation. In total, we have identified and reviewed 17 significant datasets, with the intention of regularly updating this resource to ensure it remains relevant in the future. To date, our review is the most thorough examination of its kind in the computational history community, and the associated code and output can be found on the HFUB GitHub repository for reproduction. As of December 2022, our review remains current, but we anticipate that it will require expansion in the future to account for newly established datasets. The datasets covered encompass images of inscriptions, documents, buildings, artifacts, clothing, and various other areas of historical interest. This study examines various structural parameters as tools to bound the graph's metric dimension, with a focus on underlined graphs, 2-decomposable graphs, and graphs with maximum degree Δ. We show that each vertex identification model determined by a set of structural parameters has a complexity of NP-hard, unless it can be solved in linear time, and we derive parameters that yield polynomial-time algorithms for the general vertex identification problem. For the metric dimension, which can be reduced to a more tractable problem in several cases, we obtain upper bounds in terms of the number of vertices n and other parameters: on underlined graphs, a bound of Ω(n/Δ) is demonstrated; for 2-decomposable graphs, a bound of Ω(n/Δ^2) is shown; and for graphs with a maximum degree Δ, a bound of Ω(Δ) is obtained. These results are complemented by finding lower bounds of Ω(n/Δ) and Ω(Δ) for the metric dimension and vertex identification problems, respectively, thus almost matching the obtained upper bounds. Moreover, we obtain lower bounds for the number of markers in specific vertex identification models. Recent discoveries of Weyl semimetals have led to heightened curiosity about their magnetic properties. A key feature of these materials is their time-reversal symmetry, but when an external magnetic field is applied, this symmetry is broken, resulting in the emergence of the Weyl semimetal's surface states. This paper explores how this symmetry breaking behaves in three-dimensional Weyl semimetals under external magnetic fields that are not uniform. Through a general analysis using the Berry curvature, as well as a model based on the honeycomb lattice, our research shows that a magnetic pattern that changes in strength creates semi-metal surface state pockets that are not affected by time-reversal symmetry. These findings offer an exciting opportunity to study time-reversal symmetry-violating Weyl semi-metals using techniques such as angle-dependent magnetoresistance, a method which has already proven successful in identifying symmetry violations in other materials. Moreover, our model enables the calculation of the symmetry-breaking gap size associated with each surface state pocket using this same method. Experiments on this model have confirmed that a uniform magnetic field of a certain strength can trigger a uniform gap size in the surface states throughout the entire Brillouin zone. Nevertheless, our realistic calculation of the gap size behavior as a function of magnetic frequency reveals more intricate and correlated gap size behaviors that are influenced by the lattice structure. This calculated multiband physics is expected to not only apply to the honeycomb lattice used in our model,  but also to other lattices such as the hexagonal BCN and trigonal AuPhosphides, and could potentially offer new insights into the nature of time-reversal symmetry-violating Weyl semi-metals. It's hoped that our proposed experimental strategy in our paper, specifically designed for the realistic model based on the honeycomb lattice, will lead to groundbreaking discoveries in the field of symmetry-breaking Weyl semi-metals. Research demonstrates that a specific molecular energy transfer process can be accelerated by coupled optical fields generated by the nanoantenna. When included in optical circuits, this transfer process can be utilized to produce discrete, high-frequency laser light sources. Sgr A East is a radio source situated at the core of the 2-kpc spherical bubble surrounding the young stellar population of the Galactic Center. To determine the origin of Sgr A East, we examined explosive events capable of producing young stars within this area. We identified a massive (500 solar masses) green pea galaxy serving as a stellar cradle, located 0.8 kiloparsecs from the Center and moving at 500 kilometers per second, thus explaining the spatial and kinematic relationships between Sgr A East and surrounding stars. We verified our findings through a second independent method based on an extensive 12.7-year survey by the GASKAP survey. This collaboration identified a dense ionized gas layer with 20 solar masses, 0.8 kiloparsecs from the Center, and concluded that massive explosive events are necessary to form the massive stars within the 2-kpc circle. We observed minimal star formation elsewhere across the bubble due to the low metallicity, and the absence of significant internal extinction in the Center, consistent with theoretical models of the Galactic Center's star formation. We also observed the circular distribution of explosive events outside the bubble, coinciding with the predicted explosion zones of starbursts and supernovae. However, a significant fraction of these explosive events remains unobserved because of their remoteness, yet we remain confident that a stellar population originating from Sgr A East, at the heart of the Galactic Center, has been discovered. The rapid multipole method, employed in astrophysical simulations, effectively and efficiently evacuates negative mass elements from the central region of a calculation domain. However, the standard implementation of this method is well-documented to break celestial body angular momentum, which is a critical component in astrophysical planet-forming environments. We introduce a new strategy to preserve angular momentum during the execution of this algorithm by converting the affected mass elements into spherical particles with customized properties and then relocating them outside the central domain area for further processing in a standard astrophysical simulation code. We verify the effectiveness of this approach in a test simulation involving a fast-trotting protoplanet and demonstrate its ability to conserve angular momentum while accurately replicating typical planetary motion in astrophysical environments where the rapid multipole method is typically applied. The accompanying C++ code for this project is CFAAST-2023-0001, which is available in the Cyberspace Astrophysical Software Toolbox (AASTOOH). Furthermore, we have included a supplementary Python illustration demonstrating the concept of angular momentum preservation in a simple test environment, which can also be accessed through the AASTOOH portal. The incorporation of angular momentum conservation in simulations offers significant benefits in terms of minimizing biases, which could have a substantial impact on our comprehension of astrophysical celestial formation processes. By incorporating negative mass elements as essential components in planet-forming simulations, researchers can now simulate complex planetary systems more accurately by combining standard celestial body simulations and our newly developed negative mass preservation approach. As a result, simulations assuming uniform protoplanet masses can now conserve angular momentum during the execution of the rapid multipole method, which significantly reduces simulation artifacts and inaccuracies that previously occurred in such configurations. In physics research, this laser has facilitated groundbreaking measurements, while in engineering, it drives crucial industrial processes. Although lasers have advanced technological boundaries, traditional ones all absorb light, thereby hindering certain applications, including optical coherence tomography and laser cooling of atoms. Its current major constraints are the laser's low power output and relatively long time it takes to start emitting light after activation. We are confident that future improvements in this area will bring this laser into widespread use across the fields of quantum information processing, spectroscopy, and laser cooling. This open-access article explores interconnections between K3 varieties, Picard numbers, Siegel disks, complex multiplication, and isogenies in genus 2 curves, also examining the relationships between these complex variables as well as their associations with K3 surfaces and elliptic curves. For instance, Pickering and Harvey previously demonstrated that K3 surfaces with a Jacobian Picard rank of 1 are linked to points on the Siegel disk of their complex multiplication field. We now confirm a conjecture of Pickering and Harvey that K3 surfaces with a Jacobian Picard rank of 1 are also connected to genus 2 curves via isogenies. We extend Kudla and Kudla-Tayyaballi's work on relationships between isogenies in elliptic curves and K3 surfaces to the case of genus 2 curves. Moreover, we show that K3 surfaces with a Jacobian Picard rank of 1 are associated with points on the moduli space of stable matrices, mirroring results for elliptic curves. These findings lead to the conclusion that K3 surfaces with a Jacobian Picard rank of 1 form part of a larger context, similar to moduli spaces of elliptic curves, and that they complement work in genus 2 curves. We use this knowledge to create new examples of K3 surfaces associated with points on the Siegel disk and generate examples of pairs (X, X') such that X and X' are connected via isogenies but do not satisfy complex multiplication with respect to each other. These include (the Jacobian of a K3 surface with degree 2, C) where C is a genus 2 curve, and (X, X' the Jacobian of a K3 surface with degree 2). We also explore numerical data regarding the distribution of Picard numbers among K3 surfaces, which correlates with results for elliptic curves. In addition, using computer calculations, we show that almost all K3 surfaces of a given degree have a Jacobian Picard rank of 1. We conclude with suggestions for future research. This paper presents a decentralized algorithm to solve strongly convex optimization problems with $N$ data points and dimension $d$, where each node computes an epsilon-approximate solution with only local communications between neighboring nodes and limited computational resources, as if it had all the data and the gradient information for the entire dataset, all while maintaining stability and efficient resource usage. We introduce a novel method that combines elements of distributed Newton and quantized distributed projected gradient descent, where the algorithm iteratively computes a weighted average of local gradients, quantizes and broadcasts this average to all nodes, which then compute and broadcast updated solutions, with each node responsible for computing its solution. We analyze the computational and communication costs of this algorithm, derive the required quantization step for convergence, and verify the results through simulations in non-negative matrix factorization applications. We assert that this algorithm is the first to achieve such results for strongly convex optimization in decentralized settings. Our research involves investigating the prospects of indigenizing the techniques employed by NLP practitioners in Western countries to tackle problems relevant to our native language speakers in an increasingly global world. We have selected India's two primary languages, Hindi and Bengali, along with a related third language, English. Our focus is on developing effective models to monitor and regulate online hate-speech dissemination. Given the severe consequences of hate-based movements, such as those fueling anti-minority sentiments in India, accurately detecting hate-speech across diverse languages, including English, has become crucial. We have established an innovative dataset comprised of 2,427 annotated reviews from users, split equally into training, testing, and validation sets, to facilitate comparison with the recently published HIBERT model. In a recent study, a machine learning model for evaluating commercial driving skills has been presented. This model can provide more accurate and adaptive evaluations of driving skills by considering various factors, as compared to a traditional machine learning approach. To support the use of this model in sensitive settings, two new methods for gathering expert feedback have been proposed. These methods aim to improve fairness and transparency in the evaluation process. First, a modification of the evaluation process was proposed, enabling drivers to select and justify their ratings for certain aspects of performance. Second, a technique called Post-Hoc Rationalization was proposed, allowing experts to provide feedback based on the reasoned basis for their ratings. Both methods were successfully tested in a collaborative project with commercial drivers working in local food delivery services. The project resulted in gathering a large quantity of expert feedback with improved consistency, which in turn enabled the training of more accurate and fair models. The code and model has been made publicly available to the research community at https://github.com/epicentre-utd/commercial-driving-evaluation. The research findings have also been implemented in a working collaboration with a prominent food delivery company. Our study presents novel approaches for gathering expert feedback, demonstrates their effectiveness, and highlights their value in the development of fair and adaptive evaluation systems. Moreover, the research sheds light on the process of collaboration between industry partners and researchers, which was crucial in the achievement of the study's outcomes. The research contributes to the advancement of the research field of evaluation and decision-making assistance. Lastly, the research presents a concrete example of Practical AI.

This paper reports on the outcomes of the recently concluded Out-of-Context (OoC) 
Challenge in NLP 2023, where participants tasked the winning system, TAYA, to 
process and respond to out-of-context requests appropriately, albeit with 
limited visibility of the prior conversation. Unlike other dialogue systems, 
TAYA's architecture is purposefully simplistic, given the absence of essential 
conversational cues. Despite these limitations, TAYA emerged as the top-performing 
system in four out of five robust evaluation categories, where the absence of 
scoring bias was ensured. Interestingly, TAYA's performance was found to improve 
considerably with the incorporation of a novel, noise-reduced dataset called 
noiseco. This dataset aims to boost model robustness through carefully crafted 
noise-related prompts. Couples with an accompanying tutorial on dataset 
creation, the noiseco dataset is expected to facilitate improved model 
robustness in the dialogue and out-of-context domains. Through experiments, the 
paper delves into the challenges posed by noisy text and out-of-context requests, 
attempts to gauge the impact of these limitations on model performance, and 
suggests potential future research directions. Furthermore, the paper provides 
detailed analyses of the challenge results, alongside the accompanying code and 
dataset, which can be accessed at https://github.com/gagarina/ooc-challenge.

When a wing's upper surface presents a smoother obstacle to air particles than its lower surface, it is considered a positive cambered wing. Note that while this model's justification may be applied to negative cambered wings, the upper surface of such wings present greater resistance to air particles than their lower surface except when they are operated under the conditions of rarefaction, as explained in the principles of aerodynamics.  This paper consists of three sections, the first of which describes a model's justification through the example of a square cross-section of a wing.  In the second section, the model's justification is extended to rectangular cross-sections of a wing.  The final section of this paper discusses the implications of its mathematical results from both a physical and mathematical perspective. We are presenting a novel mathematical approach, the outward complex scaling method, to solve the Schrödinger equation in the presence of a strong direct current (DC) electric field for both electrons and nuclei within a nonvariational framework. This method generates a complete set of scaling equations to determine the energies related to the states born from the ground state through a perturbation of any order. We start by applying this method to the hydrogen atom and obtain accurate results for the energies of the states in the nonrelativistic regime, especially at high orders of perturbation. We also use it to investigate the currently unresolved critical DC field that would allow the one-dimensional confinement of a nucleus, and we establish that a finite DC field exists that can achieve this confinement. Although this approach can be generally extended to the electrons in a molecule, the same cannot be said of the nuclei due to three-dimensional structures, but we can use it to calculate the DC field that would allow the one-dimensional confinement of a diatomic molecule. Lastly, we conclude with some practical comments on how to numerically compute the required inner products that appear in the outward complex scaling method. This conclusion complements our prior work on the conventional complex scaling method in the outward direction. We anticipate that our new approach will greatly aid us in the investigation of the quantum mechanics of extremely strong DC fields. We plan to use it to study the behavior of electrons in one- and two-electron atoms and molecules, and then extend it to the relativistic quantum mechanics of one- and two-body systems, including the investigation of the critical DC fields that would allow the one-dimensional confinement of structures that are both bound and unbound. This research will be reported upon in the future. Our research focuses on the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the diversity of contact interactions within cities. To investigate this, we analyzed the changes in spatial mobility and meeting patterns at the zonal level for three major US cities: Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York City. Utilizing smart device data, we discovered significant variations in the severity and duration of pandemic-related restrictions across these cities. Furthermore, we found that the implementation of these measures had a profound impact on the diversity of urban interactions, particularly among lower-income neighborhoods which initially bore the brunt of reduced economic activity. However, our analysis also revealed an unexpected increase in the concentration of an individual's social interactions after the onset of the pandemic. This anomalous outcome was particularly noticeable in NYC. We hypothesize that the underlayer driving this phenomenon involves a combination of increased reliance on personal vehicles and altered daily routines, which in turn significantly affects urban environmental diversity. Moreover, our findings suggest that the long-term consequences of the pandemic could potentially exacerbate income disparity, rather than merely postponing it. To address emerging challenges related to future crises, our research recommends the development of more comprehensive urban spatial policies. By promoting a greater sense of spatial flexibility, we aim to create a more cohesive, less segregated urban environment. Such an approach aligns with existing urban planning strategies worldwide. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of diversity in urban environments and encourages further research in this area. Given the ample availability of location data during the pandemic, our findings offer valuable insights into the intricate relationship between economic policies, human behavior, diversity, and the societal impacts of global crises. They also offer practical solutions to mitigate these adverse effects. Furthermore, our analysis employs a universal metric of spatial flexibility, enabling cross-city comparisons and demonstrations of how government policies influence urban diversity. Such research has the potential to be a valuable resource not only in the US but also globally. Finally, our study explores multiple scenarios to estimate the long-term impacts of pandemic-induced changes, demonstrating a key principle: that the end result of extraordinary circumstances is often unforeseen. Adherence to conventional pandemic protocols, for instance, unexpectedly accelerated the concentration of an individual's social interactions. Conversely, alternative policies, such as mass public transportation, amplified urban environmental diversity. Our research offers a theoretical framework for estimating the long-term effects of government responses to crises. To estimate the duration and causes of changes, we apply Markov chain analysis. To evaluate the consequences of changes, we use the theoretical framework from previous studies. Our study generates various scenarios and estimates the resulting consequences.

We have developed a novel, scalable numerical approach for simulating two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. We aim to accelerate large-scale multi-phase flow computations by leveraging parallel processing. A prerequisite for an efficient solution is achieving a stable, nearly fully linear system through preconditioning. We have evaluated the effectiveness of a pioneering field-split approach, decoupling flow and transport equations, yet introducing non-linear corrections to achieve greater efficiency. However, non-linear preconditioners lack theoretical guarantees of convergence. We have extended a widely-used field-split scheme by incorporating various non-linear preconditioners based on Newton-Krylov methods. We have computed convergence rates and essential matrix conditionality measures for a comprehensive set of non-linear preconditioners. We have also conducted extensive parallel simulations on an 80-million-point domain with a fine-grid spacing. Notably, the preconditions we proposed for flow and transport showed a 2-3 times improvement in convergence speed compared to the original Transport-First method. Moreover, our approach allowed us to conduct a 40-hour simulation of a 40-million-point domain at its finest resolution, whereas the Transport-First method failed to converge. These results validate the potential of our proposed preconditions to significantly accelerate two-phase flow simulations on an industrial scale. Furthermore, our approach has significant implications for real-world applications, such as oil reservoir modeling and cancer treatment simulations. We plan to integrate our preconditions into a publicly-available, parallel two-phase flow solver called PAThES. Our research utilizes the coherence of spin-exchange narrowed rubidium ion ensembles to examine crystalline motions within 2D crystals. The core group of galaxies with unusual microwave emission, originally identified by the GLASS survey, was selected for the present study. Initially, the analysis focused on galaxies with synchrotron emission clearly dominant in their radio spectrum. Observations of eight galaxies were carried out using the Sardinia Radio Telescope, with five detected emissions, three highly flat spectra, and four unresponsive galaxies. Data on flat-spectrum galaxies suggested weak and highly variable emissions, typically in the range of 28-33 GHz, with strength corresponding to less than 0.1% of total radio emission. It is hypothesized that unresponsive galaxies may have emissions below the SRT's detection threshold. Moreover, the presence of flat or weak spectra in these unusual galaxies poses difficulties in accurately classifying their emissions as radiative or anomalous. Notably, the present study successfully identified two previously overlooked sources, both exhibiting microwave anomalies that could be attributed to Pulsed Radio Emission (PRE). The research raises additional questions, inquiring whether the anomalies in the flat-spectrum galaxies point to more occurrences of PRE, or if the microwave anomalies are evidence of localized, highly intense particle accelerators. The study's data allows for the estimation of the total number of relativistic electrons necessary to produce the microwave emissions as $\sim 5\cdot 10^{48}$ in the 28-33 GHz range for the strong sources. The present count is roughly an order of magnitude lower than the 28-33 GHz total in the whole GLASS survey. Moreover, the study's data indicates that the microwave emissions could cover only $\sim$2% of the sources' hot gas volume, assuming the electrons' momentum spectrum given by the Bohm diffusion mechanism. Further investigations are required to resolve the nature of the microwave anomalies and their relationship with the total radio emission. Compounds displaying both ferroelectricity and calcoric properties are rare among solids. Despite detailed studies using neutron scattering, the underlying proton dynamics in these unique materials remain largely unexplained. We present evidence that neutron spin-echo spectroscopy can directly measure the fast motion of protons in both high- and low-temperature ferroelectric states of ammonium sulfate. Our results show that protons exhibit relatively simple and fast motion at both temperatures, contradicting earlier proposals suggesting a connection between caloric and ferroelectric properties and more complex proton dynamics. We suggest that the fast proton motion in both states be attributed to a universal ionic mechanism. This discovery highlights the potential of using various types of neutron spectroscopy to investigate materials and points to a need for revisiting the interpretation of previous experiments. Moreover, given that ammonium sulfate's high-temperature fast proton dynamics resemble those of other ferroelectric and caloric materials, it is reasonable to assume that these compounds may also exhibit similar proton dynamics, which could explain the unique properties of these unique materials. Such a connection could offer a new perspective for the development of correlation, functional, and topological materials, as well as a deeper understanding of the relationship between solid-state chemistry and biology. This approach incorporates complexifications of gauge groups and shows that adding complexity to physical systems increases their ability to exhibit non-local effects. Simulations of these systems with up to 240 particles demonstrate non-local behavior that cannot be explained by classical probability or the Carmichael rule. Moreover, we propose a new concept, termed quantum potentiality, and show that the level of quantum potentiality in these systems correlates with their ability to exhibit non-local effects. For metric spaces, defining close neighbors for time series under the Frechet distance leads to a complex computational problem. Various approximations have been developed to speed up computations, yet most of these methods lack guarantees for obtaining these approximations. In this context, we establish that certain approximation algorithms for finding close neighbors, commonly used in Frechet distance applications, provide guaranteed bounds on approximation error. We demonstrate that these algorithms give exact results within a distance of at most $\varepsilon/2$ to the true closest neighbor, and also show that no further reduction in $\varepsilon/2$ precision can be achieved without computing the exact closest neighbor. Our study employs the Korn algorithm for our analysis, but also shows that similar results can be obtained for the Elzey-Feldman algorithm. Moreover, we provide a lower bound on the average precision of approximate closest neighbor search in general metric spaces. Our findings have practical implications, as they motivate the use of the Korn method in applications where exact computation may be feasible. Furthermore, in scenarios where exact computation is not possible, our work suggests combining the Elzey-Feldman algorithm with a sampling technique inspired by our previous work to speed up approximate closest neighbor search. The effectiveness of our proposed sampling approach for two time series closest neighbor search under the Frechet distance is confirmed through empirical evaluation. Precision precision tradeoffs are a key consideration for measurements, as the choice of measurement parameters can affect both accuracy and precision. Typically, higher precision comes at the cost of precision, but research has revealed scenarios where post-analysis enhancements can reverse this tradeoff. We develop a method, the iterative Bayesian unraveling, to analyze how precision can be recovered from imperfect measurements. By reiterating Bayesian inference with a modified prior, the method can refine measurement uncertainties and improve precision, with the potential to do so without additional data. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach in theory and practice across various scenarios, including optimal and non-optimal measurements, and show its applicability to diverse parameter estimation scenarios. We also discuss the implications of our work for future measurement design. Our code is available to facilitate future applications. In summary, the Bayesian unraveling is a powerful tool for reversing the precision tradeoff in measurements and can be an invaluable tool for parameter estimation tasks. Its versatility and adaptability in comparison to existing tools make it a promising solution for various applications. Its primary advantages over existing solutions include its capacity to process non-optimal measurements, recover precision without data, and enhance uncertainties in a stable manner. We discuss the similarities and differences between our method and existing approaches in the context of measurement precision, demonstrating that our approach outperforms them in specified scenarios. Conversely, our method shows that precision can be improved with data, contradicting the principles of conventional unraveling. We use the confidence interval gap metric to quantify the method's effectiveness in practice. In contrast to conventional unraveling, which is confined to optimal measurements and relies on data to improve precision, our approach expands its applicability to non-optimal measurements and can achieve similar results without data, making it a more versatile and efficient tool. Our findings indicate that the Bayesian unraveling can be an efficient and versatile solution for precision enhancement in various applications. Its robust performance across different measurement scenarios makes it a promising tool for diverse fields. We further demonstrate the importance of accurate measurement parameter design to recover lost precision, emphasizing its impact when errors occur during data collection. We hope our approach will contribute to future measurement design by bridging the gap between theoretical and practical applications. As robotic assistance becomes more prevalent in everyday life, the robot's intentions and actions are evaluated against the standards of the environment they occupy. Unfortunately, the robot's expectations may not align with those of the human participants due to discrepancies in understanding the conventional use of space. This study examines how robotic assistance can impart societal norms and expectations to humans by means of shared control interaction. We designed a novel technique, Spatial Language-Based Shared Autonomy, incorporating verbal guidance to inform human-robot collaboration. A series of experiments demonstrated that prior spatial awareness informed by verbal guidance enhances human-robot coordination and recognition of the robot's goals. Moreover, the robot's goal predictions are free from preconceptions and are capable of adapting to novel situations. We discuss how the use of verbal guidance can be employed to communicate the robot's intentions and serve as a means of conveying societal norms and expectations to humans. Ultimately, the research outlines the potential for shared autonomy to play a key role in conveying robotic intent and societal norms in collaborative settings. In numerous cases, an autonomous agent requires knowledge of its surroundings to complete tasks efficiently. We concentrate on a particular class of agents that need to navigate efficiently. Developing a navigation strategy for an agent in an unfamiliar environment is complicated by (i) the absence of a map that divides the environment into manageable sections and (ii) the absence of landmarks that serve as distinct reference points. To address these challenges, we propose HiTMap - a map-making algorithm - that creates hierarchical topological layouts for navigation in unknown environments. Initially, HiTMap identifies distinct regions in the environment based on spatial features, and then it breaks down each area into smaller sub-regions to create a multi-scale topological map structure. We show that HiTMap significantly simplifies the navigation process in complex environments by leveraging its inherent properties. By using small spatial scales, an agent can quickly identify its position in the environment, and then it can focus on selecting an optimal route by higher scales representing the main paths of the environment. We validate the efficacy of HiTMap through comprehensive experiments in both real-world and simulated scenarios. We also provide empirical analysis to demonstrate the advantages of our hierarchy-based navigation approach over alternative strategies. This study proposes an abstract data type, the SLIS, which represents multivariate time-based data and facilitates parallel rendering on multiple displays. In this context, the term "longitudinal data" refers to data sets with temporal and categorical dimensions, which can be visualized using parallel lines or bars to show measurements across different categories taken from the same individuals or groups over time. To optimize visualization, the SLIS data type includes an algorithm that strategically samples categorical and temporal dimensions, allowing for a balance between detail and screen space. Moreover, the suggested class includes methods for sorting based on categorical values and spatial relationships, as well as techniques for identifying anomalies and clustering patterns. Some potential applications and extensions of this idea are also outlined, such as its use in analyzing event sequences and detecting circular patterns in time-based data. Although the initial implementation was done in Java, the concept can be easily adapted for use in other programming languages. The medical field has witnessed an extraordinary expansion in collected data, offering an unparalleled opportunity for healthcare professionals to make more informed decisions with better insights. However, the graphical structure of this data presents difficulties in incorporating relationships between variables via neural networks. To overcome these challenges, research has led to the development of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which can efficiently process the expanded medical data and uncover hidden patterns within. Despite their success, current GNNs mainly focus on optimizing individual variables for specific tasks, overlooking the complexities of medical data that demand more flexible and robust solutions. Moreover, recent advancements in diversifying GNNs with multi-task training approaches have limitations, as they cannot guarantee similarity preservation for input variables. This notion is crucial, as similar input variables should produce similar output results. To address these concerns, this paper introduces a novel Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN) with an optimized similarity graph, which combines numerous medical information types, and trains it with an innovative method of using multiple diverse inputs to enhance robustness and diversify similar results. Experimental data proves that our DSGNN model surpasses other neural networks in diverse similarity tasks, also successfully applying GNN to diverse medical problems like disease similarity and lung cancer risk prediction. Given the absence of a universal gold standard for assessing lesion extent, datasets are typically annotated by in-house experts, leading to potential biases. Consequently, models trained on these datasets may adapt to specific annotation guidelines rather than the true lesion definition. Traditional approaches, involving the incorporation of previous datasets with modified hyperparameters or weights, has been shown to hinder performance. Moreover, CarNat facilitated the first-ever benchmark for lesion segmentation across clinics and demonstrated superior real-world performance. The presence of Infrared Dark Nebulae (IDNs) in molecular clouds represents dense cores excluded from illuminating light, which belies their potential significance in massive star formation. By tracing dust continuum emission, IDNs can be studied at various evolutionary stages. Our aim is to examine whether these dense cores are generating new stars. By analyzing a sample of IDNs in the Carina Molecular Cloud with Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter-wave telescope, we identified 8 IDNs showing spectral lines characteristic of massive star formation, which we subsequently followed up with high angular resolution spectroscopic observations. Our results reveal that two IDNs are clearly engaging in star formation, whereas the remaining six IDNs show no evidence of forming stars. We deduced that the intense reddening of IDNs observed in our sample is the result of dust produced by nearby star-forming regions rather than the inherent interstellar medium background. The presence of massive dense cores which do not show signs of star formation suggests promising targets for searching for newly formed stars. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that these IDNs are located proximal to established star-forming regions, which may be responsible for triggering the formation of the stars within them. Finally, we estimate that the vast majority of massive dense cores are still hidden from view, awaiting the emergence of their stars. Current models, however, look backward and use preceding words as references for the current word's prediction. As a result, when dealing with topics that have outdated or irrelevant precedents, looking backward can be a significant drawback. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel mechanism called "look-forward attention." In this innovative approach, we allow the model to look forward and consider subsequent words as relevant references for the current word's prediction. This "look-forward attention" mechanism can be implemented using various methods, including incorporating preceding words as an additional channel in the attention computation or utilizing a constraint to ensure that the attention distribution does not focus solely on previous words. This note clarifies and updates the key findings of a prior work, offering a general framework for Asian options valuation. The original paper built on a pioneering idea in Chen and Carr (2018), yet the new analysis addresses several unresolved issues in a clear and comprehensive manner. Beyond correcting errors and adding insights, the updated framework now makes Asian options valuation accessible through a readily implementable spreadsheet. The revised work also presents a new, efficient method for pricing Asian options. Finally, the updated analysis extends the valuation techniques to more complex derivatives. 

Key among the corrections is the identification and rectification of a crucial flaw introduced in Chen and Carr (2018). The flaw related to dynamically allocating computational resources, leading to slow computation times. Additionally, the updated framework addresses an open question regarding the construction of a suitable time-homogeneous transformation. Lastly, the updated analysis constructs and exploits a useful time-invariant density, facilitating an efficient method for pricing arithmetic Asian options. 

Valued at over $2 trillion, Asian options are a crucial derivative type, widely applied in many situations, such as an options contract on the average stock price, to hedge against losses in specific price movements. Historically, exact analytical solutions have only been developed for a few Markov processes, like the geometric Brownian motion and the arithmetic/geometric Brownian motions. As a result, most studies on Asian options only considered these few Markov processes. 

Key among the newly introduced concepts is the idea of a time-homogeneous transformation, a general approach to tackle any finite Markov process. Although great progress has been achieved by deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) in semantic segmentation and image classification tasks, the mechanisms underlying their decision-making processes remain unclear. In order to shed more light on these mechanisms, we present VHFSFA, a novel interpretation technique based on attention that reveals the collaborations between DCNN's visual and semantic components. VHFSFA's structure consists of a module that combines semantic information with layer-specific visual information from DCNN, thereby facilitating an understanding of decisions at each decision stage. Multiple evaluations conducted on ImageNet, PASCAL VOC 2012, and PASCAL VOC Challenge 2015 indicate that VHFSFA achieves high accuracy without compromising performance. Moreover, we analyze the semantic interpretation of DCNN at different layers, and observed that the key contributors vary depending on the stage of the DCNN. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that by integrating semantic information, DCNN's confidence in its predictions increases, especially for difficult cases. Our final findings reveal that by utilizing DCNN plus VHFSFA, we achieve state-of-the-art results on PASCAL VOC 2012 and PASCAL VOC Challenge 2015 datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/ziplab/VHFSFA. VHFSFA was visually demonstrated at IEEE ICME 2021. The video can be accessed at: https://youtu.be/y4tY2oYk2Gw. With VHFSFA, by integrating visual and semantic information, we are able to gain a deeper understanding of decision-making processes of DCNNs, and achieve state-of-the-art performance in various evaluation experiments. Furthermore, our results also suggest a novel approach to validate and interpret the existing models, including those that have been trained on a multitude of tasks by transferring knowledge from other domains without comprehensive human annotation. Such interpretation is crucial, given the growing interest in incorporating human intelligence into machine design. Lastly, our results indicate that by incorporating human intelligence into machine design, we can achieve a more reliable and understandable AI system that is in line with human values. Such a system benefits both humans and machines, and facilitates a deeper and more constructive interaction between the two. The proposed method enables a collaborative and harmonious interaction between human and machine. The main idea was developed by Hadi Ghasemipour under the supervision of Prof. Kang K. Toh.
