In the context of the Holstein model, where one electron interacts with a Debye phonon mode and acquires mass as well as an electron-electron interaction for a better representation, the phase diagram is mapped out in terms of temperature and coupling parameters for systems of any number of units. Notably, this model exhibits a notable distinction from the previous Peierls model in that it allows for an attractive interaction, and this property becomes increasingly significant in larger systems. By distinguishing between direct and swap processes involving electrons and phonons, the influence of phonon dispersion is separated from that of electron distribution, and it is shown that the attractive interaction is predominantly facilitated by phonon dispersion. Moreover, by expanding the model to include infinite coupling of electrons, the influence of phonon dispersion on the system's properties is observed in the gap at low temperatures, and it is revealed that phonon dispersion can cause a significant deviation from BCS predictions regarding critical coupling and critical temperature. Lastly, by comparing the model in one dimension with others that have multiple dimensions, it is found that the former's interaction is primarily facilitated by phonon dispersion, and this is distinct from the latter's case, and it is also shown that the latter's behavior can be reduced to one-dimensional behavior solely under the condition of weak electron-electron interaction. The findings of this study are supported by a numerical method, and it is shown that the effects observed can last for a considerable period of time in one dimension. The study also makes a comparison with a study of cuprates and suggests that the mechanism of interaction behind superconductivity in these materials varies with temperature and is more complex than what the model can describe. Nevertheless, it is also shown that the mechanism of interaction described by the model is present in one-dimensional behavior and it is responsible for superconductivity in very low temperatures. In the realm of magnetic materials, the presence of topological defects, particularly skyrmions, has been very fruitful for scientists. Among these, the most accessible are stabilized by localized clusters of magnetic ions as opposed to being stabilized within the bulk of the material. A relatively new type of system, known as the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ cluster system, is known to exhibit extremely stable lattice formations of these topological defects even at room temperature. This study delves into understanding the melting dynamics of these cluster formations in response to electrical current when they are in contact with a Hall bar, by observing changes in magnetoresistance and magnetohostility properties, as well as conducting in situ dc-magnetization measurements. This analysis reveals that the cluster formations undergo rapid melting via what is known as the bloch wall mechanism. Moreover, the melting dynamics are found to be heavily influenced by the temperature-dependent stability of the clusters. This phenomenon could potentially offer a previously unseen level of control over these cluster formations, thereby opening up new avenues of research in the field of magnetic cluster systems. This study demonstrates that the cluster formations in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ are both stable and can be manipulated at various temperatures. This could be achieved by utilizing either magnetic fields or electrical currents at low temperatures, thereby enabling room temperature melting and room temperature control. This study therefore confirms that the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ cluster system possesses a level of stability that is greater than previously anticipated. Additionally, the system exhibits characteristics that are distinct from the recently discovered "memory" type metals that require the application of multiple magnetic fields to change the structure. Therefore, the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ cluster system possesses a unique characteristic profile distinct from the currently existing magnetic cluster formations. This study therefore identifies Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ cluster formations as ideal models to study the dynamics and long term stability of these cluster formations. Furthermore, the system exhibits characteristics that are easily accessible at room temperature and can be manipulated at both the microscopic and the material level. Therefore the Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ cluster formations offer a unique platform to study the dynamics and the material model for stable skyrmions. To capture the intricate nature of high-dimensional temporal data, researchers have turned to nonlinear modeling and causal analysis. This has led to the development of innovative methods leveraging partial information about system components and their interconnections. This study provides an overview of the current state of research in this field, focusing on dynamic influence models and their applications to biological systems, where stochastic approaches often prevail. The review will cover key aspects of model techniques, their practical implementations, and showcase prominent applications from the literature. Given the burgeoning interest in this area, the review will not only examine existing methodologies but also explore the challenges and opportunities for further investigation. The intended audience includes experts in the field, researchers entering the area, and those interested in the latest developments in high-dimensional dynamic influence modeling. Furthermore, the paper will conclude with suggestions and potential research directions that are expected to shape the future of this rapidly evolving field. The suggestions presented are informed by the knowledge gained from a workshop held in 2020, which brought together leading researchers to discuss the challenges and opportunities in the area. The written paper and associated videos from the workshop can be accessed through the provided links. This overview and associated resources aim to promote research advancements and create a platform for experts to share their knowledge, thereby advancing the field of high-dimensional dynamic influence modeling. The primary conclusion from the review is that high-dimensional dynamic influence models, unlike other topics in the field, do not have established benchmarks that allow for objective assessments of model performance. To address this challenge, potential research directions identified in this analysis include the development of suitable evaluation metrics and data sets or protocols similar to those in other areas of system identification and causal analysis. Furthermore, the review concludes with a list of key questions that are expected to shape the research agenda and drive theoretical, methodological, and practical advancements in high-dimensional dynamic influence modeling. The questions are meant to stimulate discussions, promote interdisciplinary collaborations, and inspire novel approaches to addressing the mentioned challenges. The requirement for continuous balance in dynamic game models necessitates the use of a stable point, which enforces the balance constraint at every point in time. However, when models are estimated using historical data, calculating a stable point is challenging due to the absence of information about the model's future behavior. Consequently, most balance methods applied in estimation can only ensure that the average violation of balance is minimized, and their ability to maintain balance in the long term is unverified. This paper proposes a new approach that allows the calculation of a stable point even with limited information, making it suitable for long-horizon estimation and forecasting scenarios. This method, which relies on a filter similar to the Kalman filter, not only maintains balance on the surface but also confirms balance stability through a statistical test. Moreover, our approach outperforms existing balance methods in model estimation, particularly in conditions where data is sparse. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we applied it in estimating a consumption-based asset pricing model that necessitates balance on consumption and wealth over multiple assets. By calculating a stable point using the proposed method, we obtained models with successful balance enforcement and accurate asset price predictions. Furthermore, our approach's predictive success was validated through a predictive score test. The theoretical foundations of our approach, along with the associated estimation software, have been made publicly available. Keywords: balance problem, stable point, filter, consumption-based asset pricing, predictive success, long-horizon forecasting. A special relationship between star formation and supermassive black holes exists within galaxies. The molecular outflows discovered recently are thought to play a crucial role in regulating this interaction by removing gas from the central black hole's vicinity. The transfer of this gas to the interstellar medium could initiate the formation of new stars, while excess material could accumulate into star-forming clumps. However, the stability of such clumps is still uncertain. Our observations of the spiral galaxy NGC4945 have revealed a molecular outflow similar to those found in disk galaxies but also uncovered a massive, 107 solar mass, rotating disk of molecular gas extending 435 parsecs from the nucleus. This discovery indicates substantial gas transfer from the central black hole's vicinity to the interstellar gas pool, a process potentially leading to the formation of protostellar clusters. Our findings reprieve the role of molecular outflows in galactic evolution: rather than merely driving star formation, they may actually foster it. Our data suggest that the outflow's base in NGC4945 is surrounded by a 100 parsec wide ring of star-forming clumps, indicating that the outflow gas has contributed to the creation of these clumps. Our estimates show that the mass of this ring's western clump equals 5.8 times 10(8) solar masses, indicating that the outflow has formed at least 20 new star-forming clumps during its lifetime, (2-5) times 10(6) years ago. Our image also shows that the outflow has lost (3.8 +/- 0.3) times 10(-2) per year in momentum and (1.3 +/- 0.3) times 10(-2) per year in kinetic energy since its discovery in 2013 (August). Our data suggest that the outflow's power is not sufficient to launch the surrounding interstellar gas more than 100 parsecs from the nucleus of the galaxy. Our image also indicates that the outflow has not created the extensive, 1.5 times 10(2) solar mass molecular ring surrounding a 40 parsec wide and 66 parsec deep potential well in the galaxy's nucleus. Instead, we attribute the formation of this ring to spatially inhomogeneous star formation in the galaxy. Our model of the inhomogeneous star formation in the galaxy indicates that, in its early stages (2-5) times 10(6) years ago, the outflow has created at least four protostellar clumps

A solution method is developed and tested for a set of simplified plasma equations, including Vlasov, magnetic diffusion, and ion motion. This method extends the conventional finite element method to resolve the nonlinear behavior of plasmas under external magnetic fields. Through theoretical analysis, it's shown that the proposed method always converges and preserves key properties of the original equation, such as positivity and conservation of specific quantities. To validate its effectiveness, simulations are performed on a modified version of the reduced Newcomb equation to reproduce known plasma behaviors, including Stefan problems and Machado's experiment. Additionally, the method is tested on a full magnetized Vlasov distribution, showing agreement with established plasma theories. This research provides a framework for applying the quasilinear diffusion framework to analyze complex plasma phenomena. Furthermore, the properties of the proposed method offer a foundation for extending it to more comprehensive plasma models in the magnetized regime. Finally, the theoretical insights into the convergence properties of the proposed method are extending to a broader class of nonlinear partial differential equations in the magnetized plasma context. A rigorous proof of the exponential stability for the solution of the Cauchy problem associated with a single first-order differential equation in a Banach space is provided. The stability analysis is tied to a Lyapunov condition that must be satisfied in a specific submanifold within the space. Depending on the relationship between certain parameters, two scenarios emerge: an unbounded semigroup if the parameters are not tightly constrained, and an exponentially stable c0-semigroup if the parameters are constrained. Additionally, the properties of the semigroup are extended to include operators whose resolvents satisfy specific bounds, and the notion of robust exponential stability for the semigroup is defined and demonstrated. It is shown that, when the parameters fall within a certain range of displacement from the origin in the Banach space, the c0-semigroup remains exponentially stable. Lastly, the concepts and findings are applied to a nonlinear reaction-diffusion equation bounded by its boundary, subject to homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, and are exemplified through the consideration of a specific nonlinear vector-valued equation known as the Lorenz equation. Our work thus diverges from the conventional treatment found in Standard Textbooks on the topic of semigroup theory and dynamical systems, and instead draws inspiration from the influential paper 'On the Lyapunov conditions of certain approximation schemes for abstract non-autonomous differential equations in Banach space' by K. This paper enhances the existing DocQA framework by introducing a more advanced approach for retrieving relevant documents using dense vector modeling. We present a compact yet efficient model, called C-DPR, which surpasses the performance of the pre-trained DPR engine in several key areas. Subsequently, we perfect a state-of-the-art transformer-based model, called F-TF, which builds upon the T-F model and achieves significant gains in processing speed while retaining high accuracy. Notably, the combination of C-DPR and F-TF models reaches new standards in performance, yielding remarkable results on the SQuAD benchmark. Specifically, the proposed system achieves an impressive 89.5% in mind-related matters and 90.3% in general inquiries. This breakthrough marks the first time a DocQA system has surpassed the Human Score of 89.8, as measured on the SQuAD benchmark. Furthermore, the system has been successfully applied to various real-world applications, including medical contexts. We present empirical analyses in-depth to explain and validate the contributions of each component throughout the DocQA pipeline. We will make the selected code and models available for public access at github.com/asperasoft/embedding-learning. We presented our findings at the Asilomar Conference in August 2021 and at the AAAI Conference in January 2022. Ultimately, the research highlights the importance of incorporating key aspects of a pre-trained model, albeit ones that were previously considered minor, in order to optimize the performance of downstream applications. This underscores a critical challenge for researchers working in the field of EML. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major research priority. Current state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval primarily utilize pre-trained vision backbones with rigid network architectures, thereby hindering the ability to further refine the video representation and yielding suboptimal results. To address these limitations, we present TS2-Net, a groundbreaking transformer architecture incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection, which effectively captures and refines both the text and video tokens' spatial-temporal contexts. TS2-Net comprises a novel token shifting module for adaptively adjusting the positions of tokens and a selection module for identifying salient tokens, and it demonstrates exceptional performance when combined with existing vision backbones. Furthermore, TS2-Net's token shifting and selection capabilities enable cross-modal attention to be seamlessly implemented, thereby avoiding previous multilingual bias issues. Comprehensive experiments conducted on three prominent text-video retrieval benchmarks showcase TS2-Net's superior performance, surpassing state-of-the-art approaches by over 2%, and substantiate the effectiveness of incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection in improving text and video representations. The code for TS2-Net has been made available on the CSAIL Vision-Lab GitHub Platform. The in-depth findings of this study are expected to facilitate the development of novel transformer-based text-video retrieval models in the future. The growing number of Wireless Sensor Networks and Internet of Things devices has led to a significant need to identify disturbances within licensed radio frequency bands. This thesis investigates the use of convolutional neural networks for multi-label interference detection in spectrum sensors. It introduces an innovative dataset, Spectrummy, which is comprised of spectra and sample information. This study explores the network's performance on the Spectrummy dataset and discusses its application in analyzing the output of spectrum sensors. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the network in detecting various types of interference. Moreover, the network's accuracy reaches 70% or higher for detecting all three interferences simultaneously. This research also examines the network's sensitivity to interference types and amounts. Future studies can explore the use of additional deep learning networks, such as recurrent and recurrent convolutional networks, to further improve interference detection performance. Artificial Intelligence has its set of rules and principles, but its ultimate goal is to mimic Human Intelligence, which remains unattainable for now. Achieving General Artificial Intelligence necessitates the development of Enhanced Artificial Intelligence, or second-generation AI. In this paper, we argue that second-generation AI requires Artificial General Intelligence. Additionally, we break down the terminology and concepts associated with first- and second-generation AI, as well as General Artificial Intelligence. Furthermore, we introduce key pillars and components of GAI, and explain how these elements contribute to the creation of GAI. In conclusion, we outline a three-step approach to building GAI, and justify its feasibility. In doing so, we address several crucial questions such as: What distinguishes first- and second-generation AI?, What sets GAI apart from Artificial Neural Networks, Support Vector Machines, and other polyvalent AI systems?, and What attributes must GAI possess to surpass existing AI models?. Ultimately, we posit that GAI-based machines possess the potential to surpass human capabilities in various aspects. For atomic systems featuring multiple clock states, we examine through the density-matrix renormalization group method, the effect of temporal variations on the superfluidity transition for coupled clock-bosons in a two-dimensional optical lattice, where inter-clock interaction is affected by spin-orbit coupling. It is observed that introducing temporal fluctuations, based on the Fibonacci sequence, alters the superfluidity transition relative to a static model and two other models with combined spin-orbit and Hubbard interactions. Notably, our results indicate the existence of two distinct superfluidity phases under certain conditions and suggest the potential for multiple phase shifts in response to temperature changes. Furthermore, our findings are relevant to experimental designs involving multiple clock-state atoms. They provide constraints on the related parameters, especially for systems involving the $1^1\Sigma^+$ and $^3\Sigma^-_l$ states of Rb-85. It is also suggested that superfluidity phases could be accessed via spin-orbit coupling followed by a Feshbach resonance. The related superfluid phase could be identified by the presence of persistent currents in the optical grid and Soudry's clock metric. It is found that temporal modulations can significantly impact the superfluid phase for coupled non-interacting bosons but clock metrology is impaired in such conditions. On the other hand, temporal modulations have little to no impact on the superfluid phase for coupled spin-orbit coupled fermions but fermionic clock metrology can be realized in such conditions. Therefore, bosonic clock metrology cannot be reduced to either bosonic or fermionic clock metrology. It is also shown that temporal modulations can realize multiple phase shifts not achievable through the static model, the spin-orbit coupled non-interacting system, or the Hubbard model with clock metrology. Moreover, our results for the static model, the superfluid transition for coupled clock bosons with spin-orbit coupled pairing can be related to recent experiments using $^1S_0$-$_1P_1$ system of Rb-52. We also extend our calculations to the region of parameter space that realises $\mathcalM_6$ metric in a trimer of clock bosons with nearest neighbor interactions and identify the impact of temporal variations on the superfluid phase in trimers in a incommensurate Floquet lattice. It is shown that the superfluid phase in trimers in a incommensurate Floquet lattice is influenced by the aperiodic nature of the potential and the number of states in the trimers

This study examines various strategic approaches to reduce beam-induced electromagnetic interference in large muon collider complexes, such as the ILC and CLIC, where high-energy muon collisions are achieved by combining multiple fast-rising muon beams. Optimized ring designs with enhanced focusing systems could significantly enhance collision probabilities, reaching yields of tens to hundreds of attobarns per hour, necessitating strategies for suppressing beam-induced effects. In this context, the research evaluates and compares different methods for reducing beam-induced noise, including (i) adjusting muon production parameters, (ii) implementing separated muon capture, and (iii) employing dedicated beam killers. The assessment is based on an in-depth analysis of beam characteristics combined with full-end-to-end simulator models of the ILC and CLIC systems. A four-dimensional optimization method is used to identify suitable parameter sets for each approach, with a focus on maximizing collision rates while minimizing beam-induced effects. It is found that the separated muon capture approach yields up to 80 times reduced beam-induced effects at 200-fold increased muon delivery rates, surpassing the beam killer method in terms of maximum collision yields by up to 40 times. Furthermore, the research explores the potential for improving the optimized beam delivery method in terms of maximum collision rates without altering the beam parameters. In particular, the use of fast muon ionization cooling is considered, with an estimated reduction of yield acceptance by half due to increased emittances in the horizontal plane as a result of increased muon production. A proposed fast cooling in six-dimensional space to improve the transverse and longitudinal emittances of the beam is evaluated, with corresponding increases in energy loss. The fast cooling has the potential to improve the maximum collision rates of the optimized beam delivery method by up to 40 times, with the highest improvement in terms of maximum collision rates for the separated muon capture approach. In summary, the optimized beam delivery method is effective in reducing beam-induced effects across various muon collider designs, with the separated muon capture approach yielding up to 80 times reduced effects at 200-fold increased muon delivery rates. Additionally, the fast cooling concept has the potential to further improve the maximum collision rates of the optimized beam delivery method, with the highest improvement in terms of maximum collision rates for the separated muon capture approach. A corresponding improvement in terms of observed collision yields of tens to hundreds of attobarns per hour is anticipated at CLIC. The optimal muon production parameters, with or without fast cooling, is characterized by high muon intensity

The formation of vortices within a superfluid is restricted by the pauli exclusion principle, as interactions cannot overcome the inherent impossibility of two identical bosons occupying the same spatial and quantum coordinates.  This principle previously restricted the creation of impurity-induced vortices in dilute Bose-condensates through scattering events.  However, our theoretical analysis reveals that in a system of weakly interacting bosons, separated from instability by small interaction strengths, the pauli exclusion principle can be overcome through multiparticle collisional self-interactions, enabling the production of multiple intertwined vortices.  Notably, this phenomenon occurs despite the continued weakness of interactions within the system.  Furthermore, experiments using atomic Bose-Einstein condensates could investigate the inherent boundaries of superfluid stability in highly interacting systems.  Prior theories concerning superfluid stability, based on mean-field approaches, failed to account for this phenomenon, while these theories would predict a reduced threshold for stability in systems of fewer collisional degrees of freedom, in direct conflict with our findings.  Therefore, our results suggest a significant requirement for considering the role of collisional dynamics within superfluid physics, particularly in systems exhibiting non-perturbative and highly nonlinear collisional properties.  It is also possible to extend this concept to the study of superconductivity in strongly coupled fermionic systems, potentially uncovering novel mechanisms of non-perturbative vortex production.  Consequently, our discovery may introduce an important modern constraint on the stability of superfluids and superconductors that goes beyond classical predictions.  Moreover, in the broader context of superfluid/superconductivity, our work is similar to studies of non-rigid quantum molecules and can be extended to other complex atomic systems, where a critical distinction between perturbative and non-perturbative regimes has been identified.  Moreover, our discovery implies an intriguing connection between principles of superposition (e.g. in Bose-Einstein condensation) and superfluid stability, where a distinct and unexpected non-perturbative mechanism of vortex formation can be realized.  Lastly, it is also possible to extend this concept to the study of superfluid $^4He$ by considering $^4He$-atomic mixtures, in which case the inherent walls of superfluid stability in highly coupled systems can be modified through collisional coupling to an external atomic reservoir.  Therefore, our findings suggest a significant modification to the long-standing predictions of superfluid $^4He$ stability that was based on pure $^4He$.  Moreover

The growing size of software test datasets is causing the number of test data points to increase, which is leading to a phenomenon referred to as test smearing. This occurs when flaws are present in systems where the faulty sections overlap with areas containing correct code, causing difficult diagnostic tasks to arise. One strategy to mitigate test smearing involves using minimal datasets, which are designed to focus on key program points, despite being imperfect representations of the full test suite. Nonetheless, the acceptance rate of such minimal test suites tends to be lower in comparison to full test suites, which has led some developers to question the need for minimal testing in the transition from development to maintenance. A goal of this study is to understand the perspective of developers on the use of minimal test suites to counter arguments that they are ineffective. Through a mixed-methods approach combining both quantitative and qualitative methods, the study found that a substantial number of developers (44 out of 64) indicated they would not reject minimal test suites during updates, while 19 out of 64 developers would. Interview results revealed that motivations for accepting or rejecting minimal test suites are diverse and largely independent of concerns about test quality. One key motivation for accepting minimal test suites is the potential they have to help diagnose and fix tricky bugs. Conversely, a common reason for rejecting them is the perceived lack of focus on crucial program elements. A significant finding is that developers' acceptance or rejection of minimal test suites appears to be influenced more by their personal opinions on their usefulness rather than objective measures of their impact. A notable limitation of this study was that it solely focused on the perspective of developers and did not consider the perspective of other stakeholders, such as users. A notepad format has been provided for replication purposes. Empirical findings suggest a future research opportunity to investigate the user's viewpoint on the acceptance or rejection of minimal test suites. Additionally, the study provides a definition for minimal test suites, which can inform maintenance decisions in an empirical context. A research opportunity has also been identified for developers to integrate the principles of minimal testing into the practice of Pull Request review. Our replication link is available at here. Additionally, the data can be accessed at here. Ultimately, the study's findings imply that during maintenance, developers should consider accepting minimal test suites if they acknowledge the test smearing issue and understand how minimal testing can facilitate diagnosing and fixing complex bugs. A particular group where this advice may hold true is software testers. Furthermore, the idea behind minimal testing can potentially be applied to other flaws like fragilities to improve maintenance effectiveness. A future research opportunity

This paper introduces and resolves the existence and uniqueness of solutions for a newly formulated hybrid differential equation that combines element of integral expressions and sweeping conditions, a type of monotone operator. Our strategy for proof is multi-faceted, incorporating the use of a regularized formulation, incorporating properties of the prox-regular sets, and leveraging properties of the Green function. To demonstrate its utility, this theorem is used to develop a method for solving a first-order optimal control problem with a classic Bolza functional through the application of the sweeping conditions. Additionally, a variety of examples are included to illustrate and support our results. Furthermore, by means of the Lagrange multipliers, we prove the second-order necessary optimality conditions for a class of optimally controlled hybrid problems governed by a differential equation, characterized by a nonautonomous right-hand side, with a measure control and a moving convex set in the phase space. Our multi-faceted approach to the problem resolves a challenging class of measure-data optimal control problems, characterized by lack of convexity, measurability issues, and sweeping conditions, through the use of measure-data approximations and the use of selected properties of the sweeping conditions. Lastly, a necessary optimality condition is proved for a class of optimally controlled hybrid problems governed by a differential equation, characterized by a nonautonomous right-hand side, a measure control and a moving convex set in the phase space. Our optimality conditions are of the first and the second order, and are expressed in a implicit way through the Lagrange multipliers. They are derived for a typical trajectory of the control, and a typical trajectory of the measure control. Our conditions involve partial derivatives of the cost functional and those of the Lagrange multipliers, and some of them involve a integral expression of the derivative of the cost functional with respect to the measure control. Our conditions are proved by using a regularization of the measured data, and by employing the properties of the prox-regular sets, and the Green function in the vicinity of zero. Our results are general, and can be applied to a large class of measures. The MMee program is a comprehensive, Monte Carlo-based event generator focused on creating pairs of charged leptons and quarks through the high-energy processes of $e + e -$ and $e +$ at circular leptonic facilities. Building on the proven KKMCee Fortran program, MMee aims to expand accessibility and provide event samples for a broader range of scenarios, including initial state fluctuations enabled by the QED radiation effect. Key outcomes of MMee include the ability to produce polarized $e^-e^+$, $e^-e^+$, and $e\pm e^\pm$ collisions as well as unpolarized $e^-e^-$, $e+e-$, and $e\pm e \pm$ events. The program utilizes a next-to-leading order QCD and QED theory framework to ensure accurate cross-sections and radiation effects. In addition to these fundamental capabilities, MMee offers the option to include initial state fluctuations with multiple Z boson resonances, initial and final state radiation, and rapidity and transverse momentum cuts for efficient data generation. A supplementary tool, the Fast MMee (MMee Fast) mode, is available to provide rapid, order-of-magnitude estimates of unweighted events. The program's technical details and various implementation options are discussed in Chapter 1, while practical applications and generated event files are presented in Chapter 2. As an additional resource, Chapter 3 provides a concise verification of MMee's theoretical framework through multiple comparisons with current theoretical predictions and experimental data. Furthermore, the program's Fortran source code is freely accessible for user modification and integration into their own research environments. The program's one-time compilation is achievable with a Fortran compiler such as gfortran, as demonstrated in the provided online supplementary material. And finally, users can generate MMee-based event files through the designated interface, the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO MadEE interface, described in Chapter 2, as well as the pre-built, fast event files available for direct download on the website https://hepunp.uni Bonn.de/~kayser/fastMee.html. These fast event files are generated using the MMee Fast mode, allowing users to efficiently obtain pair formation events in various scenarios using this program. The program itself can be obtained via the publicly accessible repository https://git.asdf.uni Bonn.de/MadEE/ MMee/tree/2022.2.2, a collaborative effort led by the author. Measuring inter-beat intervals in electrocardiogram signals can be difficult due to noisy environments, but this research introduces a unique model, the Tiramisu model. Based on the proposed model, the experiment showed that the incorporation of signal process techniques significantly improves the accuracy of IBP assessment. Comparing the results to a leading deep learning model, the experiment revealed that the Tiramisu model achieves superior performance with a lower error rate in IBP assessment. While the deep learning model yielded an average IBP assessment error of 20.7 milliseconds, the Tiramisu model achieved an average error of 9.4 milliseconds, indicating its potential as a more efficient and effective technique for IBP assessment. Therefore, the study suggests that the Tiramisu model be used in clinical settings for precise IBP measurements. A novel contribution of this study lies in its incorporation of IBP assessment with denoising methods to achieve noise-free results. Due to the challenging nature of IBP signal denoising, the integration of this approach with the Tiramisu model enables accurate IBP assessment even in noisy conditions. This study's findings can serve as a foundation for developing more advanced techniques to improve IBP assessment models in the future. Ultimately, the study aims to improve the precision of IBP signals in electrocardiogram measurements, leading to more accurate clinical diagnoses. When certain conditions are met, the proposed algorithm is guaranteed to converge to the t-SVD solution. We've also introduced a criterion that specifies when the algorithm can stop based on the change in objective function values. Empirical studies were conducted to examine the relationship between the proposed algorithm's runtime and the selected number of passes beyond numerical precision limits, as well as the impact of starting point variations. These investigations were carried out using the IBM LPA benchmark. Additionally, the paper describes an approach for selecting the optimal number of passes based on the desired runtime and an initial estimation of the convergence threshold. We demonstrate that, given a sufficient number of passes, the proposed algorithm is able to accurately compute the t-SVD. Finally, a comparison of the proposed algorithm with the tensor singular value decomposition variant of the multi-dimensional SVD (mTSVD) approach was performed, showing that, for 10D and higher dimensional tensors, the proposed algorithm is superior to mTSVD in terms of runtime. However, the proposed algorithm turns out to be computationally more efficient than mTSVD at lower dimensionalities through symbolic computations based on the Kronecker product. Moreover, the proposed algorithm is able to accurately recover low-rank tensor properties in a noise-perturbed environment with high levels of corruption up to the rank of the tensor itself. We attribute this resilience to the stochastic method's capability of handling large datasets independently of sizes and tensor dimensions. This paper's primary objective is to resolve the Nirenberg problem, specifically focusing on PDEs that are invariant under SO(n + 1) symmetry. We concentrate on a particular sub-group, A(n), and discover that for n equal to 3 or greater, positive energy solutions do not exist without specifying the radial component of the tensor. Additionally, we show that these solutions, when not radially symmetric, will blow up at a specific point, and our analysis also reveals new blow-up solutions for the equation that has been invariant since 1982, particularly for n equal to 5, 7, and 9. This work extends Betti number forecasts for sample covariance matrices in the sparse regime, using the theoretical framework of Gaussian linear regression. Similar to earlier research, predictions for large samples are made using expected eigenvalue counts and Betti numbers of the level-set hypersurfaces associated with the MLE correlation hyperplane. A modified formula is introduced to correct for the bias associated with the central limit theorem. This is done by replacing expected Betti numbers with stochastic components, composed of the MLE correlation hyperplane's Betti numbers and a variance term. A limiting process is used to simplify this expression. By applying the central limit theorem, the formula is transformed into a tractable expression for large samples, enabling straightforward computation. Notably, in the sparse regime, primary homology and persistence results exhibit a distinct Betti number bias of order N^-1/2, which differs from bias of order N^-1 observed in the general regime. Moreover, in the sparse regime, the second homology group vanishes as N grows. Extrapolating these findings to the case of sparse sample covariance matrices reveals that, in the sparse regime, the persistence function is solely determined by the largest eigenvalue. A critical evaluation is provided of the concepts' practical validity when dealing with real-world datasets. At the same time, it was found that the concepts' theoretical attributes are not entirely reflected in the simulation outcomes. A comparison with the persistence function's application in the generalregime highlights its distinct characteristics in the sparse and general regimes. Overall, the persistence function's utility is confined to the general regime due to its failure to capture real-value bias in the sparse regime. Consequently, valuable insights into the persistence function's behavior were obtained, which can further our comprehension of its underlying properties. One such property is that, unlike correlation hyperplanes, the level-set hypersurfaces' Betti numbers are not correlated. Automating the adjustment of an eye-in-hand camera in a workspace controlled by a robot requires complex 3D environment perception and is necessary for numerous manufacturing applications. We propose an innovative method utilizing a single image to calculate the necessary adjustments for the camera's position. We train a deep learning network to predict the desired rotational adjustments based on the image, taking into account the camera's previous orientation. While all deep learning-based solutions for similar problems use at least two images, such as RGB-D frames or stereo images, our method achieves results through incorporating spatial information from the image alone. We also develop a model to estimate expected camera orientations, leveraging the characteristics of manufacturing environments with generally horizontal planes. We conduct extensive experiments on a dataset comprising 3730 images gathered from a collaborative robot's workspace in a car parts manufacturing plant. We assess various network architectures to determine the most effective design, achieving accurate predictions for up to 90% of cases when using a hierarchical convolutional network with multiple hidden layers. Moreover, we adaptively fine-tune this network's parameters across different workflows in the manufacturing plant. We compare our method with a baseline approach using computer vision alone for calculating desired camera adjustments, ultimately achieving a 52% success rate, which is nearly five times higher than the baseline result. We introduce a groundbreaking technique for calculating desired camera adjustments: the Integration of Angular Averages. We successfully apply this method to various manufacturing applications at the companies where this research took place. We publicly release the relevant code and datasets at https://github.com/josephjz/eye_in_hand_camera. Our method won the Data Challenge at the 2021 ICRA RV-EXTENSIO workshop. Lastly, a related patent was filed with the relevant information at https://patents.google.com/patent/US2022015625A1.

In the realm of online learning, one-area bandits, specifically the linear bandit, has seen significant growth in research. Yet, in environments where action options are numerous and varied, this theory often falls short. Thus, researchers have developed new approaches, known as multi-dimensional linear bandits, targeting diverse action sets. However, these novel methods share a common limitation: they lack a connection to the traditional one-dimensional setting. As a result, they significantly broaden the confidence intervals when comparing average rewards. Our goal is to investigate this expansion relationship and demonstrate its impact on inference capabilities. We also aim to answer two open questions concerning multi-dimensional linear bandits: 1) What lies at the base of this width enlargement? 2) Can we draw a direct line between the multi-dimensional setting and the one-dimensional case? To address these queries, we first establish a baseline by quantifying the width enlargement through a multi-dimensional linear bandit's Gram matrix. Next, we present a new algorithm, simply named "SortOnce," capable of achieving similar regret to the best multi-dimensional linear bandit algorithms while maintaining a reduced width enlargement. Furthermore, we show that "SortOnce" is capable of being modified to also efficiently estimate weights with a minimal regret. Our findings on the relationship between the multi-dimensional and one-dimensional settings suggest that the best multi-dimensional linear bandit algorithms may share a bound with their one-dimensional counterparts. Finally, we also introduce a new "SortOnce"-based multi-dimensional linear bandit algorithm with a simplified computational structure. Our study's findings have also been substantiated through experiments. Overall, our research offers a comprehensive understanding of multi-dimensional linear bandits, allowing for generalizable results that can be applied to a variety of online learning scenarios. Moreover, our contributions on the connection between the multi-dimensional and one-dimensional settings may pave the way for new developments in online learning theory. Deep Graph Neural Networks have become widely used in various applications.  Reinforcement Learning has shown considerable potential in testing GNNs without relying on labeled data, which can be expensive or time-consuming to obtain.  Contaminating training datasets with anomalies is a well-known method to evaluate the resilience of models and metrics such as Robustness Depth Score (RDS).  We studied this method in the context of graph data, however we discovered a problem, as the way we currently generate contaminants and the RDS metric that measures them, is biased.  We found this bias results in GNN models being overly robust to trivial contaminants while being vulnerable to more complex ones.  As a result, our generated contaminants are not as diverse as desired.  We decided to improve this by developing a contamination generation method on graphs inspired by a similar approach already existing in image data contamination generation.  We developed a graph contamination generation method on Jason Lee's ADocker that is guided by a multi-modal distribution of diverse contaminants.  We also developed a multi-task training procedure that allows GNNs to simultaneously minimize their classification accuracy and a constraint that controls the level of contamination in training data.  We tested our approach on popular datasets and our results show that our method is more effective than existing ones.  Our code can be found at https://github.com/alexandru-mos/Adocker-on-Graphs.  We also evaluated the effect of different contamination levels and diversity on the performance of RL and RDS metrics.  We found significant impact of contamination diversity on the model robustness, while impact of contamination level also had an impact, but it was less significant.  Furthermore, we discovered that high quality contaminants are essential for optimal results, and this is in contrast to what we expected.  We found that optimal results occurred when the percentage of contaminants in training data was set to 80%, which is higher than what we expected.  We also found several strategic options to select the optimal level of contaminants, namely varying the diversity of contaminants, extending training time, enhancing GNN model capacity, increasing number of agents and ensemble prediction.  Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of a standardized metric to assess GNNs resilience in graphs.  While our contribution is still theoretical at the moment, we are confident it will be of great help to the community in the future. The process of matching astronomical catalogues can be hindered by crowding, which is mitigated when supplementary photometric data from a higher resolution dataset is combined with the existing astrometric information. This enhances signal-to-noise ratios, thereby minimizing overlap between source profiles. A method involving graphical modeling is applied to mitigate bias in maximum likelihood estimations, which are commonly used in crowding-prone matching. The algorithm's efficacy at accurately identifying cross-matched sources from various catalogues that contain different types of data is verified through the analysis of synthetic datasets. Case studies of real-world datasets from two catalogues, the Two Micron Sky Survey and the UK Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey, demonstrate the need for graphical modeling to accurately determine the associations between sources from these datasets. Furthermore, the analysis highlights the importance of utilizing higher resolution datasets for astrometric refinement of objects in crowded areas of catalogues, which results in significant improvements, with examples seen in the Two Micron Sky Survey. However, this technique may not be necessary for datasets that contain comprehensive photometric data in 15 minute intervals. A related software package, CatalogAugment, is documented such that developers can incorporate additional astrometric source data to further refine the results. The algorithm's computational complexity is noted to be O(n^3) due to the necessity of calculating a Hessian matrix, which may make it less suitable for very large datasets. Future research could explore the use of more advanced optimization techniques, such as MapReduce, to increase the scalability of the algorithm. Individual items within extensive knowledge bases frequently establish connections with multiple other entities, rendering their depiction in conventional Caley graphs impractical due to irregularly dispersed visual representations.  To address this challenge, we develop OntoPlot, a innovative visualization technique that enables exploration of datasets comprising numerous interconnected entities.  By minimizing the need to hierarchically organize or represent cyclical relationships, OntoPlot utilizes an radial layout to clearly show relationships between data sets and their components, thereby facilitating efficient visualization of knowledge bases through the integration of zooming, panning and focus-enabling interactive tools.  To showcase the effectiveness of OntoPlot, we apply it to the visual representation of two knowledge domains: a taxonomy of musical instruments and Wikipedia's incorporated knowledge graph.  Inspection of these visualizations uncovers intriguing patterns such as correlation among musical instruments and the interconnected nature of human and animal life as depicted in Wikipedia's knowledge graph.  We believe that OntoPlot, being a user-friendly interface, can uncover numerous previously unseen patterns within various knowledge domains.  The full OntoPlot code, along with the datasets and knowledge bases, is available for public access at https://github.com/ashish34/OntoPlot.  The OntoPlot demo can also be directly accessed at: https://onto-plot-ashish-demo.herokuapp.com.  Lastly, a 15-minute video detailing the creation of OntoPlot is available at: https://vimeo.org/36213223.  OntoPlot won the 2016 IEEE Conference on Visual Languages and Diplay 2016 VLDP Challenge. We introduce an inter-domain penalty to the end-to-end automatic speech recognition framework that closes the domain gap between speech and text. Our approach leverages CycleGAN to transform speech into speech-like inputs for the end-to-end ASR model, thereby facilitating its training with speech-data and transcribed text. In a related study, we examine the efficacy of several domain shift techniques and find that the inter-domain penalty is superior to existing methods. When combined with Inter-domain penalties, we observe substantial performance improvements from our CycleGAN-based technique. Notably, this method surpasses the conventional self-supervised approach based on Consistency Regularization, particularly in the low SNR regime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using only 5 minutes of synthetic data for model fine-tuning is sufficient to outperform the existing self-supervised approach on the Librispeech dataset across various signal-to-noise ratios. Our proposed method is also shown to be compatible with existing self-supervised approaches, thereby offering a high degree of flexibility. The findings presented here provide a clear roadmap for enhancing the overall model performance. For instance, employing both our proposed technique and the existing self-supervised approach yields a combined error rate that is significantly lower than that obtained with either method in isolation. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made our code available on the GitHub platform. The associated experiments were conducted using the JFT-13 open-source end-to-end ASR code developed by the Facebook AI team. The findings reported here would be readily applicable to other models, whereas our code is easily adaptable to various types of text-to-speech models. The presented work is a direct extension of the findings presented in the related study titled 'Utilizing CycleGAN for Speech-Sensitive Model Regularization'. The related study is distinct from the findings presented here in that it entails combining the inter-domain penalty with a standard self-supervised approach based on Consistency Regularization, whereas this penalty is shown in the present study to be compatible with the CycleGAN technique. The results presented here are a direct refinement of those reported in the related study, wherein the error rates were evaluated on the Clean section of the Librispeech dataset. The findings presented here are, in contrast, relevant to the Noisy section of the Librispeech dataset (SNR > 15 dB). The present study is a continuation of the findings presented in the related study and is a direct extension of the findings presented in the study titled 'Using Monaural and Binaural Speech with Deep Neural Networks for Target-Listener Dependency Modeling'. A predictive model called Profound, which is grounded in Active inference, is proposed for a planar robot navigation task. Despite the absence of a learning-based approach such as deep reinforcement learning, Profound effectively guides the robot to reach goals in a map, using dynamic time-series observations integrating prior knowledge. A novel aspect of Proference is the incorporation of prior distributions for states and actions, which are passed from parent to child in a complete tree searched at each time-step. Importantly, the tree's depth is dynamically controlled through an automated process. Experimental results reveal that Profinding's time complexity is significantly lower than that of recursive Active inference and sampling-based motion planning, yet it outperforms them in reaching targets in a map. Furthermore, Profinding's efficiency can be observed by examining the structure of time-dependent prior distributions for states and actions that Profinding learns across trials. In addition, Profinding's ability to generalize is examined under different environmental and target conditions, with results demonstrating its capability to adapt in these novel scenarios. Finally, Profinding's theoretical scalability is established through proven guarantees for its computational complexity. The analysis, built on a standard theory of Le Chatelier's response, reveals that the rate of soft molecules falling behind during thermal diffusion can be attributed to the internal structural fluctuations within the molecules themselves, rather than solely due to anisotropic viscosity variations. By accounting for the finite probability fluctuations and taking into consideration the average rate of rotational movements, a more accurate expression for contributing viscosity is derived. It becomes evident that as thermal diffusion proceeds, the disparity between parallel and perpendicular viscosities to the diffusion direction grows, yet initially, the internal structural fluctuations contribute significantly to the Soret effect, but eventually their impact lessens and the contributing factor depends more profoundly on the properties of the rotating movement within the molecules. It is found that a more substantial internal structural fluctuation in favor of the diffusion direction results in a more intensified Soret effect, but a random or reversed internal structural fluctuation has a weakening effect on the Soret effect. The study indicates that the Soret effect is generally weakened in systems of low anisotropic viscosity variations. Moreover, the internal structural fluctuations of molecules with biaxial symmetry play the most crucial role in thermal diffusion, as compared to those of prolate or oblate symmetries. To distinguish between the contributing effects of rotational movements and parallel/perpendicular viscosities, parallel measurements can be carried out by fixing the molecules in specified orientations, thereby enabling quantification of the internal structural fluctuations' impact on thermal diffusion. It is also observed that the internal structural fluctuations of samples with low anisotropic viscosity variations (such as CTB and CTBA) can produce Soret coefficients of the same order of magnitude as those of systems with high anisotropic viscosity variations (such as DCHOL and STOL). The internal structural fluctuations of chiral molecules can produce Soret coefficients that depend on the molecular helicity, thereby potentially enhancing the Soret effect. As an added benefit, the internal structural fluctuations of molecules can be controlled through various methods, such as molecular design, external electric/magnetic fields, and laser irradiation, thereby providing an extra avenue for Soret coefficient enhancement. The internal structural fluctuations of composite materials can be controlled and maximized via the selection of suitable soft and rigid segment molecular structures and the arrangement of segments along/different from diffusion directions. Consequently, the Soret effect in various fields can be effectively promoted through internal structural fluctuations. The internal structural fluctuations of molecules also contribute significantly to the self-Propulsion behavior of colloids and Janus particles by influencing the Soret effect in these particles. In the field of Music Information Retrieval, particularly in automatic music composition and evaluation, models must grasp both musical structure and expressive language to criticize composed music. However, current methods are limited by their reliance on manually annotated data and specific domain knowledge. Also, since composition is a diverse and subjective art form, models need to adapt to various genres and individual tastes. To overcome these challenges, we employed a multi-task learning approach to develop a music evaluation system using a combination of recurrent neural networks and an advanced transformer-based language model. We tested our framework across four benchmark datasets and discovered that it performed exceptionally well on music evaluation, generating highly accurate and informative reviews with fluency and versatility. Moreover, our findings reveal the capacity of this approach to tackle various NLP and music comprehension challenges, opening up opportunities for broad applicability in music composition and evaluation. We will make the source code for our framework available to the public.

We tackle the challenge of supressing false positives in pedestrian detectors' output. Although learning to ignore false positives by minimizing a classification loss is an effective approach, it is not well-suited for our needs as it tends to eliminate positive boxes. In our solution, we adopt a distinct strategy where we reject false positives through a lossless process. We incorporate an unsupervised metric that assesses the similarity between positive and negative boxes, thereby triggering a ranking adjustment during training to minimize false positives. This approach is in contrast to box regression as it operates independently of target coordinates. We also incorporate a self-supervised method for the codebook of an offline hash table to enhance pedestrian detection's query efficiency. We tested our method on the Citypersons dataset, revealing a substantial 93% reduction in false positives and an overall 7-frame per second speedup after using the hash table for search. The source code is available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/BRoP. Our method's performance is graphically illustrated in Figure 1. Visualization of the method's performance can be seen in Video 1 and Video 2. As for the method's supervision requirements, ours is largely self-supervised, with minimal need for labels - specifically only box-level annotations are required. We discuss more details about this in Section 2.3. Lastly, another key benefit of our method is that it is simple to implement, requiring roughly just 100 lines of additional code beyond the original Code 1. Our method's key lines of code can be found at the end of this file, specifically at Code 2. The reason for this is that our method is built on top of the existing Box Attention with Re-Ranking (BaRR) method by Tan et al. 2020. We decided to build our method on top of their work as their method successfully identified and localized pedestrians in images via box regression, whereas our method focuses solely on rejecting false positives. We believe that our method is the first of its kind to tackle the challenge of supressing false positives in pedestrian detectors' output through a distinct, lossless and unsupervised and tailored approach that is specifically designed for domain adaptive pedestrian detection. This research explores the potential for developing an alternative, more
general voice encoding method by examining how our perception of speech
relates to visual speech (lip movements) rather than audio. By first using
3D video synthesis to generate face images from given speech samples, and
then employing a voice codec to compress both audio and these images, we
create a unified voice representation that can potentially outdo existing
methods. When evaluated using the MOS-NLQR score on the WSJ corpus, our
novel representation surpasses both the narrowband and wideband PCM codecs.
Furthermore, using this representation allows us to create a voice codec
comprised of a lossless component for high-frequency image data, a lossy
component for low-frequency image data, and a lossy component for audio,
which further improves speaker quality at equivalent bit rates. When this
codec's performance is compared to other popular voice codecs, it achieves
better speaker quality at similar bit rates, with the bit rate required
for comparable quality being lower than that of the other codecs. Hence, our
method leads to high-quality voice representation that outdoes existing
voice codecs both in terms of speaker quality and data efficiency. When
cross-validation is used to optimize this lossy encoder/decoder pair, its
performance improves even further, with the current method being one of the
most effective voice representation approaches to date, especially in terms
of efficiency. Therefore, this research contributes to the development of
efficient voice representation techniques. An implementation of the model is
available at https://github.com/mostafaTarek/AICIV. Based on this approach,

track 1. The link to the challenge is https://ictassp2021.github.io/track1page. Furthermore, our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mostafaTarek/AICIV. Our research delves into the impact of incorrect mechanics in throwing actions on player efficacy, as measured by score and completion rate, in a 2D throwing game. By implementing a variety of techniques to simulate arm motions, we aim to understand how the mechanics of throwing function and how they can be represented. The artificial throwing system, 'FauxThrow', utilizes vector equations to simulate arm movements, and we modify these to create faulty throwing mechanics and control them via the player. When these flawed mechanics are used in the game, player performance suffers, indicating that accurate understanding of physical motions is essential for engaging gameplay. Following player feedback, we can tailor the mechanics to improve their scores, highlighting their intrinsic motivation in determining game dynamics. This research demonstrates the practical application of motion simulation in game design and provides a framework for evaluating and adjusting game mechanics based on player feedback. Ultimately, our work offers guidelines for designing throwing mechanics and control schemes. The code for our project is available at https://github.com/No-Signal/FauxThrow. To incorporate syntax into neural machine translation (NMT), we suggest combining a syntax-based decoding method with a new tree-structured neural model. This new model, called TSD, can handle the translation of short and long sentences by utilizing a tree structure. TSD considers two types of connections, a pre-defined syntax-based link and a learned neural link, to transfer information between words. The decoding process starts from the words and builds the translation tree following the predicted syntax-based link. Additionally, TSD includes a module that learns how to link words. We developed a method to mitigate the bias toward the most likely connection during decoding. We evaluated TSD on the EN-FR NMT dataset and the CoNLL 2017 Parsing dataset, and the results indicate that it outperforms the state-of-the-art model. Furthermore, we observed that the learned connections conform to established syntax while the model exhibits superior translation quality when accompanied by syntax-based decoding. Moreover, when applied to the CoNLL 2017 Parsing dataset, TSD surpassed the state-of-the-art model in all metrics. All source code is accessible via the link: https://github.com/alexkilian/tsd_nmt. In interstellar chemistry, the binding energy of small molecules to colder dust grains often sets the minimum energy requirement for the formation of specific compounds to occur competitively. Since experimental determination of such binding energies is challenging, computational models have been crucial in understanding the relationships between chemical structure and binding energies. Many studies have employed the magic angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance technique to this end, supplying valuable data on the width of molecular binding energy distributions. In this context, our new platform, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, was developed to compile and release results from quantum chemical simulations of the binding of various hydrogen species to graphite and silicate surfaces, matched with the corresponding experimental results. With the BEAP, researchers can access results from over 1000 calculations of intermolecular potentials as well as models for desorption, allowing further exploration of intermolecular forces and facilitating the comparison of theoretical and experimental results. Additionally, a section of the platform has been set aside for future outcomes from state-of-the-art molecular dynamics simulations. With the platform's first edition focusing on C-H, O-H, and N-H molecules bound to graphite surfaces, future updates are expected to include classifications of even more complex compounds such as amino acid hydrogens. By releasing source code for the platform and associated tools, we intend to involve the astrochemical community in developing new content. We anticipate that the platform, meant to be a collaborative resource, can be expanded to cover other types of hydrogen-containing molecules and even larger organic molecules such as nucleotries and amino acids. Furthermore, we aim to make the platform a hub for the assessment and evaluation of theoretical models for desorption and binding energies. Besides facilitating the evaluation of compound-specific binding energy distributions, the platform can also be employed to evaluate phase-specific binding energy models and offer recommendations for suitable model selection based on existing data. In this study, we describe the platform, provide an overview of the simulated binding energy distributions of various hydrogen-containing molecules, and compare them with corresponding experimental results. By doing so, we reveal some community trends regarding the relationship between molecular structure and binding energies. This average value is represented as $\mathcal{O}(1)$ and is achievable using a specific target value of $\mathcal{O}(poly(\log k))$, which is derived from applying a random Clifford circuit of low depth on the state $\rho$. The global solvability of the Davey-Stewartson II equations is demonstrated for initial data pairs $(u, v)$ in specific $L^2$ subspaces by using a standard Riemann-Hilbert framework. The field of text categorization (TC) has seen numerous sibylvariants proposed as robust solutions to handle exceptional conditions in TC tasks. To date, there is a lack of comprehensive research on these variants. This study aims to examine 10 sibylvariants in relation to exceptional events like misspelling, incomplete, or truncated texts. We investigated the performance of these variants using two metrics: correction of misspells and tolerance of incomplete or truncated texts. Our results indicate that some sibylvariants are adaptable to diverse TC tasks, while others are sensitive to specific tasks. We discovered that the encoder sibylvariant is effective in handling misspells, and the truncator sibylvariant is efficient in coping with incomplete or truncated texts. Interestingly, the encoder and truncator combinations did not worsen the performance in most cases. Additionally, we found that the current implementations of some sibylvariants are suboptimal. For instance, the classifier sibylvariant can be improved by employing different classification algorithms. Our research is a fundamental step towards understanding the performance of sibylvariants and may serve as a starting point for future advancements in TC. The source code is publicly available at the repository https://github.com/Anderson Santana/sibylvariants. Our experiments were performed using BERT-JUMU, a fast BERT model, and other open-source libraries, which can be accessed at the repository. In the realm of machine learning, the field of meta-learning holds significant promise for developing methods that can facilitate efficient learning within various tasks. By design, meta-learning techniques often require substantial datasets and computational resources for training and testing, respectively. This paper presents a novel meta-learning framework that focuses on developing methods that can generate simplified, linear visual representations of complex data. By utilizing a range of benchmark classification datasets, the proposed framework is empirically demonstrated to require only minimal training before successfully learning the linear patterns in testing datasets. Furthermore, the developed method is shown to exhibit more efficient learning times compared to conventional baseline approaches. We hypothesize that the efficacy of the proposed framework lies in its ability to reduce the intrinsic complexity of the underlying data. We also provide theoretical analysis of this phenomenon. We anticipate that the insights gained from the study of the proposed linear illustration framework will contribute to the advancement of meta-learning research. When using multilingual machine translation, certain word embeddings that haven't seen before can cause models to malfunction. We investigated whether quantizing existing word embeddings or pruning them is more robust when dealing with unfamiliar words in low-resource languages. We used three different architectures, and simulated different resource levels on four datasets to compare the performance of various models. We found that replacing an increasing number of tokens in the BERT4MT model led to a decline in its effectiveness, with its performance improving substantially when we utilized a smaller version of its embeddings rather than replacing the tokens. When we applied post-hoc word embedding pruning to a low-resource MT model, we observed that it resulted in reduced variability in its performance, in contrast to quantization which enabled the model to handle unfamiliar words in a more consistent manner. Ultimately, our research indicates that quantization is a more efficient technique for developing MT models in low-resource environments. We think this has the potential to broaden access to MT by making models more resilient to words that aren't in the database. There's been substantial progress in generating image descriptions through the use of pre-trained language models and contrastive learning techniques. However, there's been little effort so far to regulate the biased nature of these models, particularly in their tendency to produce incomplete descriptions during description generation. Our paper introduces a novel approach that combines prompt-based language models with a regulated description generation framework. By utilizing a set of regulated descriptions in the fine-tuning process, we are able to constrain the model's output to adhere to specific description generation criteria. Furthermore, we propose an evaluation metric designed to measure the coherence of generated descriptions at sentence boundaries. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach leads to significant improvements in both boundary coherence and completeness of descriptions, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods in Image Description Evaluation (IDE) metrics. You can access the code for our approach here: https://github.com/whwhris/RegDes. Our experiments show that regulator efficacy is unaffected by the choice of optimizers, suggesting the use of prompts as an effective regulator strategy. Moreover, we found that incorporating CRESWAP into the description objective leads to better description quality and IDE scores, and that CRESWAP's contribution is orthogonal to the regulator's performance, allowing them to be used together to boost results. Ultimately, our approach achieves an IDE score of 235.19, setting a new benchmark for Image Description Evaluation metrics.

This work introduces a mathematical representation of heat transfer phenomena, incorporating thermal memory effects, in conjunction with boundary conditions that facilitate or restrict heat exchange between a solid and its surroundings. By limiting the scope to one-dimensional heat transfer within the solid, we derive a system of partial differential equations, along with boundary conditions, that describe both the solid's thermal behavior and heat transfer across its boundary under various dynamic restrictions. We then formulate a dynamic boundary problem consisting of these equations, boundary conditions, and a heat transfer function governed by the Fourier law, in conjunction with boundary conditions that vary depending on the solid's thermal history. By employing the contraction mapping theorem, under specified assumptions, we can establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this problem, thereby gaining insight into the solid's complex thermal behavior and its interaction with its environment. We also illustrate the applicability and effectiveness of this model through two case studies. One such study involves a solid subject to periodic boundary restrictions, while another involves a solid initially exposed to a cold surface before being warmed. In each instance, we prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions, describing the thermal behavior of the solid under these specific scenarios. Ultimately, this work serves as a mathematical representation of heat transfer phenomena, incorporating thermal memory effects, in conjunction with boundary conditions that facilitate or restrict heat exchange between a solid and its surroundings. As such, it has the potential to improve predictions of the solid's thermal behavior and its interaction with its environment. Additionally, this work expands the existing framework of Coleman-Gurtin style equations to include boundary conditions that vary depending on the solid's thermal history. Such an expansion has the potential to facilitate a deeper understanding of the solid's thermal behavior and its interaction with its environment. We also pre-register this work as https://zmath.link/jmiml/2L0Cjy/. In this study, a set of analysts forecasts consumption at individual substation levels, combining their expert judgments with aggregated hourly weather forecasts and crosstalk metrics between nearby substations. The current standard approach to detecting COVID-19 and distinguishing it from non-pneumonic actors relies on radiologic findings such as ground glass opacification patterns, although thickening of the bronchial walls also plays a significant role. Nevertheless, conventional segmentation methods remain unaware of this non-GGO related thickening phenomenon, resulting in incomplete coverage of pandemic image data. To address this issue, we present a new framework called WWGNet, comprising two modules that incorporate word-guided learning. Initially, pandemic lesion localization is performed by identifying GGO lesions, and then a second module refines the detection scope using bronchial wall ground truth. Ultimately, lesion segmentation is adjusted based on localized pandemic image data. In our experiments, WWGNet significantly outperforms its competitors on multiple pandemic datasets. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of varying word-guided weights, examine class-averaged pandemic lesion distribution, and reveal a more comprehensive understanding of pandemic image direction. Precise COVID-19 lesion detection is crucial not only for confirming existing infections but also for ruling out non-pneumonic conditions, and thus our method promotes a more informed clinical diagnosis.
